Properties of semi-classical orthogonal polynomials relative to a generalized Airy weight and their corresponding zeros and recurrence coefficients are examined, where specific parameters apply. The study extends to a symmetrized form of this weight known as the generalized sextic Freud weight, resulting in a parallel investigation of the associated polynomials' properties. The analysis ultimately leads to a exploration of limits in the parameters of the generalized sextic Freud weight, enabling the derivation of explicit limits for the associated polynomials' zeros, recurrence coefficients and other key properties. The findings are further generalized to the context of non-commutative monic linear recurrence operators, whose coefficients' behavior is mapped from the context of classical orthogonal polynomials. The work is illustrated with various examples and visualizations. The research is partially motivated by a 2018 open problem posed by Morton and Wong. The paper offers multiple novel results, one of which is a new form of explicit representation for the zeros of classical orthogonal polynomials, in addition to other innovative findings. The research was partially presented in various conferences, with the first presentation occurring in the 2018 International Linear Algebra Society conference, followed by the 2019 Canadian Mathematical Society summer conference, the 2019 XIX International Conference on Higher Mathematics, the 2020 virtual meeting of the International Linear Algebra Society, the 2020 virtual meeting of the Canadian Mathematical Society, the 2020 Tenacious Conference, the 2021 virtual meeting of the Society for Industrial and Applied Mathematics, and the 2021 International Linear Algebra Society conference. The research was completed at the University of Regina. The paper contains 25 figures. The completion of the paper is attributed to support received from multiple sources. It specifically investigates how these aspects relate to a massless scalar field in globally hyperbolic 2-dimensional spacetimes.  The study identifies subalgebras that contain either chiral or anti-chiral observables, constructing these explicitly and showing they are embedded in the full theory's algebra. Laparoscopic surgery has limitations due to a narrow field of view. Smoke produced by laser ablation in such operations obstructs the surgeon's visibility, highlighting the need for smoke removal to ensure a clear view. To apply smoke removal techniques effectively, it's essential to accurately distinguish between smoke and non-smoke images, which poses a challenge as current methods are incomplete. To overcome this issue, we have developed an image enhancement technique that extracts crucial information from RGB images to differentiate between smoke and non-smoke content. Leveraging a weighted least squares optimization framework, we employ statistical features derived from bivariate histograms and specific image characteristics, which are then used to train a classifier for binary classification of smoke or non-smoke content. We have conducted extensive experiments on the 2020 Image to text challenge dataset and achieved remarkable results, surpassing state-of-the-art references with an accuracy of 95% on smoke classification. To validate our method's clinical value, we have integrated it into the live smoke removal filter (LSRF) previously developed by us, which effectively removes smoke from laparoscopic videos while maintaining surgical key frame accuracy. The improved LSRF, combined with a new post-processing filter, further enhances removal efficiency, ultimately demonstrating the clinical value of our method through surgical video examples. Researchers have developed new methods by combining the concepts of multivariate Gaussian processes with graphical models, allowing for relationships between individual components of the process to be visualized and analyzed. Two specific approaches, functional Gaussian graphical models and graphical GPs, provide different frameworks for understanding these relationships, the former using a mathematical expansion to describe the process, and the latter by combining smaller processes in a specific order. Our study connects these two models by proving that certain functional models with selected variables can be seen as graphical GPs. This finding is used to show the equivalence between truncating certain functional models and stitching lower-order GPs. These theoretical results allow for the creation of new statistical tools that can maintain accuracy in smaller samples, such as estimating relationships between variables in the process and determining the likelihood of functional data that form cycles. Existing quantum processors are prone to errors and have limited lifespan due to
imperfect gate operations. To work effectively with these processors, compilers
must optimize programs to run within the device's coherence time, translating them
into the most efficient version possible to extract maximum value from the hardware.
We have developed new optimization techniques that take into account the unique traits
of quantum gates and systems, and these methods do not assume a specific quantum
circuit architecture. By focusing on noisy intermediate-scale quantum devices, and
specifically the IBM quantum experience, our toolchain demonstrates how to utilize
these new processors to develop practical applications that can run within the device's
coherence time. We have shown that our compiler, capable of optimizing programs with
multiple instructions, outperforms current solutions and provides up to a 240-fold
improvement. Furthermore, our toolchain enables the creation of programs that can
run on any quantum device, as long as it is available through the IBM quantum experience. 
We have successfully developed working applications that can execute on these new
processors, including a customized version of the traveling salesman problem, and
we have shown that our optimized programs yield a significant improvement in execution
time, up to 360 times faster. These results demonstrate the potential for practical
problems to be solved with these new quantum processors. Our optimized programs, along
with detailed explanations, can be found at https://github.com/qiskit-education/quantum-optimize. 
Additionally, a video detailing our research is available at https://youtu.be/VwGpdMrk5RE. 
All other relevant information can be found at https://qiskit.org/textbook/governed.html. 
And finally, my source code is available on https://github.com/alextran1998/QuantumOptimize.

Additionally, the polynomial method's accuracy in estimating a normal distribution's support is assessed, and the results suggest that methodological improvements can yield more precise estimates. Furthermore, the researchers applied this analysis to optimize a standard random sampling problem on a graph, discovering that methodological improvements can yield more efficient samplers, and in some cases, ones equivalent to a greedy sampler, a previously optimal benchmark. Finally, the researchers tested these results against empirical data, retrieving a satisfying picture of a real-world company's network structure. However, standard termination criteria for the solver frequently cause excessive 'oversolving' by insisting on sufficient residual reductions. This paper presents an alternative approach to interior point methods that utilizes an inner termination criterion not dependent on the residual, as well as indicators for premature inner iteration cessation informed by IPM demands. It also modifies this criterion to accommodate Conjugate Gradient and Minimum Residual algorithms, and demonstrates substantial performance enhancements in computational experiments for quadratic optimization problems, which translates to considerable time savings in IPM solution. These improvements have the potential to significantly accelerate quadratic optimization solution times. Additionally, the potential for these indicators to be extended to other solvers and algorithms, as well as to hybrid solvers combining IPM with, for example, Active Set or Primal-Dual Path Following algorithms, is explored. It is suggested that these indicators could result in considerable performance gains for these algorithms as well. Further research is advised to fully realize this potential. It is worth noting that the concepts presented here can be generalized and potentially applied to other optimization methods that employ iterative solvers. It is possible that the greatest performance benefits could result from combining these indicators with other solver cessation methods, such as predicting impending stagnation or utilizing solver restarts. Whether this is the case requires further investigation. Nonetheless, even standalone, the indicators presented have shown potential in interior point methods, and may also prove useful in other contexts, such as in primal-dual interior point methods, where they may contribute to significant time savings. However, it received criticism from modelers for the lack of a direct biological explanation. Our study proposes an improved logistic equation with a clearer biological foundation based on cell population dynamics, incorporating discrete and distributed delay terms. The model's global dynamics are fully analyzed and proven to result in all feasible nontrivial solutions converging to the stable positive equilibrium. The main advantage of this model is its ability to represent a critical transition threshold beyond which complex dynamics emerge, making it applicable to phenomena such as the survival of the Wolbachia fungus in the Aedes mosquito and the onset of periodic and chaotic patterns in cell population dynamics. Unlike the original Hutchinson-Wright equation, our model is capable of representing a Hopf bifurcation and subsequent global stability of spatially homogeneous patterns. Furthermore, we provide specific numerical examples illustrating global stability in various delay scenarios. Notably, we demonstrate through numerical analysis that the original Hutchinson-Wright equation exhibits stable limit cycle behavior, but it does not accurately represent a Hopf bifurcation or global pattern stability, highlighting the importance of delay order in ecological dynamics. The concept of statistical depth has the potential to be used extensively for measuring the hierarchical ranking of both multivariate and functional data within temporal frameworks, however, it remains largely unexplored in the field of temporal point processes. Recent research has developed a point process depth by incorporating a weighted product of two terms - one representing the depth of process magnitude, and the other describing the temporal occurrence of events given that magnitude. The second component is challenging due to the complex nature of event timings and thus far, methods like Gaussian and Dirichlet distributions have been used despite being oversimplified representations. Consequently, current methods fail to account for the actual underlying pattern of events in the process and thus lack clarity and versatility when dealing with intricate patterns. In order to tackle this issue, a new method based on the distribution of events via the Isometric Log-Ratio (ILR) transformation is proposed, focusing on the inter-event intervals. The ILR depth measure for a wide range of temporal point processes is developed and demonstrated through simulations, while also showing its potential application in ranking processes based on their patterns using real data from a study on a major telecom company. The CMS experiment at the CERN LHC detected the production of top quarks for the first time using proton-lead data at an 8.16 TeV nucleon-nucleon center-of-mass energy. Top quark production was identified in events featuring one isolated electron or muon and four or more jets, from a data set totaling 174 inverse nanobarns of luminosity. The measured signal exceeded the five-standard-deviation threshold expected for a background-only hypothesis, and the cross-sectional measurement for top quark pairs was found to be 45 nanobarns with an 8-nanobarn uncertainty, consistent with theoretical predictions from quantum chromodynamics. Automatically creating programs from detailed specifications is a task called program synthesis. A novel framework for generating code based on flow charts is presented, where a deep neural network called GRCNN is trained to accurately interpret these visual specifications by identifying their graphical structures. By being trained end-to-end, GRCNN is capable of simultaneously predicting node and edge details in a flow chart. The framework's results reveal high levels of accuracy both in understanding the visual structure of flow charts and program synthesis tasks, achieving a remarkable 80.5% synthesis success rate when evaluating all generated code. Furthermore, program synthesis was successfully achieved in 57.2% of cases while ensuring the synthesized code accurately reflected the input flow chart's semantic meaning, exceeding the performance of other state-of-the-art approaches. The proposed framework's source code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/visual-programming/program-synthesis. Experimental results were obtained using the VisualSourceCode dataset described in [22]. Program synthesis was conducted with a maximum time limit of 10 seconds, using the GRCNN model configured with the hyperparameters recommended in [10]. The evaluation metric employed was ProgramSimilarityMeasure [19], with program synthesis success being defined as cases where the synthesized code passed both compiler checks and semantic analysis. Compositional data analysis is a technique that deals with complex datasets, which consist of several interdependent components summing to a constant value. Common constant values are 1 and 100%. This data structure is commonly found in disciplines such as biochemistry, geochemistry, and the social sciences. Researchers often examine compositional data in "omics" studies with extremely large dimensions. The method involves calculating logratios – the logarithmic expressions of component proportions. The matrix representation, calculation, and interpretation of these logratios present distinct challenges. To facilitate understanding, we introduce simple, clear explanations for these complex mathematical operations. The accompanying software, R/Ox, enables these calculations quickly and accurately even with large data sets. We also introduce a new visualization technique to display the results in a meaningful way. The proposed approach provides a fundamental framework for analyzing compositional data effectively. Additionally, we demonstrate its application to biological studies, specifically the analysis of microbial community structures in environmental samples. The methodology enables the identification of significant changes in specific microbial groups across different samples. The primary objective of this research is to examine aspects of the validity of the active galactic nucleus unification theory. Our focus lies on AGN host galaxies, specifically how their luminosities are affected by various AGN types and redshift levels. This study leverages a large, comprehensive dataset of galaxy pairs, developed using the GaBoS algorithm, to compare AGN and star-forming galaxy pairs. By analyzing the AGN contribution to the galaxy pair luminosity, specific emphasis is placed on the extent of AGN contamination in the pair catalog, and how it impacts the measurement of AGN luminosity distributions. Pair catalog AGN contamination is found to be more prevalent in type 1.7-2.5 Seyfert nuclei and near the upper luminosity range. Our analysis also reveals that AGN contamination slightly shifts the measured AGN luminosity distribution towards brighter values. To minimize AGN contamination, specific measures are proposed to select more AGN-dominated galaxy pairs. Our analysis further examines the average AGN and starburst luminosities in paired galaxies across various redshift levels. Compared to previous studies, our results reveal lower average AGN luminosities at high redshift (z=1), and slightly brighter average starburst luminosities across all redshift levels. Our analysis supports the notion that most type 1 Seyfert nuclei reside in elliptical galaxies, providing new evidence that the active galactic nucleus unification theory is valid. Our findings also imply that AGN feedback may not significantly influence the mass distribution of supermassive black holes at present. However, our results for type 2 Seyfert nuclei host galaxies are unclear, and require further verification, possibly due to AGN contamination. To ensure the accuracy of unification theory conclusions, our study stresses the importance of accurately classifying AGN types and controlling AGN contamination in host galaxy pair studies. Our research also highlights the need for continued research into the local AGN population, particularly how it compares to the broader galaxy population. To achieve this goal, our study advocates for the continued observation and study of local AGN populations, and encourages the development of more extensive, locally rooted AGN catalogs that are consistent with those at higher redshift levels. Our study is one of the first to examine the characteristics of type 2 AGN hosts in paired galaxy studies, and aims to reduce AGN contamination in paired galaxy datasets to facilitate future research into local AGN population properties. This paper delves into a comprehensive analysis of general rotational surfaces in the 4-dimensional Euclidean space, focusing on flat general rotation surfaces characterized by a 1-type Gauss map. Additionally, it's established that a non-planar, flat general rotation surface with this distinct Gauss map is a Lie group if and only if it's a Clifford torus. Furthermore, for a non-planar surface with a 1-type Gauss map that's not a Clifford torus, its second pair of 1-type vectors being parallel is proven necessary and sufficient for its first pair of 1-type vectors to also be parallel. As a result, it follows that a flat general rotation surface with a 1-type Gauss map is a Lie group if and only if its first pair of 2-type vectors are parallel. This distinct condition is a key distinguishing feature between these surfaces and bi-orbit symmetric surfaces. Finally, it's revealed that a non-planar flat general rotation surface with a 1-type Gauss map is a Lie group if and only if it has a unique axis of rotation. Conversely, a surface with a 1-type Gauss map that's not a Clifford torus can have any number of axes of rotation. This discovery provides valuable insights for future research into 1-type Gauss map surfaces. Examples are also provided to validate the findings. Lastly, the paper concludes by highlighting potential areas for future research into general rotational surfaces with a 1-type Gauss map. These findings are substantiated through the inclusion of additional numerical examples. The paper concludes with a future research outlook, suggesting areas for further investigation. Additionally, it offers a solution to a pending problem proposed by F. P. Muriel and J. D. Pérez in 2019. To this end, it proposes four new problems for future research. The document concludes by addressing a pending issue, proposing four new problems, and incorporating two additional numerical examples. Deep neural network training for semantic segmentation requires considerable time and resources.
Pre-training on large datasets such as ImageNet is a typical initial step before fine-tuning the network for a specific semantic segmentation task.
However, a more recent strategy involves using unsupervised learning from video data to improve segmentation performance, as the motion information captured in videos can aid in uncovering latent structure.
Unfortunately, current unsupervised segmentation approaches are still in their early stages and perform poorly compared to traditional methods.
To address this limitation, we introduce a novel technique that uses depth estimation from unlabeled videos for pre-training deep neural networks on semantic segmentation tasks.
The proposed method leverages the captured depth information to enhance the network's performance by incorporating long-range dependencies and removing redundant features.
We evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed method on the KITTI benchmark and demonstrate significant improvements over baseline models.
Notably, our method achieves state-of-the-art results on unsupervised semantic segmentation tasks, including road and lane marker detection. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/gukai/DepDepth. The authors would like to thank the researchers involved in the SBS-Dataset (https://sbsdataset.org/). The ability to create complex, engaging stories about the characteristics and behaviors of time-series data is extremely important in fields like geology, meteorology, epidemiology, finance, trade analysis, stock market monitoring, and sales forecasting. Currently, domain-specific time-series story creation is limited due to the complexity, diversity, and variability of data formats. While personalized narrative generation can be effective, it often comes at the cost of increased computational requirements and the need for specialized training data. Our proposed system, TCube, addresses these challenges by incorporating a knowledge graph to standardize data representation and enable efficient narrative generation from multiple data sources. TCube's narrative generation capabilities allow for the creation of attributes, events, and characters on a timeline, all while incorporating external knowledge. This results in more detailed and accurate stories compared to traditional graph-based narrative generation methods. Additionally, TCube enables attributes, events, and characters to be linked together, and its narratives are often more plausible and engaging. Our experimental results show that TCube outperforms state-of-the-art models in both attribute detection and narrative evaluation metrics. Furthermore, TCube's narrative generation can operate in three modes: attribute-centric, event-driven, mixed, and controlled by a prompt. This versatility sets TCube apart from other state-of-the-art narrative generation systems. This research introduces a novel application of the Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) neural network to tackle the challenging task of Japanese word segmentation. Building on previous breakthroughs in Chinese word segmentation using LSTM and GRU, this study tackles the more complex task of Japanese word segmentation which involves various character types such as hiragana, katakana, and kanji. These characters lead to significant orthographic variations and increase the difficulty of accurately segmenting Japanese words. To address this complexity, this study proposes an LSTM-based model for Japanese word segmentation, taking into consideration the essential global context. Experimental outcomes confirm that the proposed model attains exceptional accuracy when evaluated across different Japanese corpora. Furthermore, this study highlights the potential of leveraging pre-trained Word2Vec word embeddings in enhancing Japanese word segmentation performance. Experimental findings demonstrate that incorporating pre-trained embeddings improves segmentation accuracy on both small and large corpora, showcasing the efficacy of this technique. However, the gains were found to be more pronounced for small corpora, highlighting the limited impact of Word2Vec on large corpora due to the increasing dominance of the LSTM model. Lastly, the study investigates the utilization of character-based word embeddings to further enhance Japanese word segmentation performance. Experimental findings indicate that incorporating these embeddings leads to minor improvements in segmentation accuracy, averaging 0.14% and 0.21% errors for the Webank Japanese corpus and KUROMO corpus, respectively. Nonetheless, the incorporation of these embeddings was found to significantly reduce the dependency on the global context in the LSTM model, showcasing their potential in improving Japanese word segmentation. Consequently, the study suggests that character-based word embeddings can serve as an effective substitute for the global context in Japanese word segmentation tasks. Additionally, the study includes code and pre-trained models to facilitate replication of these findings. Furthermore, the research is made available on the GitHub platform via the repository https://github.com/yashus/JapaneseWSLSTM. On the Stack Overflow platform, users utilize 11,926,354 external connections to share relevant off-site information, augmenting the existing knowledge base. This collaborative effort involves repeated link sharing activities, where 82.5% of all links are external and 17.5% are self-referencing internal links. To enhance knowledge base connectivity and facilitate better information exchange, this study empowers Stack Overflow developers with insights into effective external link sharing strategies. Using a network science approach, the researchers apply Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to compress the data, where each user represents a node, connected by edges that represent shared links. Centrality metrics such as Degree Centrality, Betweenness Centrity, Closeness Centrity, and PageRank are utilized to analyze user capabilities in contributing new external links. Furthermore, the researchers apply Apriori and HPyrori association rule learning algorithms to uncover patterns in time, linking successful contributors, and reveal that users who share new external links are typically linked to other new contributors. Based on the analysis, recommendations for improving the current design of Stack Overflow are provided, along with proposed enhancements. This study's findings are expected to inspire new ideas for future features that can effectively foster collaborative knowledge base growth through controlled link sharing activities. Although climate change is widely accepted, meaningful conversations about it are scarce,
resulting in slow implementation of the necessary societal changes to mitigate its effects.
To enhance climate communication and promote individual actions, we are developing a system
that leverages climate information tailored to each person's values. To overcome initial adoption hurdles,
our system employs a vast knowledge base that maps climate causes and effects to relevant personal values.
Given the absence of a complete climate knowledge base, we revisit knowledge acquisition techniques and construct
a database through natural language analysis of publicly available sources. To foster further research and applications,
the knowledge base and its code will be made open-source for the scientific community. Evaluation outcomes demonstrate
that our system effectively grounds climate data in individual values, addressing a common challenge in climate communication.
To extend its reach, we propose the development of value-based climate storyboards that can be shared across social media,
enabling the sharing of climate information even among those who struggle with abstract climate concepts. This research has been
accepted for presentation at ACM CHI'20.  All related resources, including the knowledge base, code, and demo, are available at https://github.com/your-github-username/ClimateValues.

Clinical symptoms recorded in unstructured doctor's notes are inaccessible for further use.
This problem can be resolved by using information extraction techniques capable of adapting to different medical settings and professionals. 
In this research, we address the issue of extracting symptoms by using pre-trained and fine-tuned models, trained on diverse patient data, medical institutions, and specialties. 
To reduce dependency on specific data, we develop an adaptive strategy for extracting symptoms by temporarily removing commonly mentioned symptoms from the original data source.
Also, our proposed approach pre-trains the language model using relevant but unmarked text for enhanced data representation. 
Experimental results show that incorporating these strategies significantly enhances symptom extraction accuracy when comparing source and target datasets. 
This research achieves the best F1 score of 0.542 on extracting 194 distinct symptoms from MIMIC-III data, and 0.524 when applying adaptive extraction on varied institutional contexts. 
Finally, our model matches human performance in extracting symptoms with an F1 score of 0.587.

Ultimately, Pando's innovative design and exceptional performance make it an excellent solution for volunteer computing applications. Machine learning models such as random forests and AdaBoost have proven effective across many fields but their high performance comes at the cost of clarity in understanding their predictions. Users are generally unable to discern how individual attributes impact a model's output in a way that is easily interpretable. Fairness and insight into accounting are just two reasons why explainability is crucial in using these models. We introduce a new concept, Disentangled Attribution Curves (DACs), which allow for the breakdown of how attributes contribute to a model's prediction in a clear manner. We also provide an efficient algorithm for calculating DACs and demonstrate its effectiveness on popular machine learning methods, revealing that they can be fully reconstructed from those in statistical learning methods. Moreover, DACs have the unique ability to identify redundant attributes during the training process, giving guidance on feature selection to enhance model interpretability. Our method is now available through the Python package pydac. Users can access it at https://pydac-ai.gitlab.gforge.inria.fr. A tutorial is also provided to guide users in using DACs. Our method is evaluated through comprehensive testing on 126 datasets from open-source data repositories. These tests show that DACs are computationally feasible and accurate. Moreover, they are useful in solving practical problems such as attribute selection, feature alignment, and understanding causal relationships. These applications are documented in the accompanying users guide. We showcase our method's utility in enhancing the fairness of self-driving vehicle trips by allowing for the selective exclusion of certain attributes such as camera images, vehicle markings, and lane boundaries. This demonstrates the potential for DACs to increase the transparency and fairness of decision-making processes in self-driving vehicles. Finally, DACs are presented as a viable tool for uncovering hidden injustices in complex decision-making processes, as evidenced by our investigation into the alleged discriminatory pricing of insurance policies. The findings suggest that the prices charged are indeed influenced by the vehicle's make, model, and year as well as the driver's location and age, thereby potentially exacerbating existing social injustices. In federated learning, multiple parties collaborate on training machine learning models by sharing local parameters, rather than sensitive data. Despite this setup, model parameter exchanges can potentially expose confidential information. To mitigate this issue, a novel framework called HideFL has been developed, which utilizes Trusted Execution Environments to safeguard communications while implementing efficient federated learning. HideFL employs an adaptive quantization technique and a multi-arm bandit algorithm to balance data owner energy savings and potential data compression losses, while also protecting data owner privacy. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of HideFL in preserving data owner privacy and demonstrating the potential of the framework in controlling data compression losses. Furthermore, the implementation of HideFL using Intel Software Guard Extensions and an overview of the challenge are also discussed. This paper introduces a new method called Timeloops for automating system call filtering policies in containerized applications. During operation, Timeloops' analysis adapter continuously monitors system calls and, when a policy violation is detected, triggers a machine learning model to determine the appropriate action. As system calls are typically ordered and occur within specific time frames, Timeloops capitalizes on these temporal components to enhance its modeling capabilities. In contrast to static analysis-based techniques, Timeloops' dynamic approach yields more accurate models and improved scalability for modern applications. Our performance evaluation shows significant scaling advantages and superior performance, showcasing how Timeloops' adaptable architecture facilitates scalable system call filtering for complex microservices workloads. Additionally, Timeloops' analysis adapter discovers nearly 45% more errors in popular applications, demonstrating its enhanced capability in system call modeling. Finally, Timeloops' ability to accommodate diverse machine learning models allows for seamless integration into diverse filtering systems with minimal modification required. By addressing current limitations of existing techniques, Timeloops offers a versatile and efficient system call filtering solution for complex applications. Our open-source implementation, including models and data, can be accessed through the following link: https://github.com/UCBarcelos/Timeloops. Recently, Timeloops was selected as the focus of an NSF workshop exploring recent advances in system call filtering: https://www.workshop-ascf.org/2022/program. In this follow-up to this workshop, a whitepaper detailing Timeloops' potential and future directions has been published: https://www.dropbox.com/s/5y3xv9x5y7mz3zd/Whitepaper-Timeloops.pdf. As the landscape of system call filtering continues to evolve, Timeloops remains a pioneering technique for exploring the temporal aspects of system calls while contributing to the development of modern applications. Future research will center on addressing the challenges of large-scale machine learning model distribution, efficient training, and the potential for reverse engineering attacks on Timeloops' analysis adapter. These areas of investigation will be explored in detail in the following sections. In conclusion, Timeloops sets a foundation for system call filtering using temporal components, and its various components and concepts have the potential to be applied in multiple contexts. By sharing our work, we aim to facilitate innovation in the field of system call filtering and encourage the development of new ideas. Advanced techniques for representing complex data in compact, high-quality forms involve the embedding of product spaces.
We've identified a new challenge - linear classification in complex product space structures composed of different geometric environments, like Euclidean, spherical, and hyperbolic spaces.
To tackle this problem, we first establish a framework for defining linear classification models within curved, high-dimensional spaces that generalize traditional vector-based classification.
Next, we demonstrate that, regardless of the geometry of the space, linear classification models can effectively represent any decision boundary.
We then apply this framework to the specific product space structures of open complexes, surfaces, and graphs, and show that, in these cases, linear classification models can accurately represent any decision boundary, thus providing a complete understanding of their capability to generalize.
To test the effectiveness of our approach, we created a new set of synthetic data and compared it against real-world data, and found that linear classification models can indeed represent any decision boundary on various geometric surfaces, such as those found in image recognition, as evidenced by our results. This paper bridges the gap between compressed sensing and statistical learning, leveraging sparsity and structure to minimize the computational burden of learning tasks. We focus on independent component analysis through a compressive learning lens, demonstrating that certain structures within the data enable efficient recovery of its components using a smaller number of measurements. We develop a compressive ICA approach, incorporating a new penalty term that fosters specified structures, resulting in a tractable optimization problem. We prove the existence of a solution and show that under specified conditions, the method yields an accurate recovery of the data's components. We evaluate its effectiveness using both synthetic and real-world data sets, comparing its performance to established ICA methods. Our results indicate that compressive ICA yields satisfactory outcomes across a range of signal types, offering substantial reductions in measurement and computation requirements. For example, in the case of Gaussian data with specific features, compressive ICA necessitates only 1.6 times the required number of measurements, while achieving a recovery rate of 0.9 within 100 iterations. Furthermore, our method exhibits superior computation efficiency when compared to other ICA methods. We showcase the versatility of our approach by applying it to magnetic resonance imaging, resulting in reduced acquisition time and fewer measurements. Specifically, we obtain 97% effective resolution with only 2.4 times the minimum required measurements, surpassing the performance of other ICA methods on the same data sets. Continuous speech leads to consistent prosody patterns, yet current speech synthesis models often disregard context. These systems fall short when it comes to producing high-quality paragraphs, necessitating a system that integrates contextual elements. MaskedSpeech is a context-aware synthesis system addressing this limitation. By building upon a masking strategy, MaskedSpeech incorporates contextual acoustic features into each sentence, enabling a more detailed understanding of semantic relationships. Additionally, cross-sentence coarse-grained semantic features aid in the development of a natural prosody. Through augmenting masked acoustic features with contextual elements during training, an autoencoder, based on bidirectional LSTM, improves the synthesis of natural prosody. These enhancements result in superior prosody control, captured quantitatively as mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) of 7.65, outperforming previous studies. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of this method on paragraph-level synthesis, producing higher quality speech with enhanced prosody control. Recent research has demonstrated that Deep Neural Networks are susceptible to strategically crafted malicious inputs, prompting the development of countermeasures against query-optimization attacks. Our research diverges from previous studies by exploring the vulnerability of DNN models to Man-in-the-Middle attacks. From an attacker's standpoint, conventional adversarial attacks prove ineffective as they necessitate multiple interactions with the model prior to execution, whereas MitM attacks can launch without this limitation. Moreover, these attacks can only be applied to existing data sets, significantly diminishing the attacker's yield. Conversely, employing generative models can mitigate these drawbacks, enabling the creation of novel adversarial examples. Specifically, our analysis delves into the capability of generative models, particularly Variational Auto-Encoders, in creating adversarial examples. Our proposed approach utilizes a VAE decoder to generate malicious inputs or transform benign outputs into adversarial examples. Our results show that our method enables successful MitM attacks on both MNIST and CIFAR10 datasets at an impressive rate, rivaling the effectiveness of existing query-optimization attacks. Moreover, our approach boasts considerable efficiency, executing 104 times faster than state-of-the-art query-optimization attacks on the CIFAR10 dataset. Our research also sheds light on the correlation between latent code similarity and the adversarial distance to the clean input. Lastly, our findings indicate that our method proves challenging for defensive strategies designed against query-optimization attacks, deeming them ineffective against MitM attacks enabled by generative models. Climate change communication is complicated by the proliferation of conspiracy theories, particularly those found online. This research investigates prevalent conspiracy theories regarding climate change by analyzing a significant Twitter dataset and applies a sophisticated stance detection technique. Our analysis focuses on whether such conspiracy theories are more widely shared by those who do not believe in climate change or those who do. Furthermore, we examine the most popular conspiracy theories, their variations with differing levels of climate change acceptance, and reveal that non-believers predominantly disseminate messages containing conspiracy theory-related keywords. Notably, all conspiracy theories are not equally prevalent. Our findings also highlight their implications for effective climate change communication strategies. This study utilizes a novel, sophisticated stance detection approach and a large Twitter dataset, and our analysis indicates that a new framework is necessary for understanding the complex nature of the conspiracy theory problem. This approach can be adapted for identifying stance on other contentious issues across various text-based platforms. Additionally, our analysis highlights the importance of considering the context of the text and the users who engage with it when developing future stance detection methods. To advance our understanding of matter's various forms, high-energy particle collisions with a wide variety of projectiles must be studied extensively.
Although scientists have utilized beams of numerous particles to make significant breakthroughs, creating and working with beams of antineutrons, specific hyperons and their counterparts has been notoriously challenging.
However, a recent high-tech research setup known as a super $J/\psi$ factory holds the potential to greatly improve access to these elusive particles. As a result, a huge number of $J/\psi$ decays occur annually, creating favorable conditions to accurately analyze these interactions using precision-tagging of co-produced particles. 
This state-of-the-art technology can facilitate groundbreaking studies of diverse targets and open doors for new particle and nuclear physics applications, such as studying antinucleon-nucleon interaction, properties of strange nucleons and nucleon-like particles, (anti)hyperon-nucleon interaction, exotic light hadrons and more, along with advancing our understanding of hypernuclei, calibration of computational simulations in hadronic physics and medicine, and exploring numerous other related topics. 
This article presents a comprehensive overview of the potential research opportunities, served as a introductory report to a series of studies and conference documents on this subject.

Most of a multiple star system's final mass is accumulated during the first few million years of its existence, specifically during the protostellar and protoplanetary phases.  Past research on binary systems has shown that in these systems, the majority of the acquired mass is typically added to the less massive star, resulting in mass equalization.  Yet, young stellar groups are frequently composed of more than two stars that are predicted to exist in a hierarchical setup.  Notwithstanding the significant astrophysical relevance of this issue, little research has been conducted to explore differential mass acquisition in more complex systems.  We carried out a study aimed at investigating differential mass acquisition in a hierarchical setup featuring a binary system and a separate star that interacts with them.  We utilized numerical simulations of the collapse of a massive, rotating cloud to form a binary system, which subsequently interacts with a nearby star that is approximately as massive as the combined binary.  We observed that the star interacts with the binary in two distinct ways, resulting in either incorporating the less massive star into the binary or ejecting it out of the system.  The variability in the star's mass and various properties was found to affect how the binary system grows in mass.  The study revealed that the newly formed binary system has a greater average mass than its original state, while the individual star's mass remains unchanged.  We found that the change in the binary system's mass depends on several factors, including the binary's mass, the individual star's mass, their respective velocities, their orbital characteristics, their initial distances from the third star, their respective eccentricities, their orientations, and the star formation site's velocity.  The study further discovered that the binary system tends to gain more mass when it has lower-mass stars, when its stars have lower velocities, when its orbital eccentricity is lower, when it is closer to the third star, when its velocity relative to the third star is lower, when its orbital plane is aligned with the third star's motion, and when the third star is more massive.  The study revealed that the binary system tends to gain $0.45$ times the available mass, while the individual star tends to gain $0.20$ times the available mass. This manuscript examines flat spacetimes with intrinsic properties, as viable models for understanding the universe on a cosmological scale. We find that such spacetimes naturally incorporate geometric patterns suitable for describing irregular, periodically-distributed matter within the universe. We also establish mathematical proofs for their local representation, as well as the existence and uniqueness of the Einstein's equations under these specific spatial constraints. Notably, our research uncovers an interesting set of precise solutions, illustrating how these spacetimes can be used in cosmology to model a universe transitioning from homogenous, isotropic states in the early stages to more complex distributions with voids and matter peaks over time. We demonstrate that these spacetimes share many properties with the Lambda-CDM model, while possessing distinct features. Finally, we show that these flat spacetimes with intrinsic properties can serve as effective models for understanding the universe on a cosmological scale, opening up new directions for theoretical and observational research in cosmology. Moreover, we highlight the potential for these spacetimes to model irregular, non-homogeneous cosmologies, encompassing a broader range of the universe's spatial distribution than the Lambda-CDM model. Additionally, these spacetimes offer an alternative description of the universe's geometry, different from the previously proposed Minkowski spacetime, often used in cosmological models for describing an isotropic and flat universe. Furthermore, our research suggests that these flat spacetimes with intrinsic properties, can also be used as a new kind of a fluid source to model a universe bouncing against a Big Rip, using the Einstein's equations with cosmological constant, while also generalizing the models previously proposed by the authors in arXiv:1701.07717, arXiv:1709.03022, and arXiv:1804.04016. A significant type-I noise storm, lasting 166 minutes, was observed at 160 MHz with the Ooty Radio Telescope. It exhibited pronounced dynamic spectra featuring multiple burst bursts of varying intensity and duration during its lifespan. Analysis revealed two distinct periods of evolution: an initial phase where the source strength increased over 16 minutes while moving southward, and a latter phase where the source strength decreased over 32 minutes with the source moving northward. Intermediary data suggests a southward movement of approximately 10-20 arcminutes over 16 minutes, corresponding to a velocity of 7600-15200 km/s. Spectra showed two distinct components - a narrow one (240 kHz) and a broad one (20 MHz). Variations in the weaker component correlated with the multiple burst bursts observed in the dynamic spectra. In contrast, the stronger component remained steady throughout, exhibiting a steady broadband spectrum with no changes in shape or intensity over time. It is suggested that the strong component is associated with the quiet outer atmosphere of the active region, while the weaker component, linked to the multi-thermal nature of the flaring loops, undergoes cooling as it contracts. Our observations confirm that the source strength is indeed a manifestation of the electron density in the source. Additionally, it is likely that the initial increase in the source strength was a result of the initiation of the energy release process, while the decline that followed might have been a consequence of the restructuring of the flaring loop structures during the course of the microflare. Our analysis supports the notion that the energy released during the flaring activity is directed towards the outer edges of the active region rather than towards the chromosphere. It is also possible that the energy released during the flaring activity is directed towards the corona in the form of loop flaring, where the chromosphere remains unaffected. It is further suggested that the velocity of the loop movement is not unique to the observed type-I noise storm, but rather is typical of other type-I noise storms and flares of similar characteristics. It is likely that the acceleration of the loop particles occurs earlier than 16 minutes prior to the flaring activity. It is also possible that the loop movement observed in the form of the velocity of the source strength variations, the intensity variations of the weaker component, and the loop flaring, are interconnected and occur simultaneously. It is further suggested that the multi-burst bursts observed in the dynamic spectra, in the intensity variations of the weaker component, are a result of the repeated activation and cooling of the flaring loop structures

A compact magneto-optical trap has been successfully developed, using a planar-integrated design that merges an optical grating chip and a magnetic coil chip. This novel setup minimizes the size and weight of the trap, requiring only a single laser beam to capture a population of approximately 10,000 cold rubidium atoms. The improved MOT architecture has potential applications in devices such as gravimeters, atomic clocks, and quantum memory systems. Further enhancements to the system are also possible. Currently, the trap's radius is limited by the size of the optical grating, and increasing the atom population is hindered by the presence of a central void in the magnetic coil. Nonetheless, the integration of the optical and magnetic components in this design offers substantial advantages in terms of space savings. By reducing the distance between the components, the motional sensitivity to thermal fluctuations is minimized, and the compact design is fully compatible with the integrated architecture. Furthermore, the use of planar technology facilitates the easy replication of the design onto different substrates, and the trap's performance can be optimized through the adjustment of the optical and magnetic parameters. The spherically symmetric merging of a kinetic cloud of particles onto a Schwarzschild black hole is investigated. Unlike earlier research, which established boundary conditions at a distant point, we examine this process with properties of the cloud specified at its surface. We use a series of papers to explore this problem in detail, starting by considering non-advective radiation interactions. We find that when the cloud's surface is close to the black hole, its mass flows onto the black hole at a rate determined by the kinetic energy of its random motions. As the cloud expands, its accretion rate onto the black hole either increases or decreases, eventually settling at a steady-state value determined by a balance between its potential and kinetic energies. Recent advances in wide-scale photometric surveys enable us to detect massive stars in the act of forming, particularly in less crowded regions.  This study examines OB stars in the vicinity of two less crowded regions - He 2-127 and CD-38 8893 - and identifies a number of newly discovered O stars.  Our analysis reveals no clear evidence of massive star clusters or star-forming regions in these areas, instead suggesting that these stars reside in the less crowded regions in their late stages, possibly having formed there or in near-by, undetected clusters. Degraded handwritten documents, which are susceptible to damage from paper ageing and environmental factors, can significantly impair readability. Nevertheless, several restoration techniques are available to enhance their readability and usability. Although these methods are helpful, they do have limitations, particularly when dealing with highly damaged documents. In this research, we introduce an innovative technique that leverages a combination of guidance from digital ink recognition and image processing operations to effectively restore degraded handwritten documents. By integrating input from expert annotators, also known as 'digital ink', along with techniques such as deserialization, filtering, morphological processing, and color manipulation, we can generate high-quality outputs even in challenging cases. To validate our approach, we collaborated with the National Library of France to obtain a set of severely degraded handwritten documents, along with corresponding references, which we used to assess the performance of our proposed method. Our results indicate that the quality of the restored images surpassed that of existing commercial and open-source solutions, as verified by a comprehensive comparison. Furthermore, we successfully applied and adapted our developed methodology to restore over 500 historical documents, totaling over 160,000 pages, in collaboration with the Library of Congress and the German National Library. Our approach has since been formally acknowledged as a best practice in the field of Document Image Analysis. The applied technique has been made publicly accessible on GitHub, under the repository name 'DigitalHandwritingRestoration'. This open-source repository includes a custom-designed implementation of our proposed method, which is compatible with the Windows operating system. Conversely, the majority of the code for the image processing operations is available on the GitHub repository 'DigitalInkGuidedRestoration'. Despite the similarities in names and objectives, these research projects differ significantly and address unique sets of problems. Lastly, our restoration technique has the potential to significantly benefit various historical document collections, which are detailed in the associated issue on our research platform, DigitalResearchFoundation. To date, we have received inquiries from over a hundred document archives and research institutions, expressing interest in applying our developed methodology to restore their collection of degraded handwritten documents. As a direct outcome of our work, we have initiated a positive impact on the field of Document Image Analysis, which is continually evolving and expanding. Moreover, the vision-based approach presented in this research can be applied to various other visual domains, such as video analysis or medical image processing, serving as a foundation for future contributions to the field of computer vision. Ultimately, the main goal of this research was to create a practical and applicable solution to restore degraded handwritten documents, which has since been successfully achieved

The growth of Information Technology has significantly altered how information is shared, making it necessary to convert printed documents into digital formats.  Among several technologies, Optical Character Recognition (OCR), specifically RANSAC-based OCR, has proven to be an effective solution for converting images of ID cards, tickets, signs, and other documents into readable text.  This text can then be used to find the identity of the card holder, extract data for CRM systems, enable self-check-in, provide customer support, and more.  Though RANSAC-based OCR has achieved great success, it is prone to inaccuracies in cases of non-regular text, perspective, ligature-based fonts, and occluded fields.  In an effort to improve this, researchers have proposed a Multi-KNearest Neighbor-based OCR system, which outperforms RANSAC-based OCR by reducing error rates and showcasing superior robustness and accuracy.  This novel approach leverages the inherent capabilities of MKNN, including its ability to handle nonlinear relationships, accommodate outliers, and handle missing values, making it ideally suited for OCR applications.  This proposed system has demonstrated robustness and accuracy in the presence of various distortions, including random noise, elastic transformation, perspective, and field occlusion.  This breakthrough, which offers a higher degree of accuracy than RANSAC-based OCR, presents an efficient solution for a wide range of OCR applications.  Ultimately, this proposed MKNN-based OCR system presents a groundbreaking solution for a wide range of OCR applications. In vehicular communications, the complex and dispersive nature of channels makes reliable channel estimation vital for optimal system performance.
Due to safety-critical applications requiring low-latency data transmission, pilot allocation may not be feasible in some scenarios, leading to suboptimal performance.
This study investigates the impact of limited pilot allocation on channel estimation and performance in vehicular communications using deep learning-based channel estimation.
Results show that even with minimal pilot allocation, the deep learning-based approach still achieves optimal performance compared to conventional methods.
Furthermore, the study proposes a novel training scheme to enhance channel estimation accuracy without additional pilot signals.
The framework is evaluated through extensive simulations and analyzed in terms of model and real-world data sets, showcasing its potential to efficiently estimate channel frequency-selective frequency (CFSSF) models commonly found in vehicular channels. The results indicate that the deep learning-based approach outperforms traditional methods, demonstrating the framework's effectiveness with limited pilot allocation. Moreover, when applied to actual channel recordings from IEEE 802.11p, the method performs well, even without using the recorded signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) information. The study examines the approach's tolerance to electrical connections and mobility-related variations in the channel, demonstrating its ability to effectively estimate the channel structure even with limited pilot allocation. The results show that the deep learning-based approach remains effective with as few as two pilot symbols per subframe, a significant improvement over conventional methods that require at least six pilot symbols. The study highlights the potential of the proposed approach in vehicular communications, paving the way for improved safety and mobility applications. The results show that the deep learning-based approach can achieve successful decoding in 99% of cases, even with extremely low received signal power. Moreover, the method reduces the computational complexity of channel estimation while significantly improving Estimation-to-Multipath-Assistance-Coefficient (EMAC) ratio performance. The proposed approach successfully mitigates the limited pilot allocation issue in vehicular communications, opening up new possibilities for intelligent transportation systems and vehicle communications. The task of automatically assigning colors to images is referred to as colorization. This process has garnered interest in the area of visual representation learning. Colorization presents a challenge because it necessitates generating detailed, high-resolution images along with accurate color information. Traditional generative models can struggle to capture the fine details required for colorization. In particular, single-image generative adversarial networks (GANs) have received attention for their potential in visual representation learning. Despite advancements, they have been limited by their ability to generate images of relatively low resolution. In response to these challenges, we introduce an approach that combines the expertise of multiple image transformers in colorization. This method involves a hierarchical framework that generates a color map and then fills image pixels with accurate color information. We evaluate our approach through comprehensive experiments on the ImageNet dataset and find that it significantly outperforms existing colorization methods. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple image manipulation tasks, including deanimation and deblurring. In addition to its superior performance, our approach features efficient processing, producing high-resolution colorized images at 82 FPS. We've developed a novel numerical scheme to efficiently calculate Artificial Neural Networks (ANN) weights without relying on tedious iterative processes. Based on the Universal Approximation Theorem, our algorithm rapidly achieves low error rates in the regression and classification of intricate datasets, whether the activation functions are linear or nonlinear. Its effectiveness was demonstrated on the regression of a nonlinear equation and the classification of the MNIST dataset, showcasing its rapid convergence and exceptionally low error rates for both tasks. Moreover, the structure of the trained networks closely mimics the parameters of the Universal Approximation Theorem, giving further validity to the method. This breakthrough may now enable more realistic ANN simulations. Additionally, the algorithm has potential applications in tasks where partial differential equations govern data transformations, like image processing. Due to its rapid convergence, it may offer a valuable alternative to traditional numerical methods for solving partial differential equations compared to more resource-intensive techniques like Monte Carlo methods. For instance, this may be evident in processing image data, where the algorithm quickly achieves high classification accuracies on the MNIST dataset even with partial information. Further research is needed to fully exploit the capabilities of this novel numerical scheme. Based on these findings, we propose that the developed method could be used as a partial differential equation solver, opening up new avenues for scientific computation. One of the most effective approaches to building intelligent robotic systems is Learning from Demonstration (LfD), however research is still needed to overcome challenges such as multi-agent learning and prolonged autonomy.  A new architecture for multi-agent LfD is introduced which enables the creation of reliable and efficient robotic systems in complex and large-scale environments by leveraging advancements in Artificial Intelligence (AI) through the implementation of a Federated Learning (FL)-based collaborative learning environment involving both humans and robots. This novel approach capitalizes on human expertise and AI capabilities to address the computational and data demands of large-scale multi-agent robotic learning tasks, thereby enabling extended robotic operations and enhanced human-AI collaboration. Experimental validation of the proposed framework was conducted across multiple design considerations, including learning methods, communication protocols, demonstration strategies, and network settings, which demonstrated its practicality and efficiency in handling complex robotic tasks involving multiple robots and human instructors. Results show that the introduction of AI-powered learning processes and asynchronous FL interactions significantly boost task completion rates and reduce robotic operation durations by as much as 90%, in comparison to more conventional robotic learning techniques that are typically slower and less efficient but still effective in collaborative AI systems. This breakthrough research thus facilitates the development of more practical and efficient multi-agent robotic systems that are enabled by advanced AI technologies and the synergy between human and machine intelligence. This novel multi-agent LfD architecture and evaluation methodology can be applied to a wide range of robotic applications across various domains such as manufacturing, logistics, and healthcare where human collaboration and AI-assisted decision-making are pivotal to successful task execution. A new bias-corrected estimator has been created for the mean absolute deviation of a median regression model, addressing the problem of irregularity that typically hinders conventional bias reduction.  To overcome this limitation, a specific alternative strategy was implemented.  Establishing the bias correction involves verifying the local asymptotic normality property and a specific Bahadur-Kiefer representation.  Developed within the context of a traditional asymptotic framework, this proposal appears to retain effectiveness in high-dimensional settings, as evidenced by simulation results.  This proposal is further supported by a theoretical analysis demonstrating its validity and efficacy.  Due to its computational simplicity, this estimator is well-suited for regular use in statistical practice.  Two alternative variants of this estimator were explored, each exhibiting its own advantages and drawbacks.  Ultimately, this proposal offers a valuable resource for evaluating the performance of median regression models.  Selected applications, such as assessing model fit and identifying outliers, are presented to illustrate the practical utility of this estimator.  Additional research could potentially utilize this estimator as a basis for developing tests and confidence intervals, as well as investigating its potential in the context of semiparametric models. The tasks of relation extraction and knowledge graph link prediction share a
common link in their objectives, allowing them to complement each other in the
process of predicting a subject-object relationship in a sentence. Specifically,
when a model identifies an object and its related subject, this relationship can
be utilized by another model to anticipate a list of potential objects associated
with the subject, indicating the original object relationship in the process.
In our study, we showcase how existing relation extraction models can be
transformed into knowledge graph link prediction models by incorporating the
connection between these two tasks. Furthermore, we propose a novel approach,
called RE-KGLP, which simultaneously addresses both relation extraction and
knowledge graph link prediction to achieve improved results. Our RE-KGLP model
outperforms current state-of-the-art models that focus exclusively on either
task, yielding 0.013 and 0.010 empirical score enhancements on the SemMedPlus
and BioNLP'09 data sets, respectively. Additionally, we observe that the
performance enhancements provided by RE-KGLP are largely due to the reduction
in false positives introduced by the task of relation extraction. As a result,
knowledge graph link prediction achieved 5.376 and 5.546 score improvements
on the SemMedPlus and BioNLP'09 data sets, respectively. From an
application perspective, we analyze and discuss the predictions generated by
RE-KGLP, highlighting its potential in detecting ambiguities in a dataset
resulting from noisy annotations and identifying subject-object relationships that
are not explicitly documented. The code and data used in this study can be

The Analytical Exact Iteration Method has been employed to solve the N-dimensional Radial Schrödinger equation for complex-valued potentials, and further generalized to consider finite values of anisotropy, temperature, and baryonic chemical potential. Energy eigenvalues have been calculated in N-dimensional space for any n, l state. These findings have been used to investigate the characteristics of quarkonium states, such as binding energies and mass spectra, in the N-dimensional space. Notably, anisotropy was found to decrease the dissociation temperature of quarkonia in the N=0 and mu = 300MeV ground state. In the oblate case, anisotropy resulted in a lower dissociation temperature than the isotropic scenario. Furthermore, introducing a baryonic chemical potential led to the conclusion that the leading-order Debye mass exceeds the quasi-particle Debye mass. Lastly, the analysis showed that quarkonia could potentially survive finite temperatures and baryonic chemical potential but might disassociate due to anisotropy. These findings have potential applications in the study of heavy quarkonia in the quark-gluon plasma. A Python script is available upon request for these calculations. Traditional methods of covariate-shift adaptation utilize unlabelled data to generate pre-trained components of a model, typically trained with an incorrect loss function due to a mismatch between the model's targets and observed data distributions. Conversely, supervised learning models are typically designed to minimize a specific task's loss function. This paper explores the benefits of combining adaptation with supervised learning techniques, specifically semi-supervised learning (SSL), which utilizes both labelled and unlabelled data to optimize a task-specific loss function. The research reveals that combining adaptation with SSL not only pre-trains suitable initial models but also mitigates adaptation difficulties by aligning the model's targets with observed data distributions, ultimately yielding superior performance. The study evaluates various SSL algorithms in the context of covariate-shift adaptation across multiple datasets and finds that CrossEntropyNoise, an enhanced version of Cross Domain Entropy, performs significantly better than other algorithms, achieving 100% success across all evaluated datasets. The study's findings inform the development of an Adaptation-Semi-Supervised Learning Framework (ASSLF), which integrates noise-based adaptation with self-supervised learning to tackle covariate shift and imbalanced data. The ASSLF offers customizable training configurations, accommodating a range of loss functions and learning rates, and demonstrates superior performance on imbalanced datasets compared to traditional adaptation and deep learning methods. Furthermore, the study discovers that cross-domain entropy adaptation contributes to improved model generalizability, demonstrating 92% generalizability on average across evaluated datasets. The proposed ASSLF represents a pioneering effort to integrate adaptation and semi-supervised learning, offering novel insights into adaptation. The use of Virtual-Physical Perceptual Manipulations, like redirected walking and haptics, extends VR interaction beyond conventional physical limitations by exploiting the boundaries of human perception, subtly guiding users' movements to enhance interactivity. This research examines the dangers of VPPM exploitation, beginning with a conceptual framework that confirms their existence, then investigating notable cases and interviewing experts in VR, haptics, and spatial sound to better comprehend the implications. Findings suggest that the main concerns revolve around privacy, the potential for deception, the responsibility to inform users, and the need for clear consent processes due to VPPMs' potential to influence users' free will and cause harm. However, the interviews also uncover a lack of understanding and clear guidelines for VPPM modulation, highlighting the necessity for further research in this area to provide concrete guidance. Consequently, the authors propose VPPM modulation best practice principles and encourage continued discussion among experts to ensure the development of informed user experiences. Ultimately, the success of VPPMs depends on transparent communication between creators and users, and the former's responsibility to prioritize user autonomy while respecting users' right to make informed decisions. Additionally, the study recommends that VPPM-related research expand to include diverse perspectives from fields such as law, ethics, and social sciences to mitigate potential harms and ensure that the benefits of VPPMs are equitably distributed among all stakeholders. Social media platforms host an immense volume of content, encompassing a broad array of views on society. Despite the significant percentage of this content being inaccurate or misleading, verifying every post is impractical for automated systems. To address this challenge, we've developed an approach that leverages expert input to validate information, with the ultimate goal of flagging unverified social media posts. To gather trusted data, we collaborated with fact-checking organizations and obtained a set of accurately labeled tweets from their databases. Subsequently, we established a machine learning model to predict the accuracy of social media posts based on their text and associated metadata. Our model's performance demonstrates promising results when evaluated against a comprehensive dataset of inaccurate and misleading information. The unique combination of our dataset, trained model, and partnership with fact-checking organizations positions us to address the persistent issue of unreliable social media content. Our aim is to provide reliable accuracy labels, thereby supporting social media platforms and content creators in addressing the growing problem of inaccurate information. To achieve this, we've developed an open-access platform enabling platforms to request accuracy labels for their content and incorporate them into their systems. Furthermore, this platform can be utilized by content creators for personal verification or organizations to check their social media postings. The system is accessible at https://social-media-accuracy.github.io/. The underlying dataset is accessible at https://github.com/Social-Media-Accuracy/factchecking-social-media. New, high-precision data from the cosmic microwave background lensing measurements and tomographic galaxy surveys in the upcoming years will enable more efficient cross-correlation analysis. We examine the usefulness of the weighted skew-spectrum in this context, as an efficient tool to extract information from angular and radial data, particularly in the analysis of cosmic structures and parameters. We find that skew-spectra contain substantial information, leading to up to 30% lower errors in estimation for certain parameters. Furthermore, we identify a correlation between the weighted skew-spectra and the angular distance, which may provide a new, unbiased standard ruler for dark energy studies. We estimate that using the weighted skew-spectra could lead to a 15% improvement in parameter estimation constraints for the equation of state and a 20% improvement for the dark energy density, making it a promising approach for future lensing and galaxy survey data analysis.
