By integrating Bayesian learning into adversarial training of deep neural networks, we developed a rigorous framework for training certifiable Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs). This approach combines constraint relaxation and modified cross-entropy loss to achieve robustness in BNNs, which can be certified on challenging datasets like MNIST with 90% confidence. This method performs comparably to high-entropy BNNs on standard tasks, while significantly enhancing the certainty of adversarially robust predictions. This improvement is most evident in BNNs trained with tighter adversarial perturbations. This innovation facilitates the training of certifiable BNNs on more demanding datasets, which we demonstrate by providing an initially certifiable ResNet-18 for the CIFAR-10 dataset. This research provides an alternative to existing certifiable BNN training methods, which predominantly employ random noise, offering a significant enhancement in robustness and certainty. Furthermore, we derived an initial analysis of the training process, which reveals the trade-offs of varying adversarial perturbation methods. This research also presents an initial empirical comparison of certifiable BNNs trained with different loss functions, which are standard cross-entropy, mode-based, and point estimate-based losses. These comparisons are performed across multiple datasets, including MNIST, CIFAR-10, and Tiny ImageNet. Additionally, we developed an open-source library called PyBN, which includes the developed methods and is designed to facilitate the training of certifiable BNNs. This library is accessible at https://pybn.github.io/. All of the code used in this research is available on GitHub at https://github.com/PyBN/certified_bnn. Additionally, the certified models can be found on Ardent https://arctic.io/PyBN.

The COVID-19 pandemic, spread globally, has led to the rapid dissemination of online rumors regarding coronavirus prevention, diagnosis, and treatment. To counteract this issue, we investigate the factors contributing to the spread of rumors in online social networks. We develop a data-driven model, grounded in empirical analysis of Sina Weibo data, which highlights the characteristics of Chinese COVID-19 rumors. Our study reveals that these rumors exhibit sharp increases around public health events, are often promoted by verified users, and tend to include temporal references. We also find that users suspecting COVID-19 rumors are more likely to report them, especially if they've been affected financially or have family members working in key sectors. When evaluating the credibility of these rumors, users seem to prioritize whether they originate from government or health organizations rather than expert sources. Consequently, the verified status and ownership of information sources significantly influence the spread of COVID-19 rumors on social media platforms. Our research sheds light on the dynamics of online rumor spreading and provides valuable insights to social media platforms, users, and researchers aiming to mitigate the dissemination of unreliable information during public health crises. To facilitate this endeavor, we suggest implementing content review systems, incorporating third-party fact-checking services, and leveraging machine learning techniques to identify and prevent rumor dissemination. Additionally, social platforms could introduce features enabling users to report both factual and unfactual information, thus fostering a more inclusive, reliable, and trustworthy online environment. Furthermore, we propose the development of a and true information promotion system, where Sina Weibo could prioritize and amplify fact-checked content to establish a more balanced online ecosystem. To further improve this initiative, social platforms could establish collaborative projects with academic research teams, conducting extensive analysis of online content to inform policy decisions, provide critical feedback to social platforms, and produce valuable research outcomes. We maintain that social media platforms hold the potential to establish reliable information infrastructure, grounded in the consistent application of fact-checking processes, content reviews, and user reports, thus fostering greater online trust among users. To illustrate the practical implications of our research, we present a case study where social media platforms could modify their content review systems to address the dissemination of COVID-19 medical rumors. This initiative involves leveraging machine learning techniques, collaborating with academic research teams, and promoting fact-checked content to establish a more trustworthy online environment. This study investigates the impact of hyperspectral pixel dimensionality reduction on classification tasks. Four methods (PCA, KPCA, ICA, and AE) are utilized to compress high-dimensional pixels down to 301 dimensions. The resulting pixels are used for classification, allowing a comprehensive assessment of each method's effectiveness. Moreover, this study seeks to identify the optimal compression ratio for each method by examining their performance across various compression levels. Our findings reveal that PCA and KPCA are suitable for large-scale hyperspectral imaging applications, while ICA achieves the best performance in training and cross-validation scenarios. However, AE exhibits unreliable behavior across different compression ratios. Notably, our research shows that PCA, KPCA, and AE are susceptible to degradation below specific compression rates, underscoring the importance of considering both method and compression ratio when achieving accurate pixel classification. The most efficient classification results are achieved when using KPCA with a compression rate of 50.1%. In contrast, AE requires a higher number of pixels (57.3%) to yield similar accuracy levels. The classification performance of ICA remains stable across a wide range of compression ratios but demands even more pixels (65.6%) for accurate cross-validation. ICA's superiority in cross-validation suggests that this method may be more suitable for independent testing applications. Overall, our investigation highlights the necessity to consider both dimensionality reduction techniques and compression ratios when constructing hyperspectral image datasets for pixel classification. The analysis presented herein can serve as a guide for researchers working with hyperspectral images to select suitable compression methods and achieve optimal performance. The resulting pixel sets can be used for automated land use classification in independent tests. Furthermore, this research can be expanded to compare the effectiveness of different dimensionality reduction techniques in numerous image-based applications. Neural networks are highly effective feature extractors but they pose significant challenges due to their large size. Understanding the parameters within various layers is complicated, resulting in the networks often being referred to as 'black boxes.' In contrast, simpler models are more interpretable but they are also much harder to find. Identifying and utilizing a sparse network that can be trained to replicate the same results is a viable option to improve network interpretability. According to the lottery ticket hypothesis, even large, dense neural networks harbor a smaller sparse sub-network that can be trained independently to achieve the same accuracy in the same amount of time. In this study, we examined whether this phenomenon also occurs in feature extraction tasks. We conducted our investigation on the widely-used ImageNet dataset, specifically on the task of extracting robust features from images. We identified and verified the existence of a trainable sparse sub-network. We discovered that the identified sub-network is not only trainable but also a more accurate solver when tasked with performing feature extraction. We further observed that the remaining redundant parameters in the original network are correlated, forming sparse and highly efficient graphs. These correlations, in turn, influence the capacity and performance of the sub-network. We further observed that there is a positive correlation between the density and performance of the sub-network. We noted that the diversity of redundant parameters also has an impact on the performance of the sub-network. Notably, we discovered a sparse and diverse set of redundant parameters that, when removed, enhance the accuracy of the feature extraction task. A novel prediction method, referred to as ProCS, enables fast and precise calculation of crucial chemical shift indicators in proteins, thereby determining the spatial arrangements of proteins. ProCS is calibrated with the results of high-level quantum mechanical calculations, achieving remarkable agreement in predicting the amide proton chemical shifts of a small protein with a minimal error margin of 0.25 ppm (high correlation coefficient of 0.94). ProCS is now compatible with the PHAISTOS protein simulation program and used to determine the optimal spatial configurations of proteins by optimizing amide proton chemical shift indicators. ProCS successfully identified the correct protein structures of three proteins, and in the case of small proteins, ProCS is capable of predicting the spatial arrangements of proteins directly from the protein sequence. This method provides a valuable tool in determining the spatial arrangements of proteins with high accuracy. ProCS is suitable for the prediction of proteins with a small number of residues (less than 300 residues) and can be used to determine the spatial arrangements of proteins with similar structures. The choice of loss function for a neural network is widely regarded as a key decision with far-reaching implications, given the numerous loss functions developed to date, making it crucial to carefully select one. Despite its significance, research on the topic often omits explicit justification for loss function selection. We contend that this lack of justification reflects an untested assumption prevalent within the deep learning community. In this research, we investigate how loss function impacts performance in a supervised classification context. Our findings reveal that certain, previously underappreciated loss functions, including the KL divergence, can yield superior outcomes compared to established methods, underscoring the need to view loss function choice as a parameter amenable to optimization, rather than a fixed constant. To this end, we devise a systematic approach for designing loss functions, thereby providing empirical evidence of its efficacy. Ultimately, we conclude that loss function selection should be viewed as an adjustable parameter, subject to empirical evaluation and optimization. The research presented herein appears to be the first to formally treat loss function choice as an optimizable parameter. The associated code can be found on the GitHub repository https://github.com/ghtu-ai-lab/LossFunctionOptimization. Describing the behaviors of complex systems comprised of strongly interacting elements requires concise expressions for their internal relationships. Ensuring the stability of these systems is the primary focus. Parquet theory is capable of achieving a level of self-consistency that encompasses all strictly pair-based interactions among elements. This paper further extends parquet theory by incorporating higher-order interactions of up to a third element each, while maintaining its self-consistent nature. The new formulation is derived from a previously established stochastic equation set that defines a broader category of parquet theories. The extra stability criterion that arises from including this higher-order interaction is quantified through a gain in energy for all conceivable types of elements. Furthermore, this new theory is shown to be the most stable when it includes the most significant interaction terms possible. This most stable form of the theory is developed into an entirely new framework, known as the $\beta$-parquet theory. The new theory is shown to be well-suited for handling systems that are coupled to heat, in much the same way that parquet theory is capable of handling coupled elements is a key aspect. The new theory is evaluated in terms of its application to a non-interacting system and compared with a theoretical model that is known to be stable. The findings of this evaluation confirm that $\beta$-parquet theory is accurate in its predictions about the system's properties. The new theory is shown to be an advancement in the field of theoretical physics, in much the same way that parquet theory is capable of handling strongly interacting elements is a key aspect. The new theory is evaluated in terms of its application to a system that is known to be unstable when it interacts with its environment, in a manner that is similar to its relationship with heat. The process of exciton condensation leads to the spontaneous creation of electron-hole pairs and triggers a phase transition in a semimetal that forms an excitonic insulator by creating a gap at the Fermi surface. This theoretical concept has been around for decades, but current approaches only offer approximate solutions; therefore, a reliable prediction tool remains to be developed. To address this challenge, a new method was created that incorporates finite-temperature density functional theory and many-body perturbation theory to study the critical behavior of exciton condensation. Applying this method to the single-layer material TiSe2, researchers found that it exhibits lattice distortion along with the emergence of an excitonic gap through electron-phonon coupling, but without the typical indication of softening phonons. This discovery confirms that exciton condensation is responsible for the charge-density-wave state in TiSe2, indicating the developed approach is versatile and can contribute to the study of exciton condensation in various materials. Furthermore, the methodology can be extended to investigate other types of symmetry-broken states that arise from electron correlations, but a detailed examination of this phenomenon is beyond the scope of this investigation. Finally, the theoretical gap values from these calculations are compared to experimental findings, and it is found that they match relatively well, but a more precise agreement is needed to accurately predict the critical behavior of exciton condensation. In the US, various safety organizations have adopted text-based systems for processing community members' reports and connecting them with local dispatchers. Although these interactions generate a substantial amount of written data, the emotional support provided by dispatchers and community members in these conversations remains understudied. This paper utilizes a large dataset of 831,690 safety organization dispatcher-community member interactions to examine emotional expressions in these conversations. Analyzing the emotions revealed that: (1) both groups exhibit similar emotional support; (2) emotions are more prevalent in messages from dispatchers; (3) positive emotions are more common than negative emotions; (4) emotions are more evident in conversations initiated by community members; (5) emotions in dispatchers' responses are influenced by the emotions in community members' initial messages; (6) emotions in dispatchers' responses vary based on the provided solutions; (7) negative emotions decrease, whereas positive emotions increase when dispatchers respond; (8) emotions are more prominent in conversations about safety concerns; (9) emotions are more prevalent in conversations with a single participant; (10) emotions are more evident when a case is resolved. Additionally, a Bayesian model has determined that emotions are more likely to occur in certain topics of safety concerns. Importantly, a random forest algorithm found a significant correlation between the emotional support provided by dispatchers and users' response rates in these conversations. However, the support provided by community members does not seem to affect response rates as much as it seems to, suggesting a positive effect. This research provides valuable insights into how emotional support functions in these texts and highlights their significance in community safety systems. Moreover, it underscores the importance of employing data-driven methods for identifying topics and emotions in large datasets, which can positively impact response rates in these texts. Lastly, it emphasizes the value of compassion in dispatcher responses, leading to a higher number of responses from community members. Utilizing the Emotion8 model and K-means clustering, this research identifies eight topics of safety concerns: theft, domestic disputes, vehicle incidents, medical emergencies, traffic issues, accidents, noise problems, and other concerns. Developing targeted strategies based on these findings could help boost response rates in these texts. To analyze the impact of external magnetization on doped Bi$_2$Se$_3$ with spin-triplet nematic superconductivity, we computationally investigate magnetic susceptibility in nematic and chiral superconducting states using the Ginzburg-Landau formalism near its critical temperature. A key observation in this analysis is that both superconducting states exhibit identical responses to an external magnetization, which is consistent with previous findings in the context of trigonal superconductors. Furthermore, we find that as superconducting gaps decrease, magnetic susceptibility increases, ultimately adhering to the Lawrence-Doniach model of infinite-range interaction. Nevertheless, subtle discrepancies in susceptibility values persist between nematic and chiral superconducting states, which can be attributed to differences in wavevector relationships in the two scenarios. These results imply that superconducting gap size can be estimated through a non-invasive measurement of magnetization properties in Bi$_2$Se$_3$ systems. Moreover, we also compute the mixing of components of the superconducting order parameter and derive expressions for counterflow and critical fields, which display counterintuitive behavior due to anisotropic wavevectors in the superconducting state. Ultimately, our findings contribute to a deeper understanding of superconducting properties in the doped system of Bi$_2$Se$_3$. Moreover, we also comment on the recent experiments conducted by Li et al., whose observations of magnetic susceptibility in superconducting Bi$_2$Se$_3$ are indeed consistent with our theoretical analysis of nematic superconductivity. Specifically, our results show that at 2K, the ratio of magnetic susceptibility in the nematic and chiral states is approximately 1.15, which may account for experiments that recorded a susceptibility ratio of 1.23 at that temperature. However, it is to be noted that chiral superconducting phase was not stable in those experiments, which is consistent with our theoretical findings. Moreover, our results also indicate that magnetic susceptibility in superconducting Bi$_2$Se$_3$ system follows the Lawrence-Doniary model of infinite-range interaction, which may not be the case as reported by Li et al. Furthermore, our results also show that counterflow and critical field follow different scaling behaviors, which is consistent with the experimental observations of Li et al. Lastly, our results also indicate that superconducting gap size can be estimated through a non-invasive measurement of magnetization properties in superconducting Bi$_2$Se$_3$

Label-efficient active learning algorithms query specific, representative samples to be annotated by a human. Present techniques either utilize a model's uncertainty or rely on diversity measures, such as clustering or reconstruction, to choose unlabeled examples. However, model uncertainty-based methods are susceptible to outliers and diversity-based methods may overlook key information. To address this, we introduce a semi-supervised active learning approach that simultaneously considers both uncertainty and diversity in a minimax framework. Our method incorporates a network that minimizes entropy and an entropy-maximizing classifier, while a discriminator is trained to detect anomalies and guide the network's optimization. We also develop multiple variations of our method to improve performance and efficiency. Experimental evaluations on various image classification datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed techniques. Furthermore, we show that our method is resilient to noise and outlier contamination, outperforming other state-of-the-art active learning techniques in these scenarios. Our method also achieves state-of-the-art performance on datasets such as CIFAR-10 and Tiny-ImageNet when freezing the discriminator and using its features for supervised training. We also successfully apply our technique to the challenging task of detecting anomalies in ImageNet. Our method compares favorably to other active learning techniques and benchmark unsupervised anomaly detection methods on this dataset. Our approach and experiments are presented in the following video: https://youtu.be/7WpWqYXfXgc. Our code is available at https://github.com/salehafzal/semi-supervised-active-learning. Our method is expected to provide label-efficient sampling for various image classification tasks. Our technique may also be adapted for other modalities, such as video, although additional research is required to effectively apply it in this domain. Our method is capable of handling various types of noise and anomalies, but its ability to handle structured data remains limited. Our method is primarily designed to function effectively in medium-scale active learning tasks, but its scalability may be constrained by its memory requirements. Our method is expected to be more efficient than traditional active learning techniques, as well as semi-supervised and unsupervised learning methods that rely on generative models. Our method is suitable for use in human machine interactions, as well as other applications where explainable and transparent AI models are desired. Our method is expected to be more robust to data corruption and shifts than traditional active learning techniques, as well as semi-supervised and unsupervised learning methods that rely on generative models. the average. This discovery aligns with the theory that songs with moderate levels of

change, including an overall decrease in song intensity since the 1960s, an

A novel category of stochastic processes that incorporate reinforcement involves sequences of random groupings denoted as $\{\mathcal{P}_t\}_{t=0}^{\infty}$, where each $\mathcal{P}_t$ splits into a set of blocks $B_1, \ldots, B_{N_t}$ for some $N_t \geq 1$.  A random element $J_t$ is generated, governed by $N_t+1$ equally probable outcomes, where $J_t$ either joins an existing block $B_i$ with probability $N_i^{(t)}$ or initiates a new block $B_{N_{t+1}+1}$ with the remaining probability, where $N_i^{(t)}$ represents the number of elements in block $B_i$ at time $t$.  Two primary variants of this process are investigated: Independent Increment Process and a Markov Process.  For the independent increment process, where $N_i^{(t)}$ is a random variable independent of $\mathcal{P}_t$, a central tendency process $\{\mathcal{C}_t\}_{t=0}^{\infty}$ is defined and shown to converge towards a limit distribution $C$ under certain conditions.  For the Markov process, where $N_i^{(t)}$ is a function of $\mathcal{P}_{t-1}$, a convergence theorem towards a balance probability $q$ is proven.  Finally, conditions for both processes to converge towards a common balance probability $q$ are established.  As an added benefit, our research provides an alternative proof of Snell's [1988] finding on the convergence of a Markov process with a dynamic system. Enhanced data samples from Belle-II, as well as LHCb, ATLAS, and CMS, will be crucial in further investigating the topic. Additionally, insights from $\tau$ decays into its spin will be particularly beneficial. If experimental findings of new physics prevail, it is anticipated that new CP-odd phases will be required by naturalness arguments. A typical strategy for modelling extreme events involves considering occurrences beyond a high threshold as events of a non-homogeneous Poisson process. While this method has the advantage of using threshold-independent extreme value parameters, it comes with the challenge of parameter interdependence, making estimation more complicated. We introduce a novel approach to estimating the parameters of the Poisson process in a Bayesian framework, by transforming them using a tuning parameter'm'. This study develops a technique for selecting the optimal'm' value, which nearly orthogonalises the parameters, by minimising the correlation within their asymptotic posterior distributions. Following this selection, parameters are estimated using a Markov Chain Monte Carlo simulation based on an independent Bayesian approach. Simulations demonstrate that this method surpasses traditional approaches in terms of efficiency. The proposed method is also applied to real-world data, showing improved results when compared to standard techniques. Notably, this new method appears to achieve optimal performance when the'm' value is not exactly zero, indicating that a partial orthogonalisation may be sufficient to enhance model fit and accuracy. The method is implemented in an open-source R library, available at https://github.com/jmbranco/three-parameter-Bayes. A corresponding R package, called R/three.parameter.Bayes, is also provided. In the field of offline reinforcement learning, we focus on adversarial robustness, a critical consideration in RL, by studying a scenario where an adversary can alter a portion of data in offline RL. Our analysis shows that robust learning is not possible when the adversary can change the reward of each tuple independently, leading us to investigate more realistic scenarios with constraints. Specifically, assuming the adversary's changes result in at most $Delta_1$ and $Delta_2$ changes in the reward and next-state respectively, we find that a direct adaptation is impossible but achievable with additional transformations, specifically taking $O(1/(gamma^2))$ samples in the worst case. Additionally, we propose the first algorithms for robust offline RL in the tabular setting, with a focus on model-free approaches, which yield near-optimal performance in at least two different scenarios. Our work also explores the consideration of limiting the adversary's changes, showing that imposing this restriction significantly improves the learnability of robust policies. Our study ultimately sheds light on the relationships between the forms of adversarial attacks and the robust sample complexity, which may also be applicable to other fields. A clear distinction between model confidence and true accuracy is essential 
for trustworthy machine learning models. Anomalous data points can compromise
this trust by exploiting model weaknesses, resulting in inaccurate predictions.
Proposed detection methods typically rely on measures of model uncertainty and
data normality, categorized into generative and discriminative approaches. However, 
evaluations on standard datasets may obscure the models' behavior in real-world 
scenarios with concept drifts, changes in background assumptions, and shifts in 
data characteristics. Therefore, this research introduces out-of-distribution examples
drawn from relevant domain shifts in image recognition, shift-in-domain NLI, and
synthetically created datasets, provides labels for easy assessment, and compares
the effectiveness of current detection methods. Surprisingly, discriminative methods
performed better in certain types of shifts, and we also introduce new diagnostic
metrics to further enhance detection. Furthermore, this research presents a simple
yet effective technique for improving detection performance and demonstrates the
value of accurate in-distribution and out-of-distribution classification for
trusting predictive model decisions. Additionally, this research proposes using
OOD data points for enhancing generalization and providing rich information for
predictive model training. Utilizing OOD data can facilitate predictive model
training that is more robust, reliable, and trustworthy. Overall, this research
offers insights into the evolution of detection methods, provides a standardized
platform for comparison, and provides a reliable framework for empirical studies 
on OOD detection. Also provided are the code and dataset used in this research.

In this study, we investigate the concept of general convolution by considering the set of all possible $n$-dimensional vectors from a finite domain $D$, where the elements of these vectors can take on values from $D$. A specific operation, denoted as $\oplus_f$, is defined as the application of function $f$ to pairs of elements from $D$ applied element-wise. This enables us to define a new convolution, known as the $f$-Convolution, for two given functions $g$ and $h$, each mapping $n$-dimensional vectors from $D$ to integers between $-M$ and $M$. By applying $\oplus_f$ to pairs of $n$-dimensional vectors, $f$-Convolution computes the sum of $g \otimes_f h$ for an arbitrary pair of these vectors. A brute-force approach requires examining all possible pairs and summing the results, resulting in a time complexity of $O(|D|^2)$ operations. However, in cases where $f$ has an efficient implementation, computing $f$-Convolution can be done in $O(1)$ time, making it an efficient tool for combinatorial computation. Several key properties, such as idempotence and distributivity, are explored for $\oplus_f$ and demonstrate its value in designing new efficient algorithms for convolution. A notable application of $f$-Convolution is its relationship to the All Pairs Shortest Paths problem in undirected graphs with non-negative integer weights, where it can be efficiently computed in $O(n^2 \log n)$ time when combined with the Fastest Path algorithm. Furthermore, a new algorithm based on the Fast Fourier Transform can compute $f$-Convolution in $O(n \cdot 2^{c_1 (\log n / \log n)^{1/2}})$ time, where $c_1$ is a constant, providing a new solution to the All Pairs Shortest Paths problem in $O(n^2.5)$ time. Additionally, a new result shows that $f$-Convolution can be computed in $O(n)$ time by applying a new linear programming technique combined with the Fastest Path algorithm. These findings have significant implications for understanding airborne transmission in buses and informing public health policies. Double-sided auctions are commonly used in financial markets to facilitate matching of demand and supply. Our work builds on prior research, which mainly focused on handling a single quantity of trade requests. To expand this knowledge, we developed methods to support multiple quantity trade requests and established fully formalized matching algorithms for double-sided auctions. These algorithms come with rigorous correctness proofs. Additionally, we formulated new theorems for verifying the uniqueness of an exchange's output, allowing for automatic detection of potential program violations. To ensure the accuracy of our work, all the mathematical proofs were conducted using the Coq proof assistant, which did not introduce any additional axioms into the system. From these formal proofs, we were able to derive verified and executable OCaml and Haskell code for double-sided auctions. To validate the practical value of our research, we successfully tested the verified code using real market data from an exchange to automatically identify potential program violations. To further reinforce the reliability of our research, we also provided experimental evidence that verified code can run at comparable speeds to unverified code. Specifically, for a benchmark test using 100,000 random market data, the execution time for both OCaml and Haskell verified code was approximately 0.22 and 0.21 seconds respectively, which compared to an execution time of 0.21 seconds for unverified OCaml code and 0.19 seconds for unverified Haskell code. Our research provides an innovative approach to ensuring the reliability of program code, specifically for double-sided auctions, by applying formal verification techniques that can be readily applied to other program domains with minor modifications. To facilitate future research, all the verified code and associated mathematical proofs are freely accessible on publicly accessible repositories for the benefit of the verified programming community. In particular, the verified research is freely accessible at https://git.coqproofs.github.io VerifiedResearch/DoublSideAuctions/ for OCaml and https://git-coqproofs.github.io/VerifiedResearch/DoubleSideAuctionsHaskell/ for Haskell. Our research further included constructing Regge trajectories in the planes of angular momentum (J) and squared mass (M^2), yielding predictions that align neatly with Regge theory lines. These outcomes may hold significant implications for future experimental research on this topic. Our study employed both lattice QCD and potential model approaches to address the calculations, with the former proving difficult due to technical limitations and the latter facing issues related to the validity of assumed potentials. Ultimately, we suggested that Lattice QCD presents technical challenges that make it impractical for this type of calculation at present. Furthermore, our results demonstrated that the masses of S- and P-wave bottom mesons can be accurately reproduced using non-relativistic models, whereas U-waves cannot be properly accounted for by these models, highlighting their instability and decay properties. Conversely, relativistic Harmonic Oscillator models successfully predicted the masses and other properties of U-wave bottom mesons, thereby exhibiting better alignment with theoretical lines. We also derived the strong interaction components of bottom meson decay widths, with the U-wave versions exhibiting notably higher widths compared to their S- and P-wave counterparts. Ultimately, our research provided novel contributions to our understanding of bottom mesons, particularly in the context of F-wave bottom mesons where corresponding data is scarce; our findings may serve as valuable inputs for future experimental research in this domain. We also presented possible avenues for experimentally verifying some of our research predictions in both theoretical and experimental contexts. We concluded our research by outlining potential future research directions, emphasizing the necessity of preforming systematic calculations using Lattice QCD to boost the confidence in theoretical predictions. Additionally, we highlighted potential research opportunities in the U-wave bottom meson domain. In modern research on data-driven systems, a primary focus lies on overcoming challenges presented by high-dimensional complexities, hidden system dynamics, and the presence of nonlinearity.  The dynamic mode decomposition technique has proven valuable in creating models from large data sets, yet the effectiveness of this method diminishes in cases where strong nonlinearity affects its accuracy. Conversely, sparse identification of nonlinear dynamics is able to learn comprehensive models, differentiating between linear and nonlinear interactions; however, it is limited in its application to lower dimensional systems. Combining these principles, we have developed a new, efficient method for learning data-driven models of complex, nonlinear systems that operate in high-dimensional spaces. Our method, based on a sparse neural network framework, aims to generate detailed models of complex, nonlinear systems that can handle large dimensions and are easily interpretable. We have tested our approach's effectiveness by applying it to multiple benchmark systems across various fields, including mechanical and biological sciences. Our method successfully demonstrates the ability to distinguish between linear and nonlinear interactions in a system, achieving this distinction at a higher dimensionality than previously possible. Furthermore, we have integrated our approach with an evolutionary algorithm to demonstrate its effectiveness in modeling complex, data-driven systems that mimic real-world applications, such as identifying nonlinear laws governing cell migration. Our method's unique combination of sparse differentiable networks, coupled with an evolutionary algorithm, has enabled the discovery of simple, easy-to-interpret models that can accurately predict outcomes in these systems. These results have potential implications for applications in fields such as computational biology. Our approach's efficiency, coupled with its effectiveness at handling high-dimensional complexities, makes it an attractive solution for data-driven modeling in a wide range of scientific disciplines. Our method's ability to distinguish between linear and nonlinear interactions has also opened up new avenues for research, including the analysis of mechanical systems that have historically been considered linear. Furthermore, our discovery of simple, easy-to-interpret models have potential applications in areas such as process control and uncertainty analysis. We have also introduced a new, efficient search strategy called'single-step' evolutionary optimization that facilitates the search process without generating numerous data sets, thereby reducing costs associated with experiments. End-effect models utilize a straightforward statistical representation of policy effects to simulate outcomes and implement goal-oriented learning. When combined with a predictive model, they form a effective inference system, which can be viewed as inverting a target state distribution. In this combined framework, the predictive model identifies critical state features and the end-effect model uses these features to learn goal-oriented behaviors. In multiple complex domains, including a Cart-Pole environment with partial observation, an inverted Double-Q learning using end-effect drives outperformed traditional methods and achieved better results than an associated predictive model. In this context, Double-Q learning with end-effect drives successfully completed tasks even when the target distribution was non-regularized and featured non-unique effects. In contrast, attempts using an associated predictive model failed due to overfitting. In conclusion, end-effect drives prove to be a robust and efficient means of inverting a target distribution and can be used to implement goal-oriented learning in complex and high-dimensional domains. Image-based goal navigation is a difficult problem that has received significant attention in both human and animal cognition research and artificial intelligence development. Previous methods have demonstrated success by leveraging diverse representations, but these have failed to account for the cognitive advantages provided by working memory. In this paper, we introduce the MemoNav system, which incorporates a short-term memory component to facilitate more efficient image-based goal navigation. By organizing previously visited images in memory and retrieving relevant ones, MemoNav is capable of exceling previous performance levels and adapting easily to new environments. Specifically, MemoNav excels at long-distance navigation and is particularly effective in environments with few landmarks or where navigation is complex and difficult. In a comprehensive set of experiments, we demonstrate MemoNav's ability to successfully locate targets in both familiar and new environments and find that it consistently surpasses various state-of-the-art models in image-based goal navigation. In addition to these experiments, we also provide a detailed analysis of MemoNav's performance and provide a straightforward method for implementing a similar memory-based navigation system. This study examines the operator growth phenomenon in Lie-symmetric systems by utilizing concepts from quantum information theory. We specifically analyze Krylov complexity, entanglement properties, and information capacity within SU(1,1) and SU(2) symmetric systems, leveraging two-mode coherent states as a primary tool. These coherent states enable us to explore operator growth patterns and entanglement structures in a systematic manner, ultimately verifying that certain fundamental features emerge across these systems in alignment with the universal operator growth hypothesis. Moreover, our work showcases the value of leveraging Lie symmetry, which streamlines calculations and renders existing approaches like the Lanczos algorithm superfluous, instead allowing us to extract crucial insights through symmetry-based arguments. Building upon this, we extend our analysis to SU(3) and SU(3,1) systems, thereby broadening the applicability of our findings. Ultimately, our work showcases the interconnectedness of quantum information theory and group theory, facilitating the exploration of operator growth and entanglement through the prism of Lie symmetry. This research has significant implications, extending beyond theoretical calculations to the experimental realm, where its consequences are most conducive in systems with lower-dimensional Hilbert spaces. The atomic structure of the Hoyle state, a state consisting of highly clustered $\alpha$ particles at 7.65 MeV in $^{12}\mathrm{C}$, has been a topic of interest for a long time. The question of whether this system consists of three weakly-interacting $\alpha$ particles in the 0s orbital is crucial and can be answered by analyzing the decay paths of the Hoyle state. The paper provides information about the breakup mechanism of the Hoyle state by employing a novel experimental technique. The investigation of the direct 3 $\alpha$ decay of the Hoyle state, rather than through the $^{8}\mathrm{Be}$ ground state, can be performed through an advanced analysis of the energy distribution of the three $\alpha$ particles from the decay. Using beta-delayed charged-particle spectroscopy on $^{12}\mathrm{N}$ via the Texas Active Target Time Projection Chamber, a highly sensitive measurement of the direct 3 $\alpha$ decay ratio can be made without interference from overlapping events. The analysis using a Bayesian approach reveals that the direct decay fraction is less than 0.043% at the 95% confidence level. This value is in line with previous studies and the present findings suggest a minor non-sequential component with a decay fraction of approximately (2$\pm$1)% in the vicinity of the Hoyle state. The outcome of this research implies that the Hoyle state decays mainly through a pathway involving the formation of the $^{8}\mathrm{Be}$ excited state, and the structural aspect of the Hoyle state with respect to its $\alpha$-condensate nature remains unclear. Future research should focus on additional and more sensitive measurements to elucidate the delicate breakup mechanism of the Hoyle state. Additionally, the results of this study, concerning the indirect decay, can provide information on the excitation width of the $\alpha$-condensate over 2 MeV in the 7.65 MeV state. Moreover, the analysis of the structural aspect of the Hoyle state can be compared with theoretical predictions derived from the nuclear Faddeev-Yakubovsky expansion method. The discovery of a minor non-sequential component, decaying quickly from the vicinity of the Hoyle state, can be explored using a novel theoretical framework known as the nuclear Fermi-gas model. This model can be utilized to determine the width of the Hoyle state by calculating its decay width in the vicinity of the $\alpha$-condensate region.

Significant breakthroughs in understanding and computation of fracture instability have been achieved for 2D dynamic fracture. The essence of this advancement is the identification of intrinsic scales at crack tips - nonlinear elastic length and dissipation length scales - which are absent in classical fracture theory. Studies have shown that in brittle materials at high crack speeds, an oscillatory instability emerges, characterized by a wavelength directly proportional to one of these intrinsic scales, which has been observed in line with experiments. We have extended this to 3D, where an oscillatory instability in an otherwise semi-infinite crack propagating at high speed in a 2.5D material is analyzed. An analytical solution reveals that in a specific regime, the wavelength and size of the oscillations scale proportionally with the nonlinear elastic length, showing that the fundamental phenomenon of oscillations in fracture is extendable to three dimensions. However, this is accompanied by a significant difference in wavelength compared to the 2D analysis. We have also discovered that in a given material system, the frequency of these oscillations is an inverse proportion of the crack speed. Consequently, cracks in a fixed material will exhibit different oscillatory behaviors for varying propagation speeds. Moreover, as the energy driving the crack increases, both the amplitude and frequency of the oscillations change, which has been observed in line with experiments. A crucial consequence of our analysis is that in a fully three-dimensional setting, the presence of an oscillatory instability will result in the formation of ring-shaped structures forming at the crack face - a feature that can be observed both in experiments and in computer simulations of the process. Based on our findings, we propose that the presence of oscillations in both 2D and 3D fracture is an intrinsic phenomenon triggered by nonlinearity. Therefore, any numerical method aiming for accuracy in the simulation of high-speed fracture must account for this nonlinearity - either through an explicit inclusion in the equation or by ensuring that the numerical method itself is capable of resolving all the relevant length scales involved. Ultimately, the presence of oscillations in both 2D and 3D fracture provides an experimental verification of the fundamental principle that nonlinearity plays a crucial role in fracture mechanics. Moreover, the size of these oscillations in three dimensions offers a practical means of measuring the material's nonlinear elastic length, which has significant implications for understanding the material's intrinsic properties. In a general setting, we examine the properties of finite state channels equipped with feedback and state information, which becomes available to the encoder in a predictable sequence. This encompasses a broad range of channels, including memoryless channels with independent and identically distributed states (referred to as the Shannon strategy), as well as channels with persistent memory. Building upon previous research, we develop a new proof of the channel capacity with feedback, which provides a straightforward and powerful tool for determining capacity in specific cases. This capacity is defined as the maximum value of the input entropy by the transition probabilities from the initial state to the encoder, given an infinite sequence of the state sequence as input. This new capacity is equivalent to the input output capacity for channels with memory. This new capacity is also bounded by the input output capacity with no feedback, making it a valid measure for determining capacity in those cases where it is equal to the input output capacity with no feedback. This new capacity is also shown to be effective in determining the capacity for a variety of channels, including those with infinite memory, such as the arbitrary information channel, the trapdoor channel, the hidden Gaussian channel, the binary input memoryless output locally uniform ( Milo) channel, the Ising channel, and the vector Gaussian feedback capacity with a zero output entropy. Additionally, we find that the capacity with feedback equals the input output capacity with no feedback for a variety of channels, including those with memory, the arbitrary information channel, the Milo channel, the Ising channel, and the vector Gaussian feedback channel with a zero output entropy, which implies that the state information becomes essentially irrelevant to the encoder when these channels are used with feedback. We also examine the rate distortion function with feedback, finding that it is determined solely by the distortion measure and the initial state distribution, which makes it equal to the input output rate distortion function with no feedback. We also find that the conditional entropy of the state sequence given the encoder's input sequence as input goes to zero when the input sequence has infinite entropy, which implies that the feedback enables us to perfectly recover the state sequence as long as the input sequence has sufficient information. Furthermore, we find that the feedback does not enable us to perfectly recover the state sequence as long as the input sequence has infinite information but less than half of the total information, which implies a trade off between the amount of information given to the encoder and the amount required to perfectly recover the state sequence as long as the information given to the encoder is greater than or equal to half of the total information. A novel class of superconductors featuring antisymmetric spin-orbit coupling and placed within a Zeeman magnetic field may be used to create fault-tolerant quantum computations using topologically non-Abelian effects. In this study, we explore how Rashba spin-orbit coupling and a Zeeman magnetic field affect a two-dimensional superconducting state in graphene. By solving the Bogoliubov-de Gennes equations, we discovered that Rashba spin-orbit coupling can transform a BCS superconducting state into a non-abelian quantum state. Furthermore, we found that the Zeeman magnetic field can weaken but not strengthen this spin-orbit coupling's impact on superconductivity. Graphene's curvature influences spin-orbit coupling's impact on superconductivity, causing it to degrade gradually. Additionally, we established that the critical Zeeman field required to eliminate superconductivity decreases as the curvature of the band declines. Our research provides a pathway for achieving topologically non-Abellan effects in superconductivity through spin-orbit coupling and a Zeeman magnetic field in graphene. \end{document}

This study focuses on understanding and interpreting tables, requiring the ability to recognize their structure and compare cell information effectively. To address this challenge, we introduced a new dataset for SemEval 2020 Task 9: SEM-TAB-FACTS, aiming to verify factual information and identify tabular components. The comprehensive dataset comprised 981 tables from Wikipedia, along with 81 test questions and 21 answer options. The task comprised two sub-tasks: sub-task 1 (ST1) and sub-task 2 (ST2). ST1 required participants to confirm whether a statement about a table was true or false, while ST2 asked them to highlight the specific cells that supported the statement. Twenty-one teams from various academic and industrial institutions submitted a total of 2492 completed forms to the evaluation. In this report, we summarize the results of ST1 and ST2, analyzing the performance of each team and evaluating their accuracy in addressing the posed questions. The data, task annotations, and evaluation metrics used are publicly available for research purposes. These notes document my process of reviewing equations governing distant groundwater movement for a paper. By "distant," I'm referring to horizontal distances exceeding the thickness of the aquifer. They're based on assumptions discussed later on. These equations aren't an original contribution but rather a reference guide for those working with simplified numerical models of groundwater flow.

I began with Darcy's Law, revisiting the conservation equation for vertical averaging in groundwater flow. Following that, I explored approaches for numerically solving the flow equation. Then, I considered scenarios where the hydraulic conductivity varies solely with depth, simplifying the steady-state flow equation in these cases. Lastly, there's a brief examination of the transient flow scenario. These reviews are an attempt to condense and organize information, not expand upon it. That was my goal. These notes are an overview, not a comprehensive analysis, of the topics covered. 

I found the process incredibly beneficial and hope these notes will be seen as a useful resource for others as well.

Deploying machine learning in practical scenarios can often present challenges,
mainly stemming from uninterpretable models, questionable reliance on imperfect
data, or offering a sole prediction outcome without considering various
probability outcomes.
  This study proposes the concept of Indecision Trees as a modification of the
existing Decision Trees model. These revised models are designed to learn under
conditions of uncertainty, draw conclusions in uncertain situations, produce
reliable probability distributions over potential labels, and be dissected into
clear, logical arguments that can be applied to other reasoning systems. While the
inductive coefficient used to learn the trees is inspired by logic, the resulting
models are more akin to probabilistic classifiers. Consequently, we apply the
revised Brier score to evaluate their performance. Furthermore, we investigate the
indiscretion degree of trees as a measure of uncertainty, analogous to the concept
of entropy in Decision Trees. However, our primary objective is to demonstrate the
theoretical and practical advantages of Indecision Trees over existing Decision Trees.
  The capabilities of Indecision Trees are demonstrated through comprehensive
experiments in various environments: generating pre-determined data, classifying synthetic
datasets, and applying the models to real-world data. Ultimately, we outline the
potential for Indecision Trees to be utilized in genuine practical scenarios. All code
is accessible at https://github.com/sohozade/tree_grammar.

Current educational tools used in testing can either provide coverage insights comparable to professional tools or highlight instructor-defined test cases that a student has overlooked. While this feedback has its merits, it may not be as effective as it could be, and students may become reliant on the assistance. Moreover, this feedback style does not teach students the value of independently verifying that their changes have the intended effect. To address these limitations, we have developed two new approaches: limited negative feedback and key positive feedback. Small groups of students created tests to verify specific functionality, and our approaches were informed by data from these activities. We have introduced a new tool that provides two inquiry-based learning experiences: limited negative feedback, which signals areas that need additional testing, and key positive feedback, which highlights critical test cases that confirm a feature's correct behavior. Empirical data from a study involving 35 students supported the effectiveness of these new feedback mechanisms, as students performed better with these approaches compared to the original coverage insight feedback. Furthermore, we found that students developed effective strategies for test case selection, even in the initial stages, by utilizing the limited negative feedback, and incorporating the key positive feedback facilitated students' understanding of how their changes impacted the code, as evidenced by selected test cases aligning more closely with the code modifications they made. When prompted to verify whether their changes had the desired effect, students performed significantly better with the key positive feedback, and, surprisingly, students performed better in this activity when utilizing the limited negative feedback, despite not being instructed on its importance. We have opened-sourced our new feedback mechanisms and the inquiry-based learning tool to provide educational testing software that incorporates these innovative approaches. This resource complements existing tools, offering two new feedback mechanisms that provide a more student-centered and instructive testing experience. To contribute to this project, visit the repository at https://github.com/impruve-testing/test-feedback. Additionally, a video illustrating the new feedback mechanisms can be found at https://www.youtube.com/watch?vl=Vj4AlI7wNms. Both the tool and these mechanisms have been successfully utilized in instructional settings, as confirmed by our study. To ensure the tool's effectiveness, we have thoroughly tested it, and the results of these experiments are presented in Section 6 of this article. To facilitate the tool's adoption, we provide a tutorial on how to integrate it into existing testing curricula in Section 7. Consequently, we anticipate that the improved feedback mechanisms and the companion inquiry-based learning tool will serve as valuable resources for teaching testing concepts to students. Ultimately

In domains requiring reliability or transparency, explainable AI is increasingly becoming essential for accurately selecting machine learning models.  For simple, unitary models, perturbation sensitivity and causal explanations are often interconnected, yet this interdependence is obscured for complex models involving neural networks.  This paper bridges this gap by demonstrating the equivalence of perturbation sensitivity and causal explanations within the context of abstract Riemannian manifolds, providing a geometric framework that encompasses both unitary and neural network models.  This theoretical foundation enables the development of visual tools for understanding the relationship between perturbation sensitivity and causal explanations, which we demonstrate through numerical examples.  Furthermore, this theory and associated tools enable the prediction of causal features based on the geometric structure of perturbation sensitivity, which we verify through numerical experiments.  The accompanying code can be found at https://github.com/stuartpaulpool/xai.git.  Potential future research could involve generalizing this geometric framework to account for data noise and imbalances.  An alternate approach could be developed by building upon the concepts presented in [10], which proposes the use of Riemannian geometry to model the geometry of perturbation sensitivity.  Additionally, the geometric representation of perturbation sensitivity could be utilized to develop a causal feature selection method based on an annealed variation of perturbation sensitivity.  Finally, the geometric framework itself could be replaced by a more practical and generalizable topological structure, such as a Vietoris-Rips graph, to model the geometry of perturbation sensitivity.  For instance, the geometric structure could be exchanged for a topological structure in the context of [10], which proposes the use of a Vietoris-Rips graph to model the geometry of perturbation sensitivity.  Furthermore, the proposed geometric framework could serve as a reference structure to study the origin of causal features within perturbation sensitivity by examining how they transition between different topological representations.  Ultimately, the choice of either a geometric or topological structure depends on the specific requirements of reliability or transparency in the machine learning model.  For instance, the geometric structure offers a more precise and accurate representation of perturbation sensitivity, whereas the topological structure can be applied more readily to neural networks.  Therefore, the proposed framework suggests using a combination of both structures by dividing the perturbation sensitivity structure into distinct regions according to different topological representations, such as employing a Vietoris-Rips graph to separate the main body from the periphery of the perturbation sensitivity structure, or using a topological structure to model various causal features within perturbation sensitivity

Over-smoothing significantly constrains the complexity of Graph Convolutional Networks, making it crucial to understand the underlying mechanisms. Past research examined the effects of over-smoothing, but its application to Directed Networks remains unexplored. This study aims to shed light on the mechanisms driving over-smoothing in Directed Networks by analyzing the processes of message passing and message aggregation. We identify that while message passing simplifies feature representations, message aggregation contributes to the recovery of original features. Additionally, our research reveals that different aggregation functions and directional weight distributions can mitigate or exacerbate over-smoothing. This study also validates the efficacy of counter-measures for over-smoothing, thereby providing valuable insights for the development of more effective Graph Convolutional Networks in Directed Network settings. Our findings are substantiated through experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets. This study is the first to provide an in-depth analysis of over-smoothing in Directed Networks. This study discovered that when growing the Heusler compound GdPtSb on clean graphene substrates, it results in a unique 30 degree rotated superstructure, not explicable through other mechanisms. This rotation domain percentage significantly increases at lower growth temperatures. It's suggested that slower surface diffusion at lower temperatures favors the remote epitaxial process over faster surface diffusion at higher temperatures. Moreover, this study found that incorporating imperfections boosts the epitaxial process's rate and efficiency, providing a potential solution to its current growth temperature limitations. Ultimately, this research provides the first experimental evidence of a remote epitaxial process and explores its control through variations in temperature and defect presence. This understanding can enable the optimization of this innovative growth technique, possibly replacing traditional epitaxy methods with a simpler, more economical approach. We analyze how to identify common random patterns in large sets of time series data, even when individual observations are rare or unusual. A new method allows us to make this analysis without knowing whether certain assumptions hold or even what values some important statistics have. By using information about the matrix of average relationships among these time series, we create an estimator of how many common random patterns there are, even in cases with extreme data fluctuations. As sample size increases, the rates of divergence for the matrix's key properties are significantly faster than others. To improve estimation accuracy, we use this information to construct test statistics and implement a procedure for iteratively evaluating whether each key property corresponds to one of these common patterns. A related method can identify the patterns themselves and the study shows this is a consistent approach. To extend the analysis, the study considers more complex scenarios where observations change over time and shows the methods remain effective even with significant fluctuations. The research is demonstrated through analyses of real data sets, including US inflation rates and the shares of variables related to the US inflation, the Solow growth model, and the analysis of random patterns in the behavior of prices and quantities across different economies. The new methods are implemented in software available at the website of the National Bureau of Economic Research. The research extends earlier findings that related stochastic processes in time series data can provide valuable insights into these data. A key paper in this research area was by Del Negro and Schorfhage (2019) and it considered the case where the rates of divergence for the matrix's key properties are significantly slower than others. The new research considers the opposite scenario. Early detection of heart conditions is crucial, and point-of-care methods like cardiac auscultation are vital for this purpose.  However, accurate abnormality detection from cardiac auscultation sounds is hampered by background noise and the variability of recording devices.  To address this challenge, this study investigates the development of effective methods to eliminate noise and improve the quality of cardiac auscultation recordings.  Using a large dataset of 106,667 labeled recordings, obtained from the National Institutes of Health, the research explores methods to remove noise and improve the accuracy of abnormality detection in cardiac auscultation.  The findings of this study indicate that the application of a cepstral feature-based filter offers the best combination of efficiency and effectiveness in quality improvement and abnormality detection, respectively.  Specifically, this filter demonstrated a 35% improvement in signal-to-noise ratio, accompanied by a 13.8% increase in the accuracy of abnormality detection and a lower false positive rate of 12.6%.  The implementation of this filter before feature extraction further enhanced the accuracy of cardiac auscultation-based abnormality detection, reaching 99.3% for mitral heart diseases and 99.7% for tricuspid heart diseases, thereby surpassing existing state-of-the-art techniques.  The noise-reducing filter developed in this study is accessible at https://github.com/Alexandria-NIH/Cardiac-Auscultation-Noise-Filter. Academic researchers who read research papers usually seek specific information to answer particular questions, but current systems fail to provide accurate answers to forward-looking questions, particularly those requiring understanding of a paper's implicit, inferred, or future-oriented information. While machine learning models have excelled at extracting explicit data, they struggle to grasp implicit knowledge, especially when applied to natural language inputs. Furthermore, current multi-task models often overlook the distinct requirements of question types and overlook the differences in implicit knowledge extraction across various domains. To tackle these challenges, we propose an interesting approach that encourages a model to pay more attention to implicit data extraction by introducing a novel loss function minimising implicit extraction performance between different tasks. Our method utilizes domain-specific question sets that demand implicit data extraction to penalize models failing to grasp these requirements. We name this loss function "Implicit Gap", demonstrate its positive impact on extracting implicit knowledge, and showcase its efficacy on multiple datasets including Natural Questions, OpenBook Questionaries and AI2Zeshan. Our work also highlights that "Implicit Gap" can serve as an effective tool to boost a model's ability to extract implicit data and underscore the significance of evaluating forward-looking question identification in natural language inference. Quantum interference, evident in low-dimensional systems, is one of the most notable manifestations of quantum physics. Historically, quantum interference has been observed in charge transport; however, recent findings indicate that it also significantly affects thermal properties. This insight enables the precise manipulation of heat within microscopic devices through phase-coherence. This study showcases how exploiting phase-coherent edge states in quantum Hall systems allows for the realization of exceptional thermoelectric properties and efficient heat rectification. A multi-quantum point contact tunneling setup with multiple interference paths was used to demonstrate that these systems break electron-hole symmetry. As a result, an electron charge current can be directed from hot to cold or vice versa, and an accompanying heat current is also predicted. These findings can be attributed to a simple and logical physical interpretation. Furthermore, heat rectification can be achieved by combining two quantum Hall systems with distinct filling factors, and this effect can be enhanced through the interference properties of the tunnel junction. These discoveries open doors for new quantum devices that harness phase-coherent effects to manipulate heat and electric charge with high efficiency. Additionally, the use of multi-path interference provides a valuable educational tool for introducing fundamental concepts of quantum physics to students. The research was conducted by the experimental group of Professor N. P. Armitage at the University of Maryland. The theoretical framework developed in this study can be applied to analyze various quantum interference phenomena in other systems. Based on the calculated transmission probabilities, the complete transport characteristics, including electrical conductivity, Peltier and Seebeck coefficients, and thermal conductivity, can be computed. The presence of edge states in quantum Hall systems allows these to be modeled as effective one-dimensional systems that can be analyzed using the Landauer-Battara formula. This theoretical framework can be extended to systems with complex topological properties by adding a 2D thermal conductivity term. Therefore, the proposed model is suitable for quantifying quantum interference effects in other systems that possess 2D topological properties. In oscillatory media, regions that oscillate faster than their surroundings can give rise to traveling waves, propelled by pacemakers, such as spiral waves or other high-frequency hubs. These waves often originate from the pacemaker itself or nearby oscillatory sources. This research delves into how a single high-frequency region, the pacemaker, contributes to synchronization across an oscillatory system of varying frequencies. Using a mathematical model, we demonstrate that the pacemaker facilitates propagation of synchronized activity throughout the system, generating complex spatiotemporal patterns. Interestingly, the resulting wave trains are capable of emerging from the pacemaker itself or resulting from external stimuli applied at any location within the system. Furthermore, we find that the propagated wave patterns are determined by the pacemaker's oscillatory behavior and the distribution of oscillatory system frequencies. Consequently, the resulting synchronized wave patterns can differ significantly from those resulting from exclusive mechanisms, such as wave resonance or internal high-frequency sources within the system. Ultimately, the identified synchronized wave patterns, coupled with a mathematical model, can provide valuable insights into the dynamic processes underlying heart rhythm disturbances, including those triggered by pacemaker regions or spiral waves. This study's findings can also be applied to other oscillatory systems across biology, chemistry, and physics. A fundamental concept, entropy, has significant implications in both classical and quantum physics and computer science, leading to diverse applications across theoretical and practical domains. The focus is on determining approximations within a factor $\gamma > 1$ of the Shannon entropy in probability distributions and the von Neumann entropy in mixed quantum states. The key contributions are two algorithms: a quantum one for approximating Shannon entropy that requires $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(n^{\frac{1+\eta}{2\gamma^2}})$ queries, and another for approximating von Neumann entropy that necessitates $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(n^{\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1+\eta}{2\gamma^2}})$ queries. These results hold provided the entropy is bounded away from zero by a quantity linked to $\eta > 0$, and a no-go result indicates that any algorithm for approximating both Shannon and von Neumann entropies converges to a constant factor $\gamma > 1$ in the entropy value. The conclusions have broad implications, encompassing the realm of quantum computing, probabilistic computing, and the statistical behavior of quantum systems. Clinical text note encoding using ICD codes is crucial for various healthcare purposes such as clinical navigation, financial reimbursement, and epidemiological analysis. However, manually coding ICDs is labor-intensive because clinical text notes often lack essential information, requiring inference to determine the correct codes. Previous studies have applied machine learning and neural network models, but they frequently struggle with unknown words and limited training data. To address these issues, this paper introduces Double Meaning Encoding (DME), a data augmentation method that enables the analysis of medical texts without the constraints of word frequency and data availability. DME empowers tokenizers to learn from labeled texts, teaching them to ignore irrelevant information and focus on important tokens. Furthermore, DME enables special tokens to be learned, including the "mean" token, which enables aggregating the meaning of tokens groups like family of words. Our experiments demonstrate that DME enhances the performance of transformer-based models on medical text encoding tasks. Notably, DME achieves superior results when compared to other data augmentation strategies. Additionally, DME achieves state-of-the-art results when applied to the 2021 ADAHMM challenge benchmark dataset. Our source code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/qmray/transformer-means. Our pre-trained DME models can be accessed through huggingface's COCO platform at https://huggingface.co/qmray/ADAHMM-DME. Our paper is published on arXiv at https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.11016. We hope that DME will benefit the natural language processing community in the field of ICD coding. Differentiable rendering has gained significant attention in image-based inverse problems due to its potential to enhance traditional optimization-based methods and offer self-supervision for learning-based approaches, particularly those lacking ground truth-annotated training data. However, existing differentiable renderers are either limited by their failure to account for light source visibility, resulting in inaccurately rendered shadows, or hindered by slow computation, preventing them from efficiently training deep models. To address these issues, we introduce an accurate yet high-performance approach that leverages spherical harmonics approximations to model scene illumination and visibility, using spherical approximations for occluding surfaces to significantly speed up shadow computation compared to ray tracing-based methods. By formulating this approach as a differentiable system, we can efficiently utilize analysis-based algorithms for optimizing image-based inverse problems, while also enabling fast feedback and optimization during training. This allows us to leverage it as self-supervision signal for learning-based inverse problem solutions, leading to improved results in three image-based inverse problems: image-based rendering, depth estimation, and image-based facial animation. We believe our approach has the potential to be widely adopted, as it only requires access to a single RGB image and has lower overhead compared to other self-supervision methods. The well-documented Aldous-Broder and Wilson algorithms create random spanning trees through random walks, and this research examines their synergy with the aim of reducing tree construction time. Demonstrating statistical equivalence on particular stopping points by analyzing 'branches' produced by these algorithms on complete graphs reveals that these algorithms can generate uniform spanning trees in tandem. This realization enables a faster, hybrid method that leverages the strengths of both algorithms to expedite uniform spanning tree generation in complete graphs. Furthermore, a novel, two-stage approach is developed to adapt and explore this hybrid strategy across a range of graph structures, showcasing its efficacy and efficiency in examples, such as transitive graphs, where it outperforms Wilson's algorithm by generating a uniform spanning tree 25% faster. This two-stage process involves first employing Wilson's algorithm to generate a uniform spanning tree and then utilizing its structure to rapidly generate additional trees. By integrating the hybrid algorithm, a faster, full-threshold version is also presented that directly generates these additional trees without relying on Wilson's algorithm. One major obstacle when utilizing Linked Data lies in developing intuitive and user-friendly interfaces accessible to individuals who aren't technologically inclined. To address this, Ontodia enables diagrammatic data visualization, illustrated in this study with the Wikidata dataset. We've introduced enhancements to a natural language interface that facilitates the exploration of Linked Data entities, incorporating word senses and positional information. Furthermore, Ontodia's capabilities allow entities to be visually connected, creating a sense of context. User studies demonstrated that natural language queries paired with visual representations facilitated quicker understanding and execution of approximately 70% of all possible Ontodia queries. The combination of natural language and visual elements proved especially beneficial for complex, context-dependent queries. These findings underscore the significance of simultaneously utilizing visual and linguistic cues when exploring and navigating complex data graphs. The development of this interface and accompanying proof-of-concept demonstration will be made accessible to the public through our research repository. We've discovered that in the nonlinear Schr\"{o}dinger equation with variable refractive index and a defocusing cubic nonlinearity, dark solitons exhibit stability in both space and time. Previous studies demonstrated stability in space, but not in time. Our findings show that including variable refractive index significantly enhances the system's stability. We derived new equations for stability by using the stability of solitons in the "weak coupling" regime, and then analyzed these equations through a combination of methods, ultimately verifying their asymptotic validity. Additionally, we obtained conditions for modulational instability's occurrence and studied its behavior in different regions of stability. We developed an analytical stability criterion and used it to evaluate the stability of dark solitons. Furthermore, we verified our findings numerically and validated the stability of solitons through direct simulations. Our study also reveals that soliton stability is linked to the sign of variable refractive index's derivative. Finally, we investigated how soliton's frequency affects its stability, as well as how it influences the system's modulational instability. Our study provides a comprehensive understanding of dark solitons' stability in this system and offers insights into their behavior. Our findings are universally applicable and can be extended to systems with other types of nonlinearity. Moreover, we believe that our stability- enhancing approach can be applied to other physical systems.
