We've developed an innovative approach for designing stellarators with considerable versatility. Flexibility in this context refers to the range of rotational transform values the stellarator's magnetic axis can accommodate without compromising its quasisymmetry properties. Our method enhances design flexibility by taking into account coil placement when setting rotational transform targets, leveraging superposition principles to achieve this. This idea allows us to explore a broad spectrum of designs with designated rotational transform values and find optimal solutions within this range. By doing so, we've discovered that stellarator designs with extreme flexibility can maintain exceptional quasisymmetry properties, even when their twisted modular B fields have multiple non-trivial magnetic singularities. Furthermore, we've observed that optimal designs with high flexibility tend to have a more circular magnetic axis, which suggests that prioritizing axis symmetry can facilitate quasisymmetry. We've confirmed that our design strategy is robust by validating the results with established optimization methods, which reinforces the findings and demonstrating the power of our approach. Additionally, we've analyzed various design characteristics, such as volume, surface area, and module number, which indicate that further exploration is necessary to fully understand the range of design possibilities with high flexibility. This research was financially supported by the United States Department of Energy.

Achieving uniform temperature distribution within catalytic fixed bed reactors is critical for both optimal production yield and operational stability.  However, obtaining precise temperature readings simultaneously with good spatial and temporal resolution in these systems remains difficult. Our research utilizes the capabilities of real-time MRI imaging in conjunction with the temperature-dependent shift in water's proton resonance frequency to obtain in situ temperature measurements in a cylindrical fixed bed reactor. The temperature distribution was monitored as the reactor was heated from room temperature to 60°C using hot air, with three-dimensional temperature maps produced as a result. The findings show significant temperature variations along both axial and radial dimensions, corroborated by optical temperature probe measurements, with an average error of 1.5°C. The presented MRI thermometry technique presents new avenues for the in-depth study of mass and heat transfer in gas-solid fixed beds, potentially being adapted for further applications in reactive gas-solid systems in the future. Our study's data analysis methodology is presented as a potential model to estimate temperature distributions in similar fixed bed reactors, with numerical simulations included to demonstrate the model's effectiveness. The model was validated using computational fluid dynamics (CFD) with results showing reasonable agreement with the observed temperature profiles and MRI-derived temperature maps. However, slight discrepancies were observed due to the simplified nature of the model's proposed algorithm. Nevertheless, the proposed model can serve as a basis for further development to incorporate additional parameters such as heat generated by chemical reactions and heat transfer between the reactor walls and the surrounding environment as well as solvent properties in liquid-phase systems. Therefore, this study presents a novel and useful tool to estimate temperature distributions in fixed bed reactors, with potential applications in optimizing industrial catalytic processes. The presented methodology can be extended to monitor temperature distributions in various types of reactive systems where temperature and solvent properties play significant roles. Moreover, our study's innovative MRI-based thermometry technique can be applied to other types of reactive systems where temperature measurements are crucial for understanding mass and energy transfer processes. The technique offers a unique non-invasive means of obtaining in situ temperature data in both gas-solid and gas-liquid reactive systems, with the potential to be used in conjunction with NMR spectroscopy to obtain kinetic information about complex chemical reactions. The technique has far-reaching applications in both laboratory-scale studies of chemical reactions and industrial process optimization. Within a cellular environment, proteins and nucleic acids autonomously separate, resulting in the spontaneous formation of membraneless droplets. This process underlies the development of numerous sub-cellular compartments. In a model system designed to understand condensate self-assembly, interactions between a large number of different molecular species were studied and programmed to test for variability and rules. The number of different droplets formed from mixtures increased significantly as the number of different molecular species in the mixtures increased. Additionally, the color and composition of these droplets followed specific patterns if the molecular interactions within the system were similar to those found in the system's initial components. However, the presence of a third type of molecule whose addition was uniformly small throughout the system caused the color of the droplets to uniformly change even if the original components had varied colors. This result suggests that the system's thermodynamic properties confer order to the composition of the droplets. Furthermore, the droplets formed in these mixtures displayed unique physical properties and distinct sizes that followed specific patterns if the molecular interactions within the system were similar to those found in the system's initial components. The presence of a third type of molecule whose addition was uniformly small throughout the system caused the droplets to shrink or expand consistently across all droplets. These results indicate that the system's kinetic processes confer order to the droplets' size. This study shows that both thermodynamic properties and kinetic processes can determine the physical properties of membraneless compartments. This research also reveals that the principles governing the self-assembly of these condensates are universal and can be applied to biological systems by exemplifying the emergence of a new droplet color and the uniform alteration of a nucleic acid's structure within a cell model. Lastly, the possibility of naturally occurring droplets that contradict the rules governing the system's condensates was investigated and the findings suggest that such droplets could exist. This research further expands our understanding of the self-assembly processes that occur within living cells and the membraneless compartments that make up those cells. Additionally, the results of this study and its findings can be applied to both biological systems and nanomaterials by exemplifying the creation of nucleic acid-based droplets that display unique optical properties and consistent sizes within a nucleic acid system. Using the Helioseismic and Magnetic Imager on the Solar Dynamics Observatory, we studied how a major leading sunspot rotated in NOAA AR 11429 during two powerful solar flares. A notable sunspot rotated in an unconventional direction, influenced significantly by the solar eruptions. Moving disturbances within other sunspots, caused by the solar flares, traveled rapidly and altered the magnetic properties associated with the sunspots in question, providing valuable insights into the source and characteristics of the solar flares in question. Observations indicate that the solar flares may be associated with a significant change in the shape and properties of the magnetic loop structures rooted in the sunspots. If the magnetic loop predictions hold true, they imply that the solar flares in question were triggered by the relaxation of stressed magnetic properties. Moreover, the rotation of the notable sunspot, occurring in an unconventional direction, can be attributed to the reconnection of complex magnetic loop structures. Lastly, the increased activity and interaction of nearby sunspots indicate that they likely originated from a single initial stressed magnetic structure. This stressed magnetic structure initially stressed the right-hand polar magnetic properties, and subsequently the left-hand polar magnetic properties, thereby influencing the characteristics and properties of the resulting solar flares. Given this new information, we categorize the solar flares in question as mere byproducts of the ongoing evolution of the stressed magnetic structure. Moreover, we speculate that the M6.8 and X9.3 solar flares in question could have released an energy of approximately 2-3$\times$10$^{32}$ erg. Finally, the modified stress-free arcade model, used to predict the increased pressure, predicts that the energy deposited during the solar flares in question is roughly half of the observed energy deposited during the solar flares in question. This discrepancy may be attributed to the inefficiencies of the energy deposition during the solar flares in question. In conclusion, the energy deposited during the solar flares in question may be attributed to the ongoing evolution of the stressed magnetic structure. It demonstrates that the Madsen-Weiss theorem, which can be viewed as a variation of the standard Mumford Conjecture, is derivable from a specific application of the b-principle to oriented colored broken submersions, combined with the findings from Harer's stability theorem and Miller and Morita's work. This research involves comparing the efficiency of Balancing Domain Decomposition by Constraints (BDDC) and Algebraic Multigrid (AMG) methods for solving complex cardiac mechanics problems on various types of finite element grids. By modeling the mechanical properties of heart muscle tissue using three-dimensional finite elasticity equations, researchers have transformed the problem into a nonlinear algebraic system. A combination of Newton-Krylov and BDDC/AMG solvers is employed to solve this large system. A comprehensive examination is undertaken to fairly assess the impact of multiple variables on the performance of the BDDC algorithm. Specifically, the research examines: how different solvers affect the local and coarse problem solutions; how different BDDC degree of freedom options influence performance; and the impact of finite element grid resolution. Furthermore, the project is carried out using high-performance computing resources, involving up to 1024 processors in a Linux cluster, and culminates in a detailed analysis of performance for an actual electromechanical heart simulation. The results indicate that both BDDC and AMG methods are capable and versatile tools for solving complex cardiac mechanics problems. However, the research also reveals that the BDDC algorithm exhibits greater flexibility and tends to perform better, particularly on finer grid resolutions, by yielding up to 4 times faster convergence rates compared to AMG. The study suggests that these differences in performance are attributed to the differences in heart mesh characteristics, coupled with the BDDC algebraic tolerance settings. Consequently, the BDDC algorithm is deemed suitable for large-scale cardiac computation on parallel computers. The research concludes by highlighting the potential for further improvements through variations in mesh topology, alternative finite element formulations, and the incorporation of BDDC options. Additionally, the project suggests the utility of software tools, such as the BDDC implementation in NEK4RC, for accurately modeling cardiac mechanics on complex grids. The research demonstrates the efficacy of an integrated software approach for solving actual problems, ultimately enabling detailed mechanical heart tissue simulations. The resulting models are valuable for understanding heart muscle tissue deformation and for developing computational pharmaceutical models to study and predict cardiac function. The research demonstrates the EPPA model's ability to accurately predict left ventricular pressure across different heart muscle fiber orientations, thereby validating its use in heart modeling applications. The research further emphasizes the necessity of a precise and efficient computational algorithm, such as the BDDC/AMG solver, for solving complex cardiac computations on high-performance computing infrastructure and parallel computers. The ever-growing influence of user-generated content is significantly altering the digital landscape, driven in part by the proliferation of systems supporting content creation, sharing, and management. Among these systems are tag-based platforms that enable users to collaborate in annotating shared items such as images and URLs, leading to user-generated metadata and collaborative annotation. Understanding the workings of such systems is essential to determining their potential for developing collective knowledge and establishing system efficacy. This study provides a comprehensive overview of existing research on tag systems by examining their applications, identifying current challenges, and outlining future directions for further investigation. Additionally, we have compiled a list of 105 relevant studies on tag systems and their applications, as well as developed a research network to represent the research dynamics within this domain. Our analysis reveals that the primary methods for evaluating tag system performance involve comparative studies, focusing on the perspectives of system administrators and users. Notably, there is a lack of research on tag system efficacy from a theoretical perspective. Future work should encompass empirical methods to validate existing theories and establish new ones. Furthermore, theoretical research should seek to determine the system's impact on user behavior and decision-making processes. Ultimately, a practical benefit of this research could be the development of tag system design guidelines to enhance information retrieval and the overall quality of collaborative annotation efforts. This study confirms the complexity of tag system research, requiring comprehensive knowledge and a deep understanding of the subject matter. Based on our findings, we conclude that the tag system domain is characterized by diverse systems, used for both personal and organizational purposes, and often evaluated using comparative studies, while overlooking theoretical assessment. Notably, existing research on tag systems lacks a unified theoretical framework, and there is a disparity between the number of studies on user-generated content and those related to tag systems, as documented in the collected literature. This dissertation contributes to the development of a theoretical framework for tag systems by identifying the research gaps, analyzing the literature, and outlining the proposed theoretical structure, which is grounded in the NCSTI model. We also demonstrate the feasibility of this framework through an empirical study, examining the relationship between tag system design and user-generated content quality. Furthermore, this dissertation highlights the research potential of visual tag system analysis, and contributes to the field of tag system research by investigating the impact of tag system design on user-generated content quality through a visual method. Moreover, this research is among the first to apply visual encoding and semantic differential scaling to investigate the subjective quality of groups, and effectively demonstrates the efficacy of this combined approach. Additionally, this dissertation showcases the utility of tag-based data

Recently, proposed bianisotropic acoustic metagratings offer promising possibilities for passive acoustic wave manipulation, notably in flat acoustic lenses and ultra-high frequency ultrasound imaging. This concept, however, has not yet been implemented at the MHz frequencies common in ultrasound imaging due to difficulties in fabricating complex microstructures. Advances in two-photon polymerization now enable precise manufacture of sub-wavelength structures in this range. However, shrinking structures in size introduces another challenge, where increased thermoviscous effects lead to considerable energy losses, which need to be factored into the design. This work introduces three novel microacoustic metagrating designs capable of refracting normally incident waves by approximately 35 degrees at 2 MHz, utilizing shape optimization techniques and the linearized Navier-Stokes equations. Using two-photon polymerization, we fabricated and experimentally validated microscopic acoustic metamaterials, successfully redirecting incident waves and verifying that a 0.29 wavelength-thick microacoustic metagrating can efficiently allocate 90% of transmitted energy into the -1st diffraction order. This research successfully bridges the gap between theoretical design and experimental fabrication, showcasing the practical application of acoustic metamaterials in ultrasound imaging at the MHz frequency level. Furthermore, we observed that a thick microacoustic metagrating exhibits enhanced diffraction efficiency when compared to its two-dimensional equivalent. This discovery implies the possibility of designing higher-order microacoustic metamaterials with increased refracting power for the design of compact acoustic flat lenses and ultrasound imaging systems. Lastly, we found that a microacoustic metagrating's diffraction efficiency and frequency stability are directly correlated, as they are both influenced by the same geometric parameters. This relationship enables the development of acoustic micrograting designs that not only achieve an optimal diffraction efficiency but also remain stable across a range of frequencies. This characteristic is particularly beneficial for the development of frequency-agile ultrasound devices and the creation of design protocols that balance diffraction efficiency and frequency stability. This research lays the groundwork for the next generation of acoustic metamaterials created using two-photon polymerization that can effectively manipulate acoustic waves across various frequencies and directions. This innovation has the potential to revolutionize the field of acoustic imaging by enabling the construction of compact, invisible, and agile ultrasound devices. This technology can further be scaled up for application in the visible and infrared regions of the electromagnetic spectrum, opening up a spectrum of innovative possibilities. Moreover, the liquid-state two-photon polymerization technique can be utilized for the creation of acoustic metamaterials that can function effectively underwater

This paper primarily focuses on the long-term behavior of strong solutions to the two-dimensional compressible FENE dumbbell model. Utilizing the Fourier splitting technique, we demonstrate that the $L^2$ decay rate is given by $\ln^{-l}(e+t)$, with any positive integer $l$. Through the application of the time-weighted energy method, we manage to enhance this rate to $(1+t)^{-\frac{1}{4}}$. Under the condition that the frequencies are sufficiently low, by incorporating the principles of the Littlewood-Paley theory, we find that the solutions have properties belonging to certain Besov spaces of negative order and establish the most favorable $L^2$ decay rate. Finally, by leveraging the principles of the Fourier multipliers, we derive the most favorable decay rate of the $L^2$ norm for the solutions, which is given by $(1+t)^{-\frac{1}{2}}$. In conclusion, we formulate the fundamental assumptions under which the solutions will be shown to have properties belonging to certain Gevrey classes and to tend asymptotically toward the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations for small data. Some relevant results are provided in the appendix. In particular, we prove that the incompressible limit of the FENE dumbbell model, originally proposed by Beier & Zhang in 2014, is in fact a Gevrey asymptotic limit. Furthermore, we establish the sufficient conditions for the frequencies to be bounded, which resolves an issue with the original work by Beier & Zhang. Finally, by employing a similar time-weighted energy method, we show that the solutions of the three-dimensional compressible FENE dumbbell model tend asymptotically toward the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations for small data and that the frequencies are bounded. In the process, we also derive the most favorable $L^2$ decay rate of the solutions, which is given by $(1+t)^{-\frac{1}{2}}$. In conclusion, the sufficient conditions for the frequencies to be bounded, which was derived in our study, improves the existing result by simplifying the conditions found in the work of Liu, Zhang, and Pan. The final result is verified through the application of the three-dimensional compressible FENE dumbbell model to a rotating incompressible fluid. Implementing integrated access and backhaul (IAB) through wireless connections offers network flexibility and the potential for efficient, wireless-driven management of resource sharing. However, managing IAB networks as a single entity via wireless backhaul connections also introduces new challenges in optimizing the network. This work explores the possibilities of wireless-driven management in IAB networks, focusing on the specific case of using radio access technology by 5G New Radio (NR) and its impact on a network-wide optimization problem. This problem involves selecting the most suitable access and backhaul connections to maximize network flexibility, while also ensuring that local optimization goals, defined by a set of network nodes, are met. This work proposes a distributed optimization algorithm that efficiently solves this complex problem, even in large networks with many nodes. The results show that this approach can effectively utilize IAB networks, maximizing network flexibility and meeting individual node requirements. Furthermore, the performance gains achieved through wireless-driven management are substantial, with a significant improvement in network flexibility compared to a best-effort IAB configuration. The findings validate the effectiveness of using wireless-driven management in IAB networks, showcasing performance enhancements through the sharing of resources. The analysis conducted also highlights the potential issues with congestion in IAB networks, emphasizing the need for efficient management schemes that improve flexibility and resource utilization. In this study, we conduct an extensive examination of five leading global optimization algorithms as a hyperparameter configuration problem to understand the overall impact of their settings on performance. By utilizing three methods of sensitivity analysis and evaluating various adjustable parameters, such as covariance matrix adaptation, differential evolution, and non-dominated sorting, we analyze their behavior when influenced by different sampling methods and metrics, providing insights into which settings significantly affect performance and interact with each other. The ranking of influential parameters is also determined and their individual effects are quantitatively measured, allowing for more targeted tuning in the future. This research ultimately aims to guide and inform the development of future evolutionary algorithms by highlighting the importance of carefully selecting and varying parameters to best match the characteristics of the problems being solved. The findings of this research are further validated through the optimization of real-world problems. The analysis is performed using the light weight and easily interpretable PyGPC framework, whose scalability and adaptability for analyzing complex algorithms and their interactions is also demonstrated by optimizing a suite of 12 benchmark problems. The source code to reproduce the results is available at https://github.com/afooshee/pygpc. The presentation is divided into following sections: (1) background and methodology, (2) results, (3) conclusion and future work, (4) additional investigations, (5) application to benchmark problems, (6) discussion and conclusion, (7) conclusion. The presentation is accompanied by a journal publication, which is ongoing. Despite notable breakthroughs in reinforcement learning, numerous significant hurdles remain when applying it to dynamic and ever-changing problems common in critical domains, including robotics and complex gameplay. Reinforcement learning models generally struggle to generalize effectively when confronted with new tasks beyond their training data. In response to this challenge, the field is seeing an increased focus on continual learning methods, and to support this research, new tools are being developed, including carefully crafted evaluation frameworks and benchmark environments. To address this need, we present Lifelong Learning Explorer (L2Explorer), a cutting-edge, 3D game platform that facilitates rigorous testing and comparison of lifelong learning strategies. L2Explorer features an expansive, continuously updating world filled with diverse locations, objects, and challenges, which are presented in an order designed to mimic real-world exploration and learning. By presenting learners with an evolving sequence of tasks, ranging from simple to complex, in a variety of settings, and with occasional revisits to previously encountered locations, L2Explorer poses significant difficulties to both model-based and model-free reinforcement learning algorithms. These challenges are quantified through the development of quantitative evaluation metrics, and we demonstrate the efficacy of several state-of-the-art lifelong learning methods on this demanding platform, with a particular emphasis on their generalizability to new tasks and environments. Further details, including source code, video recordings, and benchmark data are available on our project website. L2Explorer offers a valuable resource for advancing the field of lifelong learning by facilitating systematic assessments of different strategies and their performance in complex, dynamic environments. With its unique blend of 3D exploration and learning challenges, this benchmark platform may also find applications in fields like computer science, where reduced and simplified versions of these problems can inform research and inform scientific discoveries in fields like biology. The results obtained extend beyond the application of the formulated equation, offering a more general framework for a broader class of nonlocal problems. The analysis is primarily conducted within the context of a $n$-dimensional space, although some of the findings are specifically demonstrated for a 2D space. In this paper, we aim to enhance this by limiting the number of possible summands available from subset B, and explore the implications of this restriction on the required similarity between subsets A and B. It's hypothesized that if subsets A and B, of size k, meet the criterion that for every four-element subset of B, the sumset A plus that subset doesn't exceed 2k, it should exhibit a significant arithmetic structure in subsets A and B. To support this hypothesis, we prove a partial result: if subsets A and B, of size k, meet the criterion that for every three-element subset of B, the sumset A plus that subset doesn't exceed 2k, it should contain, for every ε > 0, a subset A', of size (1 + ε)k, exhibiting a significant arithmetic structure. Additionally, we note a separate finding that if a subset A, of size 2k, contains no four-element arithmetic progressions, it must use at least (1/2 + 1/ku)k elements, where u is the size of a specified set A', of which we assume A and A' share a significant overlap. In pursuit of the desired result, we develop a new combinatorial tool: a general structure theorem for high-complexity, Freiman 3k-4 pairs. This tool necessitates the creation of a new type of high-complexity, Freiman 3k-4 lemma, known as the double pivot, which we introduce and prove. X-ray images contain subtle characteristics with predictive information about patients who are likely to experience severe COVID-19 symptoms.  If accurate, this hypothesis offers significant practical value in directing limited medical resources towards high-risk patients by leveraging an economical imaging method. However, confirming this hypothesis proves challenging due to the need for large, well-annotated data sets containing post-imaging severity outcome information. To address this issue, a novel approach is proposed for extracting crucial features from datasets with ICU admission labels, using interpretable models that integrate neural networks trained to identify lung abnormalities. By limiting model complexity, overfitting is minimized while maintaining the ability to interpret results. Interestingly, only a small set of features accounts for most of the variability between patients with severe symptoms. When applied to an independent test dataset, the proposed approach achieved high area under the receiver operating characteristic curve values of 0.90 and 0.85 for NICU and ICU admission outcomes, respectively. Notably, feature specificity and interpretability were prioritized, with lung region attribution being the key feature selector. Building on this work, a simple and efficient model for predicting SARS-CoV-2 ICU admission risk using X-ray images is proposed. By leveraging pre-trained convolutional features and integrating them with a linear classifier, the model's complexity is significantly reduced, outperforming more advanced approaches in multiple dataset-based comparisons. Moreover, only a small set of images is required for model training, making it more suitable for settings with limited data and resources. When applied to the COVID-19 X-ray dataset, the proposed approach achieved high area under the receiver operating characteristic curve values of 0.95 for NICU admission outcomes. Overall, the proposed approach offers a balanced combination of high accuracy, feature interpretability, and computational efficiency. Additionally, specific features and regions of interest in lung images were identified, supporting the original hypothesis that these images contain essential information for predicting severe COVID-19 symptoms. When applied to non-COVID-19 acute respiratory disease diagnosis, the proposed approach was found to have limited utility due to its reliance on pandemic-specific data, highlighting the need for further research to make it adaptable to other diseases. Based on these findings, the code and pre-trained models are available on GitHub for public use. This study re-examines the Adler-Bobenko-Suris H2 equation. The equation has a direct linear relationship with the Cauchy matrix scheme variables S0,0 and S1,0. A detailed analysis is provided of the H2 equation's bi-holomorphic transformation in a 3D complex space, specifically how the transformation affects the Cauchy matrix variables and a related 6-point matrix. Also discussed is the transformation's impact on a particular subset of these variables, restricted to the real axis, and a subset's behavior in the vicinity of singular points. Furthermore, the research derives a specific transformation for the H2 equation's Lax pair parameters S, T, U and shows these parameters follow a specific, well-documented pattern after the application of this transformation. Next, the study looks at within the subset of real Cauchy matrix variables S0,0 and S1,0, which reveals these variables' dependence on a discrete time parameter t results in a differential equation being defined on the real number line. The resulting equation has a continuum limit that resembles the equation of a geometric Toda chain. Finally, the research discusses how the subset of these variables' low-order dynamical behavior can be used to generate, via direct multiplication, higher-order geometric Toda chains, thereby establishing a method to computationally solve these higher-order chains. The study concludes with proposed applications of this theoretical model, primarily in the fields of nonlinear systems and quantum field theory. This paper delves into the source of high false positive rates in Visual Relationship Detection (VRD). During the initial training stages, it's observed that the models incorrectly associate objects with relationships, leading to random prediction class distributions. A novel self-correction approach, Self-Correcting VRD, is introduced to mitigate this issue. By maintaining a memory bank of object proposals, the model periodically samples and corrects these proposals in an unsupervised manner, ensuring better performance and faster convergence. Furthermore, an improved training method enhances the model's ability to learn from diverse proposals, by iteratively refining proposal associations in a supervised manner, resulting in better relationship detection performance. Extensive experiments on the VRD task demonstrate the effectiveness of these proposed techniques. Notably, SC-VRD makes significant improvements over the state-of-the-art, achieving a 9.5% improvement on Pascal VOC 2012 and outperforming the best existing methods on COCO-RT by 11.6% and 14.3% respectively. A new measure, referred to as quantum correlation cost (QCC), quantifies the amount of quantum correlation employed in weak measurement procedures utilizing the trace norm. It's demonstrated that the QCC is directly linked to the trace-norm-based quantum discord (TQD) by a factor dependent on weak measurement strength. However, this measure only captures a portion of a quantum system's quantum nature in contrast to the TQD. Furthermore, our results reveal that remaining quantum features can be extracted not only via further von Neumann measurements but also through a series of infinitesimally weak measurements. We exemplify these outcomes using a Bell-diagonal state. We introduce a new method to calculate the optimal weak measurement angle for maximum QCC and provide a mathematical condition to identify optimal probe states for this measurement procedure. We also demonstrate that an optimal weak measurement angle exists for infinitely close to the optimal value, conditional on the system's unitary equivalence to a Bell-diagonal state. We propose that this condition can extend to general quantum states. We examine the relationship between QCC and the quantum query complexity (QQC) – a measure of quantum correlation cost versus functionality. Our findings indicate the QQC can be efficiently estimated using a single infusion of weak measurements proportional to the inverse of the infidelity, which may be beneficial for error reduction in measurements. We discuss potential applications of this new measure, QCC, in the context of resource theory, specifically its utility in the rapid infusion of quantum correlation from the environment to the system via weak measurements. This process can be employed for the promotion of quantum computation efficiency through the infusion of quantum correlation from the environment, which may also be beneficial for the development of quantum algorithms. Our work also offers a new perspective on the role of weak measurements in the promotion of quantum features. We demonstrate that the difference between various quantum disciplines – such as quantum information theory and quantum physics – lies in the utilization of weak measurements being either non-invasive or invasive. This distinction can be attributed to the differing goals of infrastructure support versus the revelation of hidden properties. We discuss how the new measure, QCC, contributes to the advancement of quantum correlation research and potentially opens the door for the rapid infusion of quantum correlation, which may offer new possibilities for the control and management of quantum systems. Our work sheds light on the role of weak measurements in the promotion of quantum features, which may have significant implications for the use of quantum technology. Our results indicate that the new measure, QCC, is computationally efficient and can be utilized in the rapid infusion

Artificial intelligence's interest in socially-aware agents is increasing. To address this, systems capable of deciphering diverse social interactions are needed. Understanding social relationships in a visual setting requires not only object recognition but also an in-depth comprehension of relationships and attributes within that scene. An explicit knowledge graph can be employed to model human connections and attributes, allowing for advanced reasoning. A novel neural network is introduced that can generate a structured graph from an image, representing the scene's social relationships and attributes. This network is trained end-to-end by predicting a target graph based on an image. An advanced loss function is developed to accurately represent complex, structured data. Experimental results show the network's ability to accurately represent diverse social relationships and attributes, outperforming state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, the framework provides meaningful attribute annotations, demonstrating the network's ability to make attribute-specific generalizations. An evaluation of the network's ability to reason and respond to social questions in scenarios was also conducted. Generated graphs were found to have a high degree of similarity with human-provided annotations, indicating the effectiveness of the approach. Capturing long-range relationships in scene understanding tasks is a crucial goal in computer vision. While CNNs excel in many vision tasks, they have limitations in modelling global, structured relationships due to their localized nature. A fully connected graph like the self-attention mechanism in Transformers is beneficial, but graph complexity and computation costs rise exponentially with the graph size. We introduce a new graph neural network called dynamic graph message passing network that efficiently models long-range relationships in image data by adaptively connecting local nodes to global scene structures, and we demonstrate its efficacy in modelling global scenes in image inpainting and object detection tasks. We also introduce a new method for designing efficient global scene structures and provide an algorithm for optimizing message passing in these adaptive graphs. Experimental results show our approach outperforms state-of-the-art image inpainting methods and matches performance while reducing computation costs by up to 4 times in object detection tasks. The source code can be found at https://github.com/alevvi/dgmp.git. Optimized hardware is often required in embedded systems, leading to a common operation called Multiple Constant Multiplication (MCM) over integers. This operation is widespread in embedded systems, necessary for data processing and frequently involved in key tasks such as image and video processing, cryptography, and computational chemistry. A wide range of techniques has been used to optimize MCM, including bit-slicing, bit-manipulation, and circuit-oriented approaches like field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs), all of which are aimed at reducing hardware costs. This research aims to further explore and expand upon these optimization strategies, focusing on the following areas: 1) developing novel hardware structures for MCM M-8, M-16, and M-32; 2) introducing two new factors to evaluate the performance of MCM implementations, latency and throughput; as well as 3) assessing the energy consumption of the proposed MCM structures. This study employs a cutting-edge technology to evaluate the energy efficiency of the designed MCM circuits, utilizing an accurate simulation tool. This analysis shows that the proposed MCM structures can achieve significant area reductions, up to 98% in comparison to software-based MCM implementations. This research also showcases the potential of recent technology advancements, a 65nm FPGA, in hosting an extensive range of MCM applications with minimal hardware resource, covering a substantial exponent range of 0 to 127, and requiring only 55% of the available LUTs. This progress indicates that FPGA technology can efficiently accommodate various MCM-based workloads, offering promising loadable technology for various computing applications. This research contributes to the MCM field in several key areas: 1) the introduction of three innovative MCM structures; 2) the assessment of four modern FPGA FPGAs; as well as 3) an exhaustive comparative analysis of various optimization approaches. This study demonstrates that the proposed Complement Carry Structure (CCS) exhibits substantial area reductions, up to 98% in comparison to software-based MCM implementations, and shows promising potential for CCS-based MCM architectures in terms of throughput and energy efficiency. This work also documents various challenges in designing MCM structures, highlighting the difficulties in accommodating large multipliers and the constraints of different optimization approaches, and serving as a valuable reference for future MCM research and development. Lastly, this research shows that recent technology advancements, a 65nm technology, can host an extensive range of MCM applications with minimal hardware resource, and targets loadable technologies for various computing applications. Introducing the Virtual Secure Platform (VSP), a pioneering solution that brings together multi-opcode general-purpose sequential processing with Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) to enable Secure Multi-Party Computation (SMPC) at a secure computing offloading level, such as cloud computing. To achieve this breakthrough, our research combines a modified Stratus, an event-driven SMPC protocol, with a customized Digital Signal Processor (DSP) instruction set, tailored for efficient computation of sequential SMPC operations. By allowing the encryption of computations and results within a secure memory, VSP facilitates the execution of a substantial range of computations, from linear algebra and logic operations to arbitrary functions described as a sequence of DSP operations. Leverageaged, modern C++ has been used to develop VSP, which is currently available under the permissive MIT license at https://github.com/alexharris1999/Stratus-VSP. Currently, this implementation supports the encryption of computations with 512- to 1024-bit FHE, enabled by the Intel Software Guard Extensions (SGX) environment, which provides the necessary memory boundaries for secure data processing. Current performance levels, evaluated using benchmarking tools from Google and Microsoft, include up to 18,000 evaluations per second for 512-bit integers and 383 evaluations per second for 512-bit integers with memory access. Furthermore, our research indicates that VSP can carry out around 38 computations per second with the current 1024-bit FHE implementation. Although this seems slow when compared to standard CPU speeds, the incorporation of VSP's secure processing capabilities into current event-driven SMPC systems has the potential to greatly improve performance. This is particularly evident in the secure computing scenario described above, where the difference in speed can reach up to 100 times. In contrast to conventional SMPC, VSP's design empowers developers to run programs with multiple computational steps, thus expanding the scope of applications, such as blockchain and distributed system interactions, where high efficiency is critical. Additionally, our research involves the development of a secure memory management system, providing two options: a secure dynamic memory allocator or a secure copy of the standard libcs, which includes functions like strcpy and printf, enabled by the libsafe tool. Lastly, VSP's innovative design extends the use of FHE in SMPC by supporting multi-opcode general-purpose sequential processing, while its hybrid architecture, built upon DSP and event-driven SMPC, substantially reduces the number of necessary gate operations, thus facilitating the implementation of FHE. Researchers investigate polynomial-time approximation schemes (PTAS) for solving specific constraint satisfaction problems, such as Maximum Independent Set or Minimum Vertex Cover on graph classes that have limited connectivity.

A previously developed approach by Baker achieved PTAS on various graph classes including planar graphs. Further, Romero, Wrochna, and Zivny developed a simpler PTAS for certain graph classes using the Sherali-Adams LP relaxation for maximum CSPs with constraints defined by arbitrary non-negative functions.

This research is extended to CSPs with constraints that have multiple possible values. A new PTAS is developed for any fixed maximum CSP with constraints that have at most d possible values, where d is a non-negative integer.

This finding provides solutions for specific instances, such as Maximum Independent Set or Minimum Vertex Cover on graph classes, and even for some more complex graph classes that had previously eluded simplified algorithms. Furthermore, it reveals that the standard LP relaxation and the Sherali-Adams LP relaxation are equivalent for these CSPs, and finally, it shows that the LP relaxation is sufficient to achieve a PTAS for any finite CSP. Finally, a new technique to derive PTAS for minimization CSPs with general objectives is introduced. In particular, it is known that Baker's and Romero-Wrochna-Zivny's techniques can derive a PTAS for maximization CSPs with general objectives, but it was unknown whether the same was true for minimization CSPs, until this research provided evidence that PTAS for minimization CSPs exist for certain special classes of CSPs, and even for any finite CSPs with a general objective. This study reveals intriguing evidence of a complex internal rotation pattern within a less massive and less luminous star that has evolved into a giant. Typically, lower and intermediate mass stars retain their rapid rotation rates during their main sequence phase. In algorithmic literature, the underlying computation model is typically implicit and assumed to be basic instruction movements. This study examines whether more efficient algorithms can be devised by allowing more efficient memory access, specifically linearly independent movements. This investigation is rooted in separate areas of algorithmic complexity theory - the LIN class, which involves shifting inputs over a line, and property verification, which involves examining a function for a specific property. The primary question explored here is whether Property Verification can be reduced to Property Verification within the LIN class, and several variants of this question are examined. Additionally, evidence suggesting that Property Verification is likely complex within the LIN class is provided. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that if a specific algorithmic model is solvable, where a linear shift in inputs over a line allows a solution, then Property Verification can be reduced to Property Verification within the LIN class. Two other results are presented that suggest Property Verification is complex within various forms of linearly independent memory access. The main technique employed for these findings involves creating a simulation of a general computation model with a specific form of linearly independent memory access. The study also raises questions about the solvability of decision and enumeration problems for Property Verification within the LIN class. The findings are validated through simple examples, and several natural Property Verification problems are identified that are solvable within the LIN class, including verifying the parity of a symmetric function and searching for a specific element in an intersection of half-planes. Conversely, a totem pole problem is identified that remains unsolvable within the LIN class, demonstrating a separation between Property Verification and decision problems for a specific form of linearly independent memory access. The study concludes by examining the relationship between the LIN class and other forms of linearly independent memory access, such as parallel shifts and small moves. The results are based on an earlier paper by Alon, Shamir, and Tassa, which initially examined the differences between various forms of linearly independent memory access. We examine differential forms on an algebraic compactification of the metric graph moduli space, derived by mapping invariant differential forms from the tropical Torelli map. It's known that these invariant forms give rise to the stable real cohomology of the general linear group, a finding by Borel. We compute period integrals by integrating such forms across graph metrics and find them to be always finite and expressible as generalised Feynman integrals. Our integrals have further application in identifying non-zero homology classes in the graph complex, providing novel insights into the cohomology structure. Furthermore, we propose that the metric graph moduli space, now a complex variety, possesses an action by the general linear group, a claim supported by our integrals' resemblance to gauge theory principles. This relationship is a game changer, offering the potential to solve moduli space integrals using quantum field theory methods. In a specific instance, we solve a Feynman integral associated with planar graphs, enabling us to compute the first real cohomology group of the general linear group. This finding is then used to establish a relation between the connected autoduality locus of the metric graph moduli space and the space of symmetric matrices, a duality first observed in the context of local opers by the Buan-Horn-Miller. We explore examples to demonstrate that our integrals can capture graph invariants tied to the behavior of hyperbolic geometry, a field of study initiated by the influence of Thurston. As such, we present novel duality principles, including an instance involving the metric graph moduli space and the space of Hermitian positive definite matrices, a new finding. Finally, we examine the behaviour of our integrals under the substitution of complex metrics for real metrics, a transformation studied in the work of the Andersen-Lee-Polo. This analysis leads to an identification of the vanishing cohomology groups across graph moduli spaces, a result applicable to the study of local opers, a field first explored by the Loeser-Schulze-Pillot. All cohomology groups relevant to this problem are themselves expressible as generalised Feynman integrals. Through the application of our quantum field theory methods, we are able to solve differential forms across graph metrics, a problem left unresolved by Andersen-Lee-Polo. In various object categorization tasks, particularly in visually complex conditions, it has been demonstrated that recurrent neural networks (RNNs) can outperform feedforward models.  This research aimed to uncover the specific role of RNN recurrence in aiding object categorization.  We trained RNNs on an object categorization task and discovered through linear diagnostic analysis that auxiliary variables such as object position, orientation, and size are communicated through recurrence and contribute significantly to performance improvement.  This evidence confirms our hypothesis that auxiliary variables are utilized to optimize object categorization in cluttered environments.  We also developed an attention mechanism to selectively focus on relevant auxiliary variables to minimize information overlap and improve categorization efficiency.  Experiments confirmed the efficacy of our approach, yielding improved performance and efficient resource allocation.  This research was inspired by previous studies on visual pop-out and attention modulation.  We conducted our analysis on the modified Multi Object Tracking (MOT) dataset, which we created by incorporating additional categorical objects.  We validated our findings through extensive empirical evaluations.  These studies identified recurrent pathways for object feature propagation, aux2cat and aux3 variables as key information sources, and aux3 variables as the most critical for object categorization.  These findings are in line with our initial hypothesis.  Additionally, we observed that aux3 variables are utilized for object categorization, which is consistent with previous research on visual pop-out studies.  We developed and tested three different modulation policies for our attention mechanism, which successfully improved performance by eliminating redundant information.  These experiments confirm the effectiveness of our approach and demonstrate how attention modulation can enhance object categorization efficiency.  This research is significant as it showcases the efficacy of attention modulation in improving object categorization both theoretically and empirically. Social media platforms are facing significant problems due to the presence of toxic content like hate speech, off-color language, and misogyny. These difficulties have caught the attention of the Natural Language Processing (NLP) community, driving innovative research in the field. In this study, we report on the performance of our models in the inaugural Arabic Misogyny Identification challenge, where we evaluate three models that can learn multiple tasks simultaneously, alongside their individual-task counterparts. Our approach relies on the pre-trained MARBERT language model to analyze text inputs. Our results indicate that the proposed models achieved top-tier outcomes, securing first, second, and third place in both the misogyny identification and classification tasks. Furthermore, our models demonstrated substantial time savings during processing. Our analysis highlights the benefits of pre-trained language models and multi-task learning in the context of complex NLP problems. Our code is publicly available on GitHub.

Designing effective collision avoidance systems for mobile robots remains a key challenge, particularly when accounting for the robot's spatial structure.
In this paper, we develop a novel control approach that leverages Control Barrier Functions and Quadratic Programming to enable safe navigation for mobile robotic arms around obstacles, factoring in their unique geometry.
Our proposed method successfully incorporates geometric constraints by converting them into control constraints, allowing for seamless integration with the robot's spatial structure.
Simulation results for both a simple rod and a modeled robotic arm validate the method's efficiency and scalability, demonstrating its ability to adapt to varying levels of complexity without excessive computation time. Additionally, we highlight the method's potential extension to more complex robotic systems. 
Ultimately, this research paves the way for developing practical, real-world collision avoidance systems capable of considering a robot's inherent geometry. 
The associated code can be found at https://github.com/frc-rocketz/CBF_QP_Safe_Navigation.

Natural language processing, a crucial field of study, strives to comprehend text via digital analysis, despite the inherent imperfections arising from diverse forms of written and spoken language. This work delves into employing various graph-based methodologies for resolving the challenge of text summarization via a selective extraction technique. Two key indicators – sentence overlap and edit distance – are employed for gauging sentence similarity. We investigate the utility of edit distance through graphical representations stemming from different mapping methods, including the well-known dynamic programming algorithm. Notably, our research introduces a novel graphical model built upon the random walk principle. Building upon these findings, a fusion approach combines the strengths of overlap and edit distance measures. This study culminates in the development of a hybrid system, boasting a high accuracy of 94.08%, outperforming existing state-of-the-art techniques. Furthermore, our proposed solution boasts computational efficiency, requiring only a few milliseconds to process each text input. Experimental evaluations conducted on diverse text datasets, comprising Reuters, Reuters-256, and DUC summaries, firmly establish the ground-breaking potential of this technique. A related implementation is available online at https://github.com/TanmaySanyal/Graph-based_Text_Summarization. Additionally, our code has also been uploaded to https://github.com/TanmaySanyal/Tanmay. This research was carried out at the Indian Institute of Technology Roorkee, under the guidance of Dr. Sushil Jajodia.

As a novel area of study within high-energy astrophysics, pulsar halos offer a unique opportunity to explore cosmic-ray propagation in the Galaxy's local environment. This research aims to investigate the possible connection between the Fermi-100 Myr halo and a nearby spiral arm in the Galaxy, specifically the Aquila Rift. Transportation systems are frequently hindered by unpredictable weather conditions.
Current methods for weather prediction, relying on a network of sensors, are often inadequate due to sparse coverage, costly installation, and maintenance.
A more efficient approach is proposed, using deep learning to identify weather conditions from images captured by cameras, thus enabling outdoor navigation system failure detection.
An exhaustive dataset has been compiled, the Resolved Forgetting Set (RFS), containing 125,000 images from various environments, categorized into distinct weather conditions, including clear, cloudy, light rain, heavy rain, shine, night, and obstruction.
An advanced Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) was designed to accurately classify weather conditions in the RFS, surpassing existing techniques and demonstrating superior generalization capabilities.
Moreover, a novel algorithm was developed to quantify the reliability of weather predictions from sensors, outperforming existing reliability estimation methods and providing a more accurate assessment. Both the RFS dataset and the weather classification, as well as reliability estimation algorithms, are made available for further research. An online simulator is also provided to replicate the results, showcasing its application in a navigation system failure detection framework. Soft grippers are increasingly popular across various applications due to their versatility and flexibility, yet accurately modeling and controlling them to grasp objects efficiently remains challenging. Soft grippers' infinite-dimensionality and non-linearity make traditional control approaches difficult to implement. In response, researchers have turned to data-driven methods. However, current methods typically require extensive model learning through simulations or offline processes, which often fails to adapt to novel scenarios or real-time physical robot control requirements. In this research, we propose an innovative online algorithm that uses the Koopman operator theory to update and refine a dynamic model in real-time. By integrating the updated model into a Model Predictive Control (MPC) structure, our approach enables successful deployment on multi-fingered soft robotic grippers. Our results demonstrate a high success rate in grasping diverse objects, even those initially unknown to the controller, as compared to other model-extraction methods. Additionally, our approach has been validated through a series of experimental trials, as showcased in a publicly available video. These experiments highlight the algorithm's ability to adapt to new objects, as well as its performance in handling multiple grasping scenarios of known objects. In one such case, our algorithm successfully transitions from grasping a small block to holding a larger bowl. A comprehensive discussion of our findings, along with potential future extensions, are presented. High-energy emissions from ancient supermassive black holes can mimic the characteristics of a compact symmetric object (CSO), which is considered an early stage in the development of a supermassive black hole. A CSO, characterized by two jet structures of similar strength pointing in opposite directions, can exhibit variations in the alignment and strength of its jets. Observations of high-energy emissions from a CSO, designated Pictor A, suggest it may be a black hole of intermediate age rather than a traditional CSO. Notably, Pictor A's jet variations can model spiral structures observed in its jets. Additionally, its double jet pattern can be explained by a jet that has moved beyond its initial emission point due to its faster speed. Changes in its energy emissions, classified as "low syndrome," may be the result of blocks in the jet flow causing pressure to build up and eventually release. Observations of Pictor A's behavior suggest that its characteristic double jet pattern will soon disappear, and it will then be considered a quasar rather than a CSO. This transformation indicates a possible progression from CSO to quasar for objects like Pictor A, where the "low syndrome" and double jet features appear simultaneously. Conversely, other objects with these characteristics may be undergoing a different evolution stage. Moreover, a potential discrepancy between optical and radio emissions from a CSO, characterized by a double jet pattern, may indicate a variation in its energy production sources. This possibility could lead to a classification system that is independent of emission type. Furthermore, a relationship was discovered between a CSO's age and its distance from other, more advanced black holes. This finding suggests the presence of a "zone of active evolution" surrounding a black hole, within which certain active states (characterized by a double jet pattern) disappear and reappear. This phenomenon, the "active evolution zone," may be missing from current black hole evolution models. Conversely, a model describing how a black hole's active states change over time (the "jet evolution model") suggests that the "low syndrome" and double jet features appear at different ages of a black hole. This difference highlights the need for further study of these active states, whose characteristics may vary based on the observer's angle. Lastly, a study found an association between a particular orientation of certain structures in a black hole and its active states. This finding, the "orientation hypothesis," suggests a possible connection between a black hole's orientation and its known active states. This research focuses on improving survival time prediction for lung cancer patients, which, despite significant progress in recent years, still lacks effective solutions that leverage the complete set of digital medical data. Our goal is to incorporate the rich information provided by multimodal clinical data, including text-based medical records and visual scans, to enhance survival time prediction. Our proposed method, MRCN, features a dual encoder that processes these modalities separately but combines them to produce a unified representation, which is then input into a survival time predictor. Our results show that MRCN outperforms state-of-the-art methods on data from the Baja Lung Cancer dataset and a combination of public datasets, with significant improvements in concordance statistics and lower error measures. Furthermore, we conducted extensive ablation studies to validate our findings and examined the effectiveness of different feature extraction techniques. Our study demonstrates that MRCN is a robust and efficient solution for predicting survival times in lung cancer patients through combined analysis of multimodal clinical data. A novel approach combining machine learning is introduced, enabling the accurate reconstruction of high-redshift cosmological density perturbations through observed quasar spectra analysis. By leveraging sophisticated simulations of cosmic structure formation, a substantial synthetic dataset is generated to serve as training grounds for the machine learning model. The effectiveness of this method is validated by calculating the statistical discrepancy between the reconstructed and true density perturbation spectra, yielding an error rate of less than 1 percent across all considered redshift ranges. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this technique can successfully recover the linear component of the density perturbation spectrum, thereby providing valuable insights for future observational quasar research. The associated code and dataset are publicly available for further research purposes.

This paper examines certain types of non-weight modules connected to Lie algebras of the Weyl type. Firstly, we establish the characteristics of modules whose restrictions to $U(\frak h)$ are one-dimensional over Lie algebras representing differential operators on a circle. We then identify the requirements for the irreducibility of tensor products between quasi-finite highest weight modules and modules free over $U(\frak h)$. Additionally, we show that these tensor products are isomorphic only if their corresponding base modules are equivalent, before expanding our findings to cover general Lie algebras representing differential operators. Finally, we investigate some specific examples involving sl(2) and dihedral Lie algebras VI_{n,1}. Our study partially responds to queries posed in a by Y. Shageda in 2019. Since some of our outcomes have broad applications, such as in the study of quantum field theories, the level of generality achieved in this work is valuable. Moreover, one of our key findings relates to an irreducible module whose restriction to $U(\frak h)$ is two-dimensional, a novel discovery in this field. This module may serve as a model for understanding quantum field theories involving soliton-like states. Finally, we conclude with an investigation into the quantum field theory rooted in dihedral Lie algebra VI_{3,1}, revealing which irreducible modules could represent physical states. This analysis fully resolves the antipode conjecture for this specific algebra. Furthermore, our research offers potential future directions by asking whether similar approaches can resolve the antipode conjecture for other Lie algebras representing differential operators. Additionally, one of our key contributions is the introduction of a new method for solving the antipode conjecture, which may be applicable in a broader context. The binary black hole merger's aftermath leaves a lasting mark on space-time known as gravitational wave memory, and multiple events create a background of residual disturbance known as the stochastic gravitational wave memory background (SGWMB). Researchers found that this phenomenon can be modeled using the concept of Brownian motion. The strength and distribution of SGWMB are directly tied to the frequency and occurrence rate of binary black hole coalescences, and its power spectral density is proportional to the inverse square of frequency. Unlike the more common gravitational wave background produced by binary black holes, SGWMB's characteristics allow it to span a broader frequency range than any other cosmological foreground, and thus holds greater potential for being detectable through ground-based gravitational wave detectors. Furthermore, analyzing SGWMB may provide valuable insights into the Brownian effect and the gravitational wave memory phenomenon. Lastly, we explore possible methods for identifying SGWMB and have proposed a potential approach to achieve this goal. Finally, we briefly discuss the potential future contributions of SGWMB to ground-based and space-based gravitational wave observatories. The research presented here provides an opportunity for further scientific and methodological investigation.

A reliable and efficient communication system known as semantic communication aims to minimize data transfer and ensure seamless connectivity to diverse users and services. A promising innovation in this field is the use of emergent language, which enables precise and efficient communication through the use of unique words and reduced bit rates. This paper presents a novel approach to learning these specialized words and their meanings from random binary messages by utilizing a combination of maximum likelihood decoding and Markov decision processes. The results show that emergent language performance compares favorably to an optimal baseline assumption where the source and codeword distributions are known. The approach also allows for the simultaneous optimization of both the language and the encoder, leading to improved output quality and reduced bit rates. Specifically, emergent language achieves 75% of the baseline data transfer at just 55% of the baseline error rate. Furthermore, encoder efficiency is within 90% of the optimal value. The proposed method is slow and power-hungry, but shows significant potential as a long-term solution as the need for efficient communication systems grows in line with the expanding deployment of unmanned aerial vehicles. A comprehensive analysis of the trade-offs between output quality, bit rates, and power consumption, along with implementation details and design choices for optimizing emergent language, is presented. A variant of the approach known as hidden emergent language is also developed to provide additional security by incorporating a secure encoder that ensures both confidentiality and integrity. The resulting system offers a level of security that approaches Shannon's limit at an acceptable cost in output quality, while still achieving significantly better results than standard approaches to codeword masking. The hiding of specialized words in this manner comes at a cost of slightly poorer output quality and reduced encoder efficiency, but still achieves nearly all of the benefits of emergent language. A suitable set of hyperparameters for hidden emergent language is presented that balances security and efficiency. The resulting system, which is within 90% of the optimal value for encoder efficiency, requires only 57% of the output quality needed to achieve the best possible security. The integration of hidden emergent language in semantic communication systems is expected to play a major role in the long-term development and expansion of this technology. The Natural Language Processing area has garnered disproportionate interest from researchers in the past. A primary factor driving this attention lies in the word prediction challenge, where given a sequence of words in a sentence, a model is tasked with recommending the subsequent word. Researchers have addressed this issue through various techniques, combining either syntactic or semantic analysis methods in the past. However, individually, these approaches often fail to yield practical results in real-world applications. For instance, latent semantic analysis can capture semantic relationships, yet it disregards syntactic constraints in sentence structure. In contrast, more advanced models like Deep Learning integrate both methods to achieve impressive outcomes. Despite these advancements, word prediction models often overlook the errors made in previous words, predicting the next word in isolation. In this research, we introduce a novel word prediction model that takes into consideration the context of previously input words. The proposed model is based on a Long Short-Term Memory network modified to handle sequences of words. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this model by comparing it to other prominent methods, including a dataset comprising Wikipedia articles and a database of chat logs. The results show that our model substantially boosts the accuracy of word predictions in both datasets. Furthermore, to validate the theoretical underpinnings of this model, a corresponding theoretical model was developed and tested. The outcome confirms the superiority of the proposed model. To facilitate the replication of these results, the source code, pre-trained models, and associated datasets are available for download at https://github.com/raphitw/WikiChat-LSTM. In the near future, the planned update will incorporate the capability for the model to learn and process sentences asynchronously. The model's potential applications extend to various areas, such as information retrieval, where it may be utilized to reconstruct truncated sentences from the search query and the document abstract. The model may also be applied in the completion of forms based on conversation, where it may help fill in form fields by drawing from the chat log. Lastly, the model could be used in the automatic summarization of sentences, where it may be used to reconstruct a sentence from a chat log and a query. Recent advancements in Session-based recommendation systems have gained popularity for providing personalized, real-time suggestions with high recall rates compared to conventional techniques. Recent examples include STAMP and NARM models, which, however, did not perform as expected on Zalando's Fashion-Similar dataset in comparison to a basic collaborative-filtering method. This study centers on low-energy collision avoidance and formation restoration for autonomous drone swarms. Developing efficient algorithms for collision avoidance in high-density aerial situations is crucial for applications like search and rescue operations. A key challenge lies in designing collision avoidance strategies that prioritize energy efficiency to prolong flight times. To address this, we've created a novel control strategy combining a polynomial-based trajectory planning method and a control correction system. A polynomial-based approach guarantees smooth, continuous trajectories with minimal energy expenditure. Following the initial trajectory, a control correction system ensures accurate formation restoration via the least-squares method. We've conducted simulations to demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed control strategy, focusing on a basic structure with specific considerations for when targets are within the boundary of a safety sphere or not. Test results show that this strategy yields efficient collision avoidance with minimal energy consumption and preserves the original formation structure. Furthermore, we've verified the applicability of this approach in more complex drone swarm formations with arbitrary shapes. Selected simulation results are presented to illustrate the method's performance in various formation restoration situations. Notably, we've found that our proposed controller exhibits desirable scaling properties, reducing the impact of parameter variations on collision avoidance and formation restoration. To validate the feasibility of our approach for actual drone swarms, we performed physical tests using 10 quadrotors with the results confirming our theoretical predictions. To save space, we present two of these test scenarios in video format, highlighting our method's effectiveness in complex drone swarm formations. These experimental findings demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed control strategy in achieving both efficient collision avoidance and precise formation restoration, making it suitable for autonomous drone swarms in real-world applications. In our investigation, we focus on a mean-field optimal control issue for stochastic differential equations featuring time-delay, which are influenced by fractional Brownian motion with a Hurst parameter exceeding 0.5. Given the fractional Brownian motion's nature, which defies the criteria for being a Markov process or semi-martingale, we resort to the fractional White noise calculus and specialized tools for differentiating functions of measures to establish necessary and sufficient stochastic maximum principles. This approach is further exemplified by two applications, including solving a delayed consumption optimization problem from a cash flow and a linear-quadratic problem under delay constraints. Both problems yield a unique solution verified through both the maximum principle and a dynamic programming equation adapted for fractional state variables. Moreover, we demonstrate the maximum principle's applicability to a variety of related problems. For specific Hurst parameters, including the special case of 1 (Brownian motion), we establish corresponding results, which resemble those found in standard optimal control theory. Furthermore, our study derives new interpretations for both the delayed consumption problem and a modified version of the linear-quadratic problem. Lastly, we examine the minimum variance heuristic for a related problem, showing it yields a solution that, under certain conditions, converges to one obtained through the maximum principle. In doing so, we illustrate the varied behaviors of minimum variance heuristics for stochastic control with delay, which arise from different paths of the fractional White noise. In particular, when the Hurst parameter equals 1, our findings align with those of [Overkalk and Zhang, 2019], who explored similar scenarios, but instead used different approaches, which included a quasi-sde and a rough Volterra equation. In contrast to their work, our fractional White noise calculus perspective allows us to extend their results to a broader class of SDEs involving delay, which are often referred to as fractional SDEs or SDEs with Hurst parameter greater than 0.5. In addition to these comparisons, our study also establishes relationships between the fractional maximum principle and both a differentiable equivalent for the fractional variational principle and a nonlinear variation of the quasi-synchronization property. Ultimately, our results provide new insights into the structure of the fractional maximum principle, demonstrating its distinct relationships to these fundamental concepts. To verify our findings, we also introduce and prove a specific useful lemma, which demonstrates that any solution obtained through the maximum principle remains bounded. To thoroughly analyze the Dirac operator's spectrum, we've made connections between periodic/antiperiodic eigenvalue problems for the operator, equivalent tridiagonal operator actions in weighted Hilbert spaces and relevant Heun equation connection issues. This, in turn, ties into four related non-self-adjoint, unbounded tridiagonal operator eigenvalue problems which surprisingly possess real eigenvalues. A real eigenvalue problem for the Dirac operator corresponds to a specific eigenvalue problem for one of these tridiagonal operator actions, which itself is linked to a Lax pair. This framework allows us to show that the operator's spectrum remains bounded, with the same number of eigenvalues relative to a given reference operator whose spectrum remains bounded and is self-adjoint. We also find that any real eigenvalue of the Dirac operator corresponds to a $2\pi$-periodic solution of the associated Heun equation. We plan to extend our findings to higher-band elliptic potentials, allowing for more general couplings, in a future paper. This will involve using the findings from the current study in a structured and related series of papers, where a key example will be used - the elliptic version of the non-self-adjoint Cremona transformation operator. This operator has a spectrum that remains bounded and is self-adjoint, while its corresponding Jacobi elliptic potential has a finite-band nature. Furthermore, all of the eigenvalues of the operator are real and correspond to $2\pi$-periodic solutions of the associated Heun equation.
