This was done under the condition that the eigenfunction does not become zero as the parameter varies over the range from 0 to 1. Wikipedia's ultimate goal is to be an authoritative reference on various topics.  However, due to a limited number of editors and a vast amount of articles, only 0.6% are considered of high quality according to their established criteria. To enhance article quality through machine learning, we must first label individual sentences as high or low quality, a task that is both time-consuming and labor-intensive when done manually. To address this issue, this paper examines the effectiveness of using neural machine learning models to make these labels more accurate and efficient. We assess the effectiveness of several models that utilize surface-level, contextual, and rich editing history data, and discover that a model combining these elements outperforms others by achieving an accuracy of 76.82 when evaluating edited articles on a random Wikipedia category involving weather. Notably, this model requires no training on the Wikipedia data it is evaluating, thereby maintaining neutrality. Furthermore, we analyze the characteristics of articles that are difficult for the model to identify and propose potential improvements for an enhanced machine learning experience. To facilitate further research, we provide the annotated dataset used to train and evaluate our model. Ultimately, we hope that the techniques presented in this paper will contribute to the development of high-quality Wikipedia articles more efficiently. Based on our results, we believe that the combination of human and machine editing has the potential to greatly increase the number of articles rated as high quality. To support the Wikipedia community in this endeavor, we provide recommendations for integrating our model into the standard article assessment process. In the near future, we aim to expand our study to cover the entire Wikipedia, as well as investigate other information sources such as Knowledge Graphs and structured documents. This research is part of the Wikipedia Species project, which focuses on studying and improving Wikipedia's diverse content and contributors. To facilitate further research, we invite others to participate in this effort through collaborative development of the Wikipedia Species framework. Knowledge distillation is a successful method for accelerating deep neural networks by training a compact model to mimic the behavior of a high-capacity network. Traditionally, this relies on having access to the original network's training data and parameters, which isn't always feasible due to storage or privacy constraints in real-world applications. This study introduces decision-based black-box knowledge distillation, allowing a model to be trained on the behavior of a network whose internal workings are inaccessible, given only its input-output decisions. Through theoretical analysis and experimental evaluation, the research demonstrates that such a distillation process can effectively transfer knowledge, yielding a model with performance comparable to one trained conventionally. Moreover, the study shows that the distilled model can achieve comparable accuracy on the original dataset, in addition to achieving similar results on other related tasks. Comprehensive empirical evaluations across various image classification tasks validate the method's efficacy, which is also found to have a positive effect on the distillation model's robustness against adversarial attacks. Reinforcement learning efficiency can be significantly enhanced through imitation learning by leveraging expert guidance. However, relying on expert demonstrations is often impractical or too costly due to the high expense of gathering them. In this research, we introduce a pioneering Co-Imitation Learning framework to circumvent this issue. CoIL leverages peer agents' successful experiences by training two distinct agents in an alternating exploration-exploitation process. Although agent experiences may be both beneficial and misleading, our method employs value function expected gain estimation to filter out less useful knowledge. As a result, the agents learn from each other, selectively imitating valuable information and rejecting unnecessary data. Experimentation across multiple scenarios highlights the superiority of our Co-Imitation Learning framework, confirming the benefits of inter-agent knowledge exchange in the absence of external supervision. Additionally, we investigate the effects of agent collaboration on performance and find that the collaborative effort is more efficient than individual efforts. Our findings are further validated by comparing CoIL to existing imitation learning techniques. A new model is introduced to describe treatment interference in units, 
where the response is influenced solely by its treatment status and neighboring units within a defined radius of influence (K-neighborhood). Traditional approaches for identifying interference involve controlled randomized trials and statistical tests focused on specific, selected units (focal units). We provide criteria to select these pivotal units under the given interference framework and conduct a simulation to assess existing methods for detecting interference in networks. By implementing this selection process, highly effective tests of treatment interference are achieved, surpassing the efficacy of standard experimental methods. Moreover, the developed approach is adaptable to various scenarios of limited unit influence. Additionally, we introduce a novel strategy to determine the radius of influence for units displaying treatment interference. This innovative method relies on the hyperparameters estimated through a nonparametric model or maximum likelihood estimation and is applicable across different types of networks. Furthermore, simulations reveal that the one-size-fits-all approach of traditional methods is suboptimal when compared to the network-specific radii of influence. We illustrate the efficacy of the proposed methods through numerical examples and an analysis of treatment effect moderation in a network of 250 US counties based on data from the Anti Smoking Treatment study. This study optimizes the execution time of established algorithms for classically simulating quantum circuits comprising Clifford and T gates. The efficiency improvement stems from deriving a novel upper limit for the number of stabilizer states required to express $m$ copies of the magic state, $|T\rangle$. The findings reveal that a superposition of no more than $O(2^{\alpha m})$ stabilizer states can accurately represent $|T\rangle^{\otimes m}$, where $\alpha\leq 0.3963$, surpassing the previous best-known estimate of $\alpha\leq 0.463$. This advancement allows for the development of a classical algorithm capable of approximating the output probabilities of $n$-qubit Clifford + T circuits $U$ within a specified inverse polynomial error margin, using a time complexity of $\mathrm{poly}(n,m)2^{\alpha m}$. Furthermore, the investigation yields refined bounds on the stabilizer rank of symmetric product states $|\psi\rangle^{\otimes m}$, ultimately leading to the creation of a strong simulation algorithm for circuits comprising Clifford gates and multiple instances of a fixed single-qubit Z-rotation gate, operating at a time complexity of $\text{poly}(n,m) 2^{m/2}$. An additional suggestion is presented for potentially enhancing the upper bounds through the design of specific linear codes. The supporting code can be accessed at https://github.com/qsystem/quantum_simulator/tree/stabilizer_rank_update. Previous research has suggested the use of SRAM-based TRNGs for extracting entropy from SRAM arrays. As these arrays are commonly employed in specialized or general-purpose chips for data storage, SRAM-based TRNGs provide an economical alternative to dedicated hardware TRNGs. Nevertheless, existing SRAM-based TRNGs suffer from reduced throughput, elevated energy expenditure, prolonged latency, and a limitation to generating random numbers continuously. In order to overcome these shortcomings, this paper presents an SRAM-based TRNG that can sustain long periods of operation. To accomplish this goal, the proposed TRNG incorporates a linear feedback shift register to accomplish fault-tolerant data sampling, thereby enhancing its throughput capacity. Furthermore, the integration of a multiple-input signature analyzer provides an additional boost to throughput while simultaneously supplying an internal clock, thus eliminating the necessity for an external clock. Consequently, the proposed TRNG exhibits considerable improvements in throughput, energy efficiency, and operational duration. In particular, the design demonstrates 10 to 131 times greater throughput, 11 to 205 times greater energy efficiency, and 11 to 131 times shorter initialization time when compared to current state-of-the-art SRAM-based TRNGs. It also establishes necessary and sufficient conditions for the weak quantum uniqueness theorem and the strong quantum uniqueness theorem. Ultimately, the study offers an investigation into the uniqueness of the wave function for one-dimensional strictly ergodic quantum walks. The research finds that these walks exhibit unique wave functions for almost every initial state. Furthermore, the study reveals that the unique wave functions of group quantum walks and orthogonal group quantum walks can be expressed in the form of a specific stochastic process, known as the two-state continuous-time exchangeable partition chain. Automated essay grading has been a persistent challenge in Natural Language Processing.  Despite years of research, it remains an only partially resolved issue, with notable practical applications and research implications.  Techniques such as transfer learning and data augmentation have significantly improved the accuracy of state-of-the-art models in this domain.  Past research has explored the potential of Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) and variants like Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) for essay grading, although they have largely been surpassed by more recent transformer-based models like BERT and RoBERTa.  Building on these developments, our study presents four new approaches to enhance essay grading models:  three of these involve incorporating paragraph-level data augmentation, while the final one involves leveraging multiple models to inform its predictions.  By evaluating these strategies on a widely used dataset from the Amazon Mechanical Turk platform, we found that they consistently outperformed a strong baseline model based on RoBERTa. This perspective also motivates future research into new techniques for improving these models, while sparking interest in the potential for applying similar approaches to related problems in Natural Language Processing.  In addition to these contributions, our study more broadly addresses several key challenges in the field, including the management of computational resources, the handling of missing data, the measurement of model performance, and the development of open-source repositories for NLP applications. Recent studies on large language models have demonstrated in-context zero- and few-shot learning abilities with promising results, yet their underlying dynamics are not yet fully understood. For instance, there is limited knowledge about how learning in-context changes when using varying training corpora. Our research aims to explore the influence of a pretraining corpus's origin and size on the performance of a Korean-centric model. Notably, we discovered four crucial findings: Firstly, a pretraining corpus's domain significantly affects the model's ability to learn in-context. Conversely, a pretraining corpus's size doesn't guarantee in-context learning to emerge. Furthermore, a pretraining corpus composed of multiple domains may facilitate the development of in-context learning, even when each domain doesn't result in in-context learning alone. Lastly, a pretraining corpus related to a downstream task may not always ensure a high in-context learning performance for that specific task, especially when it comes to the few-shot setting, and that language modeling performance and in-context learning do not always correlate as one might expect. To better comprehend these results, we developed various pretraining strategies and tested their effectiveness, ultimately suggesting the utilization of adaptive knowledge selection as a viable approach to enhance in-context learning performance. Additionally, we found that a fine-tuning technique can significantly improve both out-of-domain and in-domain language modeling performance, as well as a variety of downsteam tasks, indicating that early stopping could be an important factor to consider when engaging in in-context learning. Our research provides significant insights into the in-context learning phenomenon, paving the way for future research on zero- and few-shot learning. Moreover, our study is one of the few to explore in-context learning in the Korean context, contributing largely to the advancement of Korean language technology. Lastly, our proposed adaptive knowledge selection strategy could potentially be applied to other zero- and few-shot learning techniques to come out of a larger, more comprehensive language model. For example, it's possible that early stopping, which we've identified as a key factor in in-context learning, might be an important factor in other zero- and few-shot learning techniques that arise from more extensive language models. For this reason, we've decided to share our code through which a comprehensive Korean language model can be generated. Specifically, we recommend utilizing the Hugging Face transformer library to create a state-of-the-art Korean language model. When creating this model, it's essential to note that the code needs to be modified in order to prevent the pretraining corpus from being downloaded multiple times, as this could result in unnecessary data transmission.

The objective of zero-speech synthesis is to create a vocabulary-independent speech system without transcription data, requiring the transformation of training data into acoustic units for test synthesis. This study explores identifying and modeling the fundamental acoustic units in speech, comprising both transient and steady-state regions. The transient regions are equivalent to consonant-vowel and vowel-consonant units, while steady-states include sonorants and fricatives. The speech signal is first segmented into CVC units based on a short-term energy contour and then grouped using graph clustering. The clustered units are categorized into transient and steady-state regions based on their acoustic characteristics. We have developed two overarching methods to quantify the manipulation of quantum states using probabilistic protocols constrained by specific quantum resource limitations.
Initially, we formulated a fundamental criterion for achieving a physical transformation between quantum states using a previously introduced resource metric.
This approach led to the derivation of a unified method for calculating the maximal achievable gain in resource value when converting a quantum state into another of potentially greater resource value.
Additionally, this method was applied to a range of resource theories, including the theories of quantum coherence and quantum work.
Furthermore, we established a relationship between geometric measure of coherence and the maximal gain in coherence value, which was verified through multiple special cases.
These findings demonstrate that geometric measure centrality can serve as a useful tool for analyzing the resource-constrained transformations of quantum states. 
This method can be readily adapted for scenarios where the target state has a potentially lower resource value, yielding necessary and sufficient conditions for achieving this transformation.
Furthermore, we introduced the notion of quasi-free operations, a relaxed version of the weak asymptotic equivalence relation, to study resource conversion phenomena in multiple scenarios. 
One such example is the quantum work generated by the black-box algorithm, which fails to achieve the optimal gain in work value predicted by the geometric measure.
These findings collectively offer a deeper understanding of the resource metrics used to constrain quantum operations and reveal new insights into the concurrent behavior of multiple resource conversion phenomena. 
Ultimately, this knowledge can inform the development of more practical and efficient resource-tillting algorithms, which are essential for harnessing the power of quantum resources in a wide range of practical applications. 
In fact, we present a simple and efficient protocol for converting a geometric measure of coherence, which performs better than the previously reported protocols in multiple scenarios. 
This includes the conversion of thermal states with zero coherence into maximally coherent states, which takes approximately $\log_2 101$ times fewer resources than the best available protocol in the literature. 
In another example, we show that the geometric measure of work generated by black-box algorithm is insufficient to achieve the optimal gain in work value predicted by the geometric measure, which is an instance of the broader phenomenon known as the Lovász's problem. 
This problem is a long-standing open challenge in the field of convex geometry, which has remained unresolved since its initial formulation in the 1970s. 
Therefore, our findings offer novel connections between the theory of resource conversion and the geometric properties of convex bodies, which may be useful for developing new protocols for the practical manipulation of quantum states.

We investigated the dynamic behavior of a cup of coffee being carried while in motion, by applying a lumped model that combines characteristics of a planar nonlinear pendulum. This model was subject to two types of excitation - parametric in the vertical plane and a combination of parametric and direct in the horizontal plane. The position of the pivot changed over time, inducing these excitations. In the scenario of vertical excitation, the averaging method helped to determine stability boundaries, while vertical excitation and the response amplitude were analyzed through a scaling approach. For the combination of excitations in the horizontal plane, the averaging method helped to determine stability boundaries. Our findings show that as the amplitude of the pivot position increases, the system's stability decreases, ultimately losing it. Additionally, we observed a significant effect of the excursion of the pivot position on the system's response amplitude. Our study concludes that considering the excursion of the pivot position is crucial for accurately estimating the dynamic behavior of a cup of coffee. The results are supported by three-dimensional visualizations of the system's trajectory in phase space. The stability of the system is primarily influenced by the excursion of the pivot position rather than the excitation parameters. As a consequence, this model can be utilized to evaluate the dynamic behavior of objects in various scenarios of motion. We examine the techniques of simulating light-matter interactions within tight-binding models that derive from first-principle theory. The conventional method for describing optical properties uses a velocity-based approach tied to the vector potential. An alternative method exists, where a finite system is represented through the electric field, resulting in a dipole-based model inspired by Peierls substitution. This study evaluates the accuracy of both methods in relation to gauge invariance, utilizing TB models constructed from maximally localized Wannier functions and applied to two-dimensional paradigm materials. We calculate the electromagnetic responses under linear and strong excitations, comparing the outcomes to converged first-principle simulations to validate our TB models' accuracy. The results indicate that the dipole-based model yields a more precise description of light-matter interaction, whereas the velocity-based model introduces errors in the context of non-perturbative light driving. We demonstrate that these inaccuracies stem from an incorrect description of certain electronic transitions. To rectify this shortcoming, we incorporate occupation numbers derived from first-principle ground-state calculations into our TB model, enabling the accurate simulation of velocity-based models under dipole gauges. The enhancement of numerical gauges to a perfect electric-field gauge further improves the accuracy of our TB models, resulting in the correct simulation of optical transitions. The research provides a systematic approach for constructing accurate TB models capable of describing strong light-matter interactions, accelerating the efficient modeling of light-driven phenomena in 2D materials and systems. Moreover, the methodology is applicable to the modeling of certain chemical reactions accelerated by light, potentially enabling the prediction of new, light-driven chemical reactions. In a problem focused on category-level perception, we consider utilizing sensor data to identify and understand objects within specific categories despite variations within those categories. An active shape model, where pre-defined CAD models of various objects are used as a reference, is employed to determine the 3D pose and shape of an object. Our first achievement is developing a CAD-neutral representation of categories that can accurately predict poses and shapes within each category using available CAD models. For real-world applications with limited or no CAD models, we propose two approaches: one uses CAD models with similar structures to "borrow" shapes and poses, and another uses shape and pose predictions as features in a classification task to improve object classification. Our results demonstrate that these methods can improve accuracy in detecting the object type on Lytro and MiniSun datasets. In addition to these contributions, we address the issue of determining the object's identity within a specific category. If the identity of an object can be defined as a unique combination of shapes from a particular category, we show that Lytro dataset objects' identities can be defined as a combination of their poses and shapes. However, we also find that, in general, using shape and pose features from our active shape model do not differentiate one object's identity from another within the same category. To improve this, we propose an approach that uses object tracks to identify distinct identities within each category. Our finding is that using CAD models with similar structures can improve distinguishing one object's identity from another within the same category. Lastly, we explore identifying multiple objects of the same type in a image, and propose an approach that uses a multi-object learning technique to improve accuracy in identifying multiple objects. Our results show that this method can improve the performance in identifying multiple objects of the same type on Lytro dataset. This proof-of-concept implementation showcases the substantial potential for improved performance in variable position systems using modern DACs with rapid data transfer. Moreover, the proposed control designs can be adapted for other variable position systems with different performance requirements, highlighting their broad applicability. We introduce a general, flexible framework called Partial Registration Network (PRNet), designed specifically for aligning partial point cloud views. Building on learning-based registration methods, PRNet employs deep networks to overcome complex alignment and correspondence issues. Unlike existing methods that require a fully observable shape, PRNet is suited for partial-to-partial registration tasks, surpassing traditional and deep learning-based approaches on synthetic datasets. Our approach features self-supervised learning of a suitable geometric representation and a keypoint detector for common point identification, alongside learned keypoint-to-keypoint correspondences. Experimental results demonstrate PRNet's ability to consistently predict keypoints and correspondence across varying views and objects, while its geometric representation is also transferable to classification tasks. Moreover, PRNet's keypoint network enhances the performance of point cloud registration when combined with alternative geometric representations. The proposed method achieves state-of-the-art results on various benchmarks, including 3D object, chair, and synthetic object recognition, reducing the error rate by 14%, 12%, and 10% respectively, and shows promising results on real camera views. Additionally, we decompose the nilpotent quotients $\Gamma_{n,c}$ as semidirect products of finitely generated abelian groups, and we identify which invertible matrices can be extended into automorphisms of $\Gamma_{n,c}$. Ultimately, we conclude that $\Gamma_n$ has the $R_\infty$ property for every non-negative integer n, and we compute the $R_\infty$-nilpotency degree for each $\Gamma_n$. Conversely, we claim that \Gamma_n has the $R_\infty$ property for every non-negative integer n if and only if n is 0 or 1. Determining the top quark mass is crucial in understanding the stability of the Higgs potential and predicting its predicted value from data. The top quark mass can be measured by analyzing the behavior of top quark pairs produced together with an additional jet that exhibits similar characteristics to a b-jet. This can be done while taking into account various background influences. Recent studies have achieved a level of precision of approximately 0.5 GeV but face significant challenges due to background uncertainties, particularly those related to the identification of heavy jets and event topology. Highly automated driving systems designed to operate in case of failure demand robust architecture and contingency planning mechanisms. To safeguard against electric and electronic failures, a backup system is triggered by an arbitration logic that prioritizes functional safety above all else. To uphold the standards set forth by ISO 26262, rigorous testing of this logic is mandatory. Through this validation, one can confidently ensure that system-wide failure detection and recovery processes are both timely and error-free. Traditional formal verification methods are inadequate for this type of evaluation and have given way to advanced simulation-based evidence collection and formal verification techniques. Within the scope of this study, a formal model of the failure detection and recovery logic from ISO 26262 is created and formally verified in the Coq proof assistant, with a Simulink-based simulation model developed to validate the model's functionality. Any discrepancies found during comparison of the formal model to the formal verification model are documented and resolved. Methodologically, this study aligns with the standards set forth by the SAE Onboard Short-Circuit Testing Method and provides a new approach for designing and implementing fail-operational systems. This study represents the first known application of the variable substitution calculus to the formal verification of automotive control algorithms as specified in ISO 26262. Additionally, this work provides Coq and Matita verification tools for the formal model, as well as a Simulink-based simulation model, open-sourced on GitHub, facilitating the replication of this study and potential application of this verification method to other fail-operational architectures. To ensure the accuracy and completeness of the formal model, additional tools were used, including the N.B.J. Fourney's context-free parser and the SMT solver in Matita, as detailed in the supplemental materials available on GitHub. Matita verification tools were used, providing further assurance for the formal model's correctness as set out in the Coq verification. In contrast, the Simulink-based model was implemented with a focus on efficiency rather than formal correctness. To validate the formal model, the Matita verification was coupled with a rapid prototyping approach using Coq, as detailed in the results presented later in this document. Following validation, the formal model was found to be correct in relation to the Simulisk model. However, discrepancies were discovered in the Simulisk model, leading to proposed amendments as detailed in the proposed amendments to the Simulisk model, open for public review. Identifying clusters in complex systems across various fields such as power, genetics, finance, and astronomy is a pressing challenge. These systems often evolve dynamically, rendering traditional static clustering methods ineffective. In this paper, a novel approach is presented that leverages time-series data to detect communities within dynamic systems by defining a state similarity measure that reflects mutual influence and utilizes the Koopman operator to handle nonlinear relationships, thus extending the approach to a broad spectrum of applications. This method's effectiveness is demonstrated through clustering of a linear system, the non-linear 39-bus transmission network, and variables derived from atmospheric data in the Amazon rainforest. Furthermore, a proposed refinement improves performance by adjusting for noise and accommodating non-linear dynamics. This study's findings provide a framework for detecting clusters in complex, nonlinear systems and have practical implications for data analysis in various fields. One key limitation of recommender systems is data scarcity resulting in substantial variability. Various approaches have been implemented to optimize recommendations by leveraging link prediction, item ranking, and joint model training. Notably, the latter has become the standard strategy in current systems. Despite ongoing efforts to improve, systems still experience data shortages and the recommendations they produce are subpar. This paper presents a groundbreaking solution called COLD, an open-source countermeasure that accelerates training of collaborative filtering models by eliminating data variability through sampling. COLD's efficiency is showcased through experiments on well-known datasets, and its potential as a reusable module is also explored. Additionally, a comprehensive investigation of state-of-the-art personalization techniques using small datasets is conducted, and the findings are shared publicly for further evaluation by the research community. This study marks a significant progression towards developing more effective recommender systems that thrive in data-constrained environments. This paper revisits monitoring real-time systems by leveraging properties described either in Metric Interval Temporal Logic or as Timed B\"uchi Automata. We propose effective, symbolic, and online monitoring methods in several contexts that take advantage of 'zones', a concept familiar from efficient model checking of Timed Automata. These contexts encompass improved treatment of timing discrepancies, monitoring under timing ambiguity, and the extension of monitoring to provide earliest time estimates for when decisive verdicts can be rendered. Moreover, our method facilitates a straightforward adaptation to handle large numbers of time parameters by employing region-based analysis, a technique also applicable to other complex analysis techniques. We demonstrate that, in this particular monitoring scenario, the complexity of analysis is significantly reduced. Nevertheless, a contrasting example illustrates that, in general, the application of region-based analysis does not necessarily yield considerable analysis efficiency. The monitoring methods we have developed are implemented in the tool, mital. This tool, designed for online, symbolic evaluation of Metric Interval Temporal Logic formulas, allows for automatic generation of monitoring machines, capable of handling timing discrepancies, large zones, and complex formulas with multiple time parameters. Furthermore, our method also accommodates other analysis techniques, like, for instance, the use of Boolean programs, as long as these are encoded in the POZ-verifier format. We also provide experimental comparisons with other relevant approaches, namely, the original PZA and MZV methods, as well as the verifiers in MZV and Mital, which rely on Boolean programs, in the context of a simple yet time-consuming practical example. In particular, our zone-based monitoring method, designed for online analysis with timing discrepancies, outperforms other methods, even those that are exact but offline, like, for instance, the verifiers in MZV and Mital. The decay reactions $\eta \to \pi^0\pi^0\pi^0$ and $\eta \to \pi^0\pi^0\gamma$ are analyzed to assess isospin breaking in the standard model. Isospin breaking in meson-meson transitions primarily arises from different quark masses, whereas the radiative decay also involves the difference between the $U(3)$ charm and strange masses of mesons. Both contributions to $\eta \to \pi^0\pi^0\pi^0$ are relevant and need to be calculated using the kinematic amplitudes for $\eta \to \pi^0\pi^0\gamma$. Our calculations yield a value for the ratio $R_\eta$ of $\Gamma(\eta \to \pi^0\pi^0\pi^0)$ to $\Gamma(\eta \to \pi^0\pi^0\gamma)$ as $1.84 \times 10^{-3}$. This result agrees with Ritzinger, Kublitz, and Meissner's prediction, thereby validating their isospin-breaking analysis. Our analysis also reveals that the standard model contributes to the physical branching ratios of these decays with a contribution of $1.64 \times 10^{-5}$ to $\Gamma(\eta \to \pi^0\pi^0\pi^0)$ and an upper limit of $1.73 \times 10^{-10}$ to $\Gamma(\eta \to \pi^0\pi^0\gamma)$. These calculations imply that new physics beyond the standard model could cause a enhancement in the standard model predictions for both decay channels. Finally, our analysis suggests that the standard model contribution to $\eta \to \pi^0\pi^0\gamma$ could be tested through an experiment with a sensitivity of $10^{-10}$ in a decay width. \end{abstract}

The GRAVITY acquisition camera utilizes four distinct optical capabilities to track multiple beams from the Very Large Telescope Interferometer (VLTI): a pupil tracker, a reference sphere, a beam shifter, and an image processor. These functions are critical in maintaining the accuracy of the GRAVITY instrument, which is capable of forming high-stability beams from up to four telescopes into a single interferometric pattern. In order to verify the performance of the GRAVITY acquisition camera, a comprehensive testing procedure was established. During these tests, the camera's components were examined individually, and subsequent simulations were conducted to analyze the impact of the pupil tracker and reference sphere on the instrument's overall performance. Additionally, a detailed mathematical model of the GRAVITY acquisition camera was created to enable the calculation of its Abbe offset, which is essential in facilitating precise angular measurement. Following successful completion of these tests, the GRAVITY acquisition camera was deemed ready for use in the instrument's regular observing procedures. Furthermore, these experiments have provided valuable insights into the optimal operating parameters of the camera, enabling the improvement of future instrument designs. The resulting findings have significant implications for current-generation interferometric systems and the next-generation Extremely Large Telescope. Based on the test data collected, a thorough statistical analysis was conducted to assess the variability of the camera's sampling patterns. These analyses, combined with the established mathematical model, can be employed to evaluate the performance of the GRAVITY acquisition camera in a dynamic environment. In the event that the camera's control system experiences disruptions, such as those resulting from loss of signal conditions, a developed recovery strategy can be utilized to rapidly restore precision sampling of the interferometric pattern. The strategy involves implementing a quick-switching mechanism between different sampling patterns and leveraging the instrument's inherent symmetry to facilitate seamless transition. The proposed recovery strategy is expected to be effective in the majority of situations in which the camera loses signal. However, in extreme cases of severe signal degradation, the use of a restricted set of sampling patterns becomes necessary to ensure the maintenance of accuracy. In such instances, the application of a limited set of sampling patterns is necessary to maintain the level of precision required for the generation of a high-stability interferometric pattern. The implementation of this recovery strategy, along with the proposed alternative set of sampling patterns, is currently being integrated into the GRAVITY acquisition camera's control software. The proposed modifications are set to enhance the camera's resilience to signal disruptions, thereby extending its operational lifespan. Based on this equation of state, mathematical expressions for key thermodynamic properties and characteristics have been obtained, thereby substantiating the principle of corresponding states within the group of alkali elements. In the context of vector-meson dominance model, properties of light vector mesons in local parity breaking mediums with chiral imbalance are explored. By utilizing a finite lowest-order local effective Lagrangian derived from QED for vector ρ and ω mesons, a mass spectrum as a function of momentum and chiral chemical potential is determined. Furthermore, in addition to the existing Chern-Simons effect, which differentiates the transverse polarizations of these mesons, a significant radiatively induced contribution arises at a few hundred MeV for momentum and chiral chemical potential. Both effects are comparable in magnitude. This investigation also confirms previous findings and extends them correctly. Additionally, a significant correction due to light quark mass is considered, revealing that it has a substantial impact on the mass spectrum for momentum and chiral chemical potential up to a few GeV. These results have significant implications for the behavior of vector mesons in quark-gluon plasma and chiral matter. For example, the mass spectrum in chiral matter could provide crucial information about vector-meson decay widths and the existence of vector mesons in quark-gluon plasma. Finally, potential avenues for experimental verification through heavy-ion collisions are discussed. We examine the fundamental challenge of estimating a sparse network's node count under conditions of uncertainty, specifically when the network contains a large number of malicious nodes with complete network knowledge, unbounded processing power, and the ability to manipulate the protocol freely. Our main achievement is a probabilistic algorithm designed to estimate a sparse, complex network's size, even in the presence of an unspecified number of malicious nodes not exceeding O(n^(1-delta)) - where delta can be any arbitrarily small positive constant. The algorithm generates an approximate estimate with a fixed constant factor, specifically a fraction of the logarithm of the network size, and this estimation is accurate to a large extent (up to 1 - epsilon) among the genuine nodes for any arbitrarily small positive epsilon. The algorithm runs on n nodes with the properties of being fully decentralized, low overhead, and uncomplicated in implementation. However, common enforcement methods fail when the spacetime geometry becomes highly distorted or when the matter patterns exhibit complex, nonlinear characteristics. A recently developed method using multigrid techniques successfully resolves these issues, allowing for the construction of well-behaved spacetime metrics even in the presence of intricate matter configurations. This approach has been successfully applied to simulations of binary neutron star mergers and other complex systems, demonstrating its effectiveness and flexibility. This enforcement method is highly adaptable and can be implemented with varying accuracy, making it a valuable tool for a wide range of numerical relativity simulations. This technique has been implemented in the code calledboard, which is part of the Co-Design Framework. A detailed description of the method and enforcement techniques is provided in a companion paper.

The main objective of the JUNO experiment involves identifying the neutrino mass ordering by utilizing a large, 20-kt liquid-scintillator detector equipped with photomultiplier tubes. For optimal results, the experiment's instruments require precise energy resolution and quality, which necessitated a thorough assessment of the chosen photomultiplier tubes. In this study, we investigate the performance of 20 15-inch PMTs by documenting their individual characteristics, such as the pulse shape, waveform, quantum efficiency, and dark noise, through an extensive testing process. In addition, we establish the calibration method of the experimental setup in the laboratory, as well as the data acquisition system that monitors the signal intensity and pulse shape of the PMTs under various conditions. In accordance with the requirements of the JUNO experiment, our research verifies the meeting of the necessary standards for the selected PMTs in both of the mentioned aspects. In particular, the 20 tested PMTs exhibit an average pulse shape purity of approximately 90.6%, with an average pulse width of 7.75 ns, an individual pulse height maximum of 69.8 photoelectrons, and an average dark noise rate of 0.18 kHz within the signal band in the laboratory illumination. In the field conditions similar to those of the JUNO experiment, our collective 20 PMTs show exceptional quality and uniformity, as evidenced by their average properties such as the pulse shape purity of 90.5%, the pulse width of 7.66 ns, the signal intensity of 70.6 photoelectrons, and the dark noise rate of 0.17 kHz within the signal band. In conclusion, the experimental results confirm that the selected 15-inch PMTs not only fulfill but also surpass the specified requirements for the JUNO experiment in various aspects. Therefore, it is reasonable to infer that the identical 20-inch PMTs would likely exhibit even better performance and thus be suitable for use in the experiment. In view of the above outcomes, our research successfully verifies the compatibility and quality of the selected 20 PMTs for the application in the JUNO experiment. In practical scenarios like power consumption forecasting and air quality analysis, long sequence time-series forecasting (LSTF) is indispensable. The complexity of multidimensional time series data presents significant model demands, necessitating precise representation of long-term input-output relationships and relationships across multiple dimensions. Recent work employing the Informer model based on the Transformer architecture has yielded impressive results for long-term forecasting, yet it falls short in addressing dimensional interactions. Our enhancement of the Informer addresses these limitations in multidimensional forecasting through several key approaches. Firstly, we incorporate an adaptive graph neural network to identify dimensional connections often hidden in time series data. Secondly, we incorporate adaptive graph convolutional networks into spatio-temporal prediction models, enabling these models to recognize dimensional interactions. Our empirical evaluations with diverse datasets have revealed that the integration significantly boosts model accuracy and often surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, our models exhibit considerable scalability, enabling them to effectively handle large data sets and provide reliable predictions for complex dimensional time series data. Our source code is available at https://github.com/guopengf/MT-Informer.

Astronomical observations from ground-based telescopes can be distorted by Earth's atmosphere due to differential dispersion that varies by wavelength. Current designs of these correctors are based on atmospheric models which have yet to be verified through on-site measurements. We've carried out a detailed analysis of these models over the 315-665nm wavelength range using cross-dispersion spectrographs, which have an accuracy of 18 milliarcseconds. By comparing various models in detail, we're now in a better position to inform the development of improved ADCs for the future, and advise against relying on the Zemax model, especially when blue spectrum accuracy is critical. Instead, a hybrid of these models, as applied in the Case-Invariant Model, provides the most accurate results with an average precision of 3.4 milliarcseconds. This has implications beyond atmospheric correction, as this model can also be used to optimize optical systems in various applications. We've made these findings, as well as various model modifications suggestions, available to guide the development of more effective ADCs. This paper explores the recovery of one-dimensional Radon measures on a torus from their low-frequency Fourier components up to a given cutoff frequency, denoted as Kc. The proposed method involves minimizing the total variation among all compatible Radon measures through the problem of basis pursuit in the continuum (BPC). Building on the work of Adcock et al., we establish the uniqueness of the solution for BPC by adapting their arguments to our problem, achieving this for any positive integer K, regardless of the value of c. The effectiveness of our approach is demonstrated through numerical experiments, with the results indicating that the accuracy of the method can be augmented by incorporating additional constraints derived from the Plancherel estimate of Fourier series. The development of these new constraints enables the recovery of Radon measures from their Fourier transforms within specified frequency and spatial domains, a problem termed basis pursuit in the continuum with frequency and spatial localization (BPC-FSL). We derive stability estimates for the original and the FSL variants of BPC, establishing that the number of data points required for stability grows logarithmically with the desired accuracy. The study also reveals that the use of an optimized basis leads to superior recovery of Radon measures, a finding corroborated by numerical experiments. The implementation of our method is validated through several real-world applications, including the reconstruction of light fields from their low-frequency Fourier components, a problem that cannot be solved uniquely without additional constraints, as well as the reconstruction of Radon measures from their low-frequency Fourier components on a circle. Additionally, the research achieves a novel application - the reconstruction of Radon measures on a circle from their low-frequency Fourier components at arbitrary frequencies. The methods developed in this study are general and applicable to the recovery of other types of measures, a new form of inverse problem. Furthermore, the research is a foundational element in a new set of techniques for the construction of complete Radon measures through approximation, a innovative idea in mathematical science. The remarkable effectiveness of deep learning has sparked various concerns regarding ethics, encompassing skewed predictions and data security risks. To address these problems, experts employ fairness metrics, accountability techniques, and privacy preserving methods, respectively. A key challenge lies in the disparate nature of these endeavors, stemming from distinct origins and purposes. Fairness approaches often leverage model characteristics, while privacy methods prioritize operational efficiency. Moreover, the computational demands of these techniques can hinder their deployment on edge devices. This thesis seeks to bridge the gap among these parallel fields by developing innovative techniques for ensuring fairness, accountability, and privacy, tailored for resource-constrained devices. Initially, we focus on extending network disconnection, a key tenet of local privacy, to deep learning models, yielding significant time and space savings. Next, we build on this work and introduce the concept of differential fairness, protecting both model and data from inequality. Finally, we create the first framework combining local privacy and fairness, yielding a general framework for semi-local privacy and fairness, which is formally proved to meet established criteria. The proposed solutions are highly efficient, providing substantial computational savings, and can be easily integrated into existing systems, including popular deep learning platforms. Experimental results on two key applications highlight the advantages of our techniques. First, for image classification on edge devices, our methods surpass alternative privacy and fairness approaches. We re-examine a well-known model for complex semiconductor production lines and develop it into a control problem. Due to the complexity of the system's velocity, it cannot be represented solely based on its state, which poses difficulties for modeling, control, and optimization. To overcome these difficulties, researchers have resorting to numerical methods that rely on complex software. In this study, we introduce a simplified model that captures the essential characteristics of the original system while also yielding a more manageable velocity profile, also known as a diagonal approximation. Building on this revised model, we successfully apply contemporary control techniques to optimize a linear cost function while observing constraints on the system's states and velocities. The resulting optimal control strategy is then tested in simulations that compare the performance of different production strategies for a two-product system. The simulations demonstrate the efficacy of our approach and reveal a significant production cost savings of nearly 10%. Additionally, our simplified model enables rapid calculation of optimal control strategies, with a computational time that is roughly 15 times faster than standard methods. The proposed solution represents a significant advancement, as these savings and performance metrics can translate to real-world cost reductions of hundreds of thousands of dollars per week. Finally, we confirm that the optimal production plans obtained from the diagonal approximation of the original model are also viable in the full system, as validated through simulations. The resulting production schedules, which were identified using the simplified model, can be applied to the more accurate system without compromise. Therefore, our approach provides a valuable solution for optimizing complex semiconductor production lines, facilitating efficient and effective scheduling of these high-tech manufacturing systems. Modern artificial intelligence (AI) techniques are now applied to discover physics laws, with the aim of mimicking how humans derive principles from observational data. However, conventional AI models have significant limitations when transferred to entirely new situations. This raises the question of whether it's possible to automatically establish universal physical principles that work across all cases. This paper discusses the difficulties of achieving this goal, which stem from the inherent uncertainty in empirical measurements and the complex interdependence of observed phenomena. These obstacles make it likely that any AI-trained model of the world will be inaccurate to some extent. This inaccuracy can then be used to develop a more reliable physical model, but one that is necessarily different from the original representation. Ultimately, the most effective approach will likely involve a balance of both human expertise and artificial intelligence algorithms in the discovery of physical principles. This will likely involve the use of multiple, diverse models of the world, which can provide more robust and trustworthy insights into its behavior. This perspective is illustrated through the application of multiperceptual neural networks, which can be trained to generate accurate physical models from basic data, similar to how humans do, and then utilize these models to make predictions about new situations. This is particularly shown in the case of predicting the behavior of gas mixtures, for which the training data doesn't include information about the individual components involved. This capability makes the network useful for generating hypotheses about previously unknown physical systems, which can then be verified experimentally to produce reliable predictions. The Stable Roommates problem concerns pairing a set of individuals according to their unique preference orders for one another, with each stable matching respecting the principles of stability. Through an examination of large groups of triples, we demonstrate the existence of stable matchings that prioritize individual preferences, while also revealing a relationship between these preferences and stable matchings of a related graph structure. Finally, this study explores the relationship between the quantum Fisher information and the performance of the quantum feedback control, offering a valuable tool to evaluate the effectiveness of the quantum correlations and the potential of the system to extract information about the unknown variable. We conducted an exhaustive examination of non-hierarchical three-body systems where two bodies initially move in opposing directions while the third body is positioned at the center. The aim was to calculate the probability of the central body escaping within a specified time frame and escape velocities for various configurations. The study found that the probability of escape is influenced by the mass ratio of the bodies, their initial energy, and duration, with no universal value that can accurately predict escape probabilities in all scenarios. Furthermore, we identified that the previously suggested formula is accurate for a limited mass range but becomes less reliable for larger mass ratios. The research also revealed that the average escape velocity cannot be predicted without knowing the initial conditions of the systems, highlighting the significance of statistical analysis in future studies. By studying three-body escape in astro-geophysical contexts, our findings provide insights into various phenomena, such as atmospheric escape, the gravitational impact of small bodies on large planets, and the stability of planetary systems. The results of this research can be utilized to simulate high-energy impacts and the collisions of bodies in astro-geophysical contexts. A new technique is proposed to forecast suicidal ideation based on the integration of Electronic Health Records and Ecological Momentary Assessment data utilizing advanced deep sequential models. These datasets consist of asynchronous, variable-length, randomly sampled sequences which are modelled separately using Recurrent Neural Networks and combined through the alignment of hidden states, along with attention and pre-training schemes to handle differing sequence lengths. Experimental outcomes using 1023 patients' data demonstrate that the incorporation of Ecological Momentary Assessment records significantly increases the recall of the model in predicting suicidal ideation, from 48.13% using Electronic Health Record data alone to 67.78%. Furthermore, the proposed method exhibits enhanced performance of 72.46% when using a subset of 200 patients for validation, along with 68.021% using leave-patient-out cross-validation on the entire dataset. Additionally, the method offers superior classification performance when compared to state-of-the-art baselines, with a significant increase in area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.073. This suggests that the integration of Ecological Momentary Assessment records can yield more accurate and robust predictions of suicidal ideation using Electronic Health Record data. In this work, we introduce a method to extract the key information needed to track their development via a process called skeletonization. By applying a modified version of a previous technique combined with a new approach to address partial volumes, we are able to accurately identify the critical points of these interfaces. This novel skeletonization method allows for the efficient capture and representation of interfaces presenting high spatial and temporal resolutions. Furthermore, we demonstrate its effectiveness by applying it to a range of phenomena including a falling liquid drop, a swirling liquid bath, and a gas jet interacting with a liquid surface. The resulting extracted structures present a high degree of accuracy and enable us to introduce a new metric to characterize critical points in terms of their multiplicity. This new metric enables a detailed classification of these critical points into distinct categories. This approach opens up new possibilities for the operation of fluid-based mechanical systems that present unique geometries. Additionally, this method presents a valuable tool for use in computational fluid dynamics, where it can be integrated into an iterative solver to improve the accuracy of numerical simulations of interface movements. We analyzed over 8,000 massive, edge-on disk galaxies from the SDSS dataset, classifying them into 'S' and 'U' shapes based on isophote asymmetry measurements, and found that U-type galaxies are more likely to be blue, have higher star formation rates, and contain younger stars than S-type galaxies. However, both types of galaxies have similar stellar masses, and frequencies of U-type galaxies decrease with increasing stellar mass. In contrast, S-type galaxies with 'boxy' cores are more common among more massive galaxies. Our findings indicate that U-type galaxies are characterized by higher star formation rates and younger stellar populations across a wide range of stellar masses. Additionally, U-type galaxies show a linear relationship between central and outer color differences, while S-type galaxies with 'boxy' cores exhibit a different behavior, with a breakdown of this trend at high mass levels. Our discovery of a clear distinction in color distributions between S and U galaxies contradicts previous theories, and suggests that U-type galaxies are more broadly associated with active star formation across various mass ranges. Our research further demonstrates that the 'U'-type classification is not solely influenced by color or star formation rates, but rather is a distinct feature. Moreover, a comparison of U-type galaxies in the SDSS and the SAMI galaxy survey shows that, despite similarities, U-type galaxies in the latter exhibit higher stellar masses, and are less likely to contain hot stars. This leads us to consider that U-type galaxies might be less common in massive galaxy populations generally, and could have local variations affected by selection biases. Nonetheless, our research highlights the need for further investigation into the origins of U-type galaxies, and their connection to major galaxy mergers and star formations. Proximal methods can efficiently solve complex optimization problems by finding suitable solutions with minimal constraint violations. However, the original method is limited to smoothing certain nonsmooth objectives, which limits its application. We have developed an alternative smoothing technique for use with proximal methods, which is based on the Bregman splitting model. This new method allows for a more precise optimization with less constraint violations and, in contrast to the original method, does not require smoothing the objective function. Instead, we use a smoothing term for the loss function and maintain the original data point. The resulting algorithm, Bregman proximal splitting (BPS), is a universally applicable method that can be applied to a wide range of problems. We have tested BPS on several real-world tasks, including matrix lasso and robust cosine measurement, and the results show its efficiency and effectiveness. The numerical analysis confirms that BPS has a lower computational cost compared to other methods. The implementation of BPS in MATLAB is available online. This was achieved by designing photonic devices with intricately modulated transmission spectra, thus performing cross-correlation without the need for dispersion. Consequently, our device simplifies the apparatus while reducing its overall cost, enabling precise detection of atomic/molecular substances as well as accurate radial velocity measurements of astrophysical objects.

We are confident that this innovative technique will inspire the development of unique and groundbreaking photonics devices in the future.

Imitation learning seeks to bypass the complexity of creating optimal reward functions for agent training by utilizing expert behavior instead.  The challenge lies in environments that are modeled as Markov Decision Processes, and current imitation algorithms often rely on access to expert demonstrations within the exact same environment in which the imitation policy is to be learned.  However, in many practical scenarios, the expert demonstrations are obtained from a different version of the environment.  For instance, a robot may learn to mimic human cooking based on videos shot in a different kitchen from the one it is supposed to cook in.  In this paper, we explore the problem of adapting imitation algorithms to deal with discrepancies between the tutoring and student environments.  The main issue arises from the fact that these environmental differences may lead to behaviors that are inconsistent with both the tutoring and student environments.  Therefore, we propose Discriminative Imitation Learning, in which we model the probability of an action given a state by considering both the tutoring and student environments.  Furthermore, we demonstrate that our method is capable of learning an invariant policy across various variations of an environment by modeling the probability of an action that is consistent with both the tutoring and student environments.  The main advantage of our method is that it allows the use of a broad range of representations that can learn both the desired actions and the differences between various environment versions without becoming confused about which actions are desired and which are not.  We test our method using simulated versions of two practical scenarios: driving and kitchen navigation.  The results show that Discriminative Imitation Learning successfully learns both the desired actions and the differences between various environment versions. Association rule analysis is a widely used technique in Data Mining. This method involves partial implications between binary variables, which can be constrained by parameters such as confidence and support levels. We delve into the concept of redundancy among association rules from a theoretical perspective. Each transaction in a dataset can be viewed as a logical statement, and we investigate existing notions of redundancy among association rules. We explore alternative definitions of redundancy and introduce new characterizations, highlighting relationships between these concepts. We demonstrate that two distinct notions of redundancy exist, differing in how full-confidence implications are treated. We establish a deduction calculus for each of these concepts, show how to create the smallest possible bases, and also examine redundancy with multiple target variables. We fully dissect the case of redundancy involving two target variables, while, in the context of multiple target variables, we identify a specific subset of the most influential rules that can uniquely describe the redundancy relationship. We further explore how redundancy can be applied to the removal of irrelevant variables in Data Mining and highlight potential practical applications. Ultimately, we discuss possible approaches for implementing the proposed algorithms. We conclude by outlining significant challenges that require attention. Due to the complexity of the problem, several questions and propositions remain unresolved. Throughout the paper, we employ the language of Lattice Theory and Polyhedra to illustrate key concepts, using simple yet clear examples. In particular, we visualize association rules on a lattice and connection numbers, which represent the strength of association rules, as a crucial component of the study. To establish the uniqueness of the smallest base, we reduce the problem to a linear programming problem and use polynomial equations to determine the validity of association rules. We also represent the redundancy relationship between association rules and connection numbers as a polyhedron and derive necessary and sufficient conditions for full-confidence implications. We examine the computational complexity of the redundancy problem and show that it belongs to NP-Complete, a property we prove by introducing a SAT-Problem formulation. We conclude the paper by outlining possible approaches for the efficient computation of the smallest base of association rules. We propose reducing the problem to a Polyhedra cutting problem, which is known to be solvable in polynomial time under specific conditions. However, the efficiency of the solution heavily depends on the simplicity of the lattice. When dealing with complex datasets, this approach becomes impractical, leading to a new area of study that requires further research. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first comprehensive study on the application of Polyhedra cutting methods in Data Mining. This work presents the Generalized Maximum Likelihood Estimators for any parameter related to a mixing distribution, provides conditions for its existence and uniqueness, offers methods for its calculation and simulation-based validation, particularly introducing a new algorithm for calculating MM-estimators in such scenarios. Additionally, this research includes simulations to compare the performance of different estimators, such as the Product Moment Estimator, its modified version, the Generalized Maximum Likelihood Estimator, the antithetic Monte Carlo estimator and a newly developed MM-estimator. It is observed that the MM-estimators are more robust and efficient than the traditional PME and GML estimators, especially when utilizing Monte Carlo methods to handle complex integration issues. These findings are further exemplified through real-world data analyses. The research outcomes demonstrate that using Monte Carlo methods can successfully handle complex estimation problems related to mixing distributions and that utilizing MM-estimators yields more reliable results. It is noticed that the estimators obtained are invariant to the specific sampling mechanism used, such as whether sampled en bloc or individually. Based on this discovery, a modified version of the Metropolis-Hasting Algorithm is introduced for sampling from complex distributions by breaking down the distribution into a simple component and a rare component. The utility of this sampling technique is demonstrated through examples. Achieving dependable data privacy while ensuring data utility is an intricate problem in various real-world applications. To address this issue, a novel framework known as One-Sided Differential Privacy (OSDP) has been developed. OSDP enhances data utility by recognizing that not every data record contains sensitive information. However, the previous approaches in this field made the assumption that data records were statistically independent. Inspired by occupancy data analysis in building management systems, the current research builds upon the one-sided differential privacy framework by accounting for inter-record relationships. Furthermore, the paper quantifies utility losses resulting from the imposition of privacy constraints, thereby establishing a relationship between privacy parameters and utility depreciation. To validate the proposed method, an experimental dataset comprising of building occupancy records is utilized, and the results demonstrate that the data utility losses can be substantial, emphasizing the need for optimizing privacy parameters in accordance with the data's statistical properties. Ultimately, the work facilitates the effective alignment of data utility and privacy considerations. For visually appealing outfits, individual garments must harmoniously fit together based on factors like style, type, and color. Current studies view visual compatibility as a straightforward'match' or'mismatch' classification problem, where each garment item is labeled as entirely compatible or incompatible. Yet, this simplistic approach is impractical for real-world Outfit Maker apps where users must identify which specific items might clash with their creations. To address this limitation, we introduce the Visual InCompatibility TransfORmer (VICTOR) that's tailored to tackle two distinct challenges: quantifying an outfit's overall compatibility and pinpointing individual mismatched items. Leveraging a fashion-oriented language-image contrastive pre-training framework, we fine-tune VICTOR on a wide range of fashion visuals. We expand upon the Polyvore outfit benchmark, introducing a dataset dubbed Polyvore-MISFITs comprising imperfectly matched outfits, to train and test our proposed model. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that our proposed VICTOR outperforms or matches state-of-the-art performance on the Polyvore dataset while achieving an impressive 88% reduction in computational requirements, striking an ideal balance between accuracy and efficiency. A floating raft made of particles offers a clear model for observing material breakdown. Due to the slow timescales, both how the particles move and the expansion of the surrounding liquid play crucial roles. Experiments with a 2D raft of circular particles floating on a liquid that expands at a constant rate are presented here. Initially, the authors expected the particles to arrange themselves in a series of concentric circles. However, this study shows that a more complex, chevron-shaped pattern often forms before the particles break and spread out. A basic theory is developed to explain how this chevron pattern forms. Two types of instability are identified - a gentle, continuous expansion and a more abrupt, layered pattern - and the conditions for these instabilities are determined. These findings are relevant to a range of materials that undergo gradual expansion, such as rocks with expanding crystals or polymers with seeping fluids. Additionally, the authors suggest that more intricate, curved patterns may be common in nature. This is likely because many situations involve a combination of different expansion rates, not just one. This is shown through further analysis, which suggests a more general approach is possible. This approach uses a unique property called the Arondec rule, which describes how multiple forces can produce curved patterns. This theory is applied to a series of different materials, including a unique example of a caustic pattern seen in ice and a possible explanation for the unique shapes seen in salt crystals. Our novel TD learning approach overcomes several challenges robots encounter when navigating underwater.  By leveraging Gaussian Process regression, our method significantly enhances data efficiency by limiting TD updates.  To facilitate online learning, we developed a approximation algorithm utilizing the Kalman filter, which greatly improves the calculation's speed while maintaining accurate predictions.  By deriving the covariance of the advantage, we optimized update rules and reduced noise.  Furthermore, we developed a new criterion for terminating learning episodes.  The performance of our approach is showcased through simulations and practical underwater learning experiments with our buoyant robot. The resulting predictions enabled it to achieve high scores on 'Beep' both on land and underwater.  To our knowledge, this is the first time 'Beep' has been solved using online learning. The consideration of temporal contexts in knowledge graph embeddings poses a significant enhancement for numerous applications utilizing knowledge graphs. Notably, existing work in this area concentrates on developing novel architectures for embeddings that account for temporal factors, whereas the potential for temporal attribute manipulation in KGE models remains poorly explored. In this study, we introduce Time2Vec, a straightforward technique that modifies the multiplication layer in a composite KGE model to incorporate temporal attributes. Our results show that Time2Vec consistently boosts the performance of composite KGE models when applied to RE-RELEVENT-KGE and SEME datasets, covering diverse knowledge graphs such as Wikipedia, Yelp, and semantic medical information. Furthermore, we highlight that Time2Vec is versatile and can be integrated with various architectures, including attention-based models, triplets, graphs, and convolutional neural networks, thereby demonstrating its broad applicability. Additionally, we obtained state-of-the-art results on KEELPAD, a dataset for evaluating entity linking and knowledge graph embedding methods. Our source code is available at https://github.com/diml0o/Time2Vec.

In this research, we have examined the complex aspect of the Heavy Quark potential, focusing on its dissociation at high temperatures and strong magnetic fields. Our work builds upon previous studies by introducing three distinct features: comprehensive calculations of Landau levels, a novel gauge boson propagator in a magnetized plasma, and an intricate, direction-dependent heavy quark potential. To showcase our advancements, we have generated detailed visualizations, such as heavy quark potential tomography and dissociation probability diagrams, at various temperature and magnetic field conditions. Interestingly, a strong magnetic field induces the dissociation of heavy quarkonia at lower temperatures than a weak magnetic field. Additionally, we have identified temperature-induced heavy quark potential anisotropy in isospin-invariant plasmas. Our findings are anticipated to contribute meaningfully to the study of heavy ion collisions. All generated images can be reproduced using the PyHEAVY package. To effectively answer complex questions, large language models need information about specific entities, but can't store all necessary knowledge themselves, so they rely on external sources like knowledge graphs to fill gaps. Our proposed solution, OREO-LM, includes a special layer that lets a language model work together with a knowledge graph to find the best answer, and in return, the language model becomes more accurate. By integrating OREO-LM with existing language models, such as RoBERTa and T5, we achieved record-breaking results and also got better explanations for the models' choices, thanks to the ability to infer new relationships between words. Experimental results show that OREO-LM outperforms other approaches, like multi-task learning and graph neural networks, and even more importantly, it improves the models' ability to make sense of their decisions, which is crucial for trustworthiness. We have developed a novel method of constructing high dimensional expanders by utilizing covering spaces of simplicial complexes. Building upon expander graphs, high dimensional expanders play a vital role in theoretical computer science but unfortunately, there are only a few constructions available that meet the required threshold of a constant $0.01$ for their coverings.

Our research involves a detailed exploration of covering spaces of simplicial complexes and establishing a general construction of high dimensional expanders through covering numbers of such spaces. We have set out to apply this framework to two specific types of expander graphs - Betzalel and Tarski expander graphs - in order to develop new constructions that meet the aforementioned threshold of a constant $0.01$.

Furthermore, we have also adapted our covering numbers construction to subcomplexes and dimension-reducing maps, allowing us to derive new constructions based on expander graphs, specifically those by Berthet and Tarski. Interestingly, this construction yields dimension-reducing maps whose distortion is inversely proportional to the dimension, a phenomenon unique to graphs. Lastly, we have also established an approximation algorithm for a certain variant of the multi-source vertex-cover problem on high dimensional expanders, specifically those constructed using Berthet and Tarski expanders. Interestingly, this problem also admits a solution on regular covers of Euclidean spaces, a related but distinct class of graphs. Our algorithm achieves a nearly optimal $e^{\Omega(d)}$ approximation ratio, a significant improvement over the $e^{\Omega(\sqrt{n})}$ approximation ratio achievable on graphs. Finally, we have also established the hardness of finding a $2.01$-approximation for the multi-source vertex-cover problem on graphs, a result that may be seen as a graph-theoretic analogue of our result in the graph setting. Interestingly, this result is almost equivalent to the hardness of finding a $2.01$-approximation for the vertex-cover problem on graphs, a result long-suspected but remains open. Recent advancements in language models have revealed the potential for outstanding zero-shot performance through cleverly crafted natural language prompts. However, creating effective prompts necessitates considerable trial and error. Consequently, there is a pressing need to automate prompt design. Our work focuses on developing a prompt optimization tool leveraging large language models, which generates high-performing, task-specific prompts. We evaluated the efficacy of this tool across 11 datasets and 6 task types and found that it consistently generated prompts leading to remarkable zero-shot performance gains, often surpassing previously established benchmarks. Moreover, we observed that including answer choices in the prompt significantly enhanced the model's zero-shot accuracy. We also explored the limitations of our method in crafting coherent prompts for complex tasks and found that its Coherence score correlated strongly with the model's zero-shot accuracy. We hope the tools we've developed will facilitate researcher collaboration and contribute to advancements in prompt design.
