The Gaussian distribution is uniquely determined by the distribution of a linear combination and a power function of independent identically distributed random variables. We identify the a-adic solenoids for which this relationship holds, effectively proving a theorem analogous to the generalized Polya theorem. This proof relies on solving a functional equation for a specific class of functions associated with the character group of the a-adic solenoid. The key to this solution is a newly developed a-adic version of the Boas-Wengenroff theorem. The properties of the Gaussian distribution are then shown to arise from specific properties of this function. The study also considers similar relationships for radial distributions in $d$-dimensional spaces and identifies the uniquely determined distributions in this context. The methods used in this research involve a novel calculation of specific functions and properties of special distributions, as well as functional equations for distributions with restricted growth rates. The results obtained are then generalized to the settings of locally compact Abelian groups and vanishing sequences. The main text of the paper is accompanied by an extensive list of open problems and additional information in the appendix. Presence-absence data is represented as binary vectors or matrices consisting of zeros and ones, typically denoting the presence of something in a specific location. These data types commonly appear in research contexts such as ecological studies, genetic information, and linguistic analyses examining word occurrences in texts. Clustering methods can effectively group similar items, but they often struggle to account for different dataset sizes or varying numbers of present features. To address these challenges, we developed a new approach (named $A_{A^2}$) that utilizes abstract simplicial complexes to cluster such data effectively. This method can be viewed as a reduction to a standard clustering problem in a particular metric space. We also proved that this reduction does not lose information, offering guarantees for its accuracy. Furthermore, we provided an algorithm to compute the clustering assuring a minimum level of similarity for the resulting groups. Our findings were substantiated through experiments involving artificial and real data. These tests demonstrated the superior performance of $A_{A^2}$ in clustering binary data, outstripping existing methods in terms of accuracy and fidelity. Specifically, we applied this approach successfully to (1) organize species presences in ecosystems, (2) categorize words occurring in texts, and (3) group genetic information. Overall, our proposed method offers an effective solution for clustering the presences or absences of items with varying feature presence. This technique offers versatile applications across data types, offering promising possibilities for research in the fields of ecology, linguistics, and genetics. A cross-attention context extraction module is designed to fuse the features of images at different resolutions, enabling the output of a low-resolution network to be refined by leveraging high-resolution features. A cross-attention fusion module is then employed to combine the refined low-resolution features with the original high-resolution features. The proposed framework refines both the input map and the corresponding mask, enabling the generation of accurate salient maps even from low-resolution images. A number, N, can be termed a palindrome if its binary format is symmetrical. In this paper, the relationship between the quotients of these symmetrical numbers is explored and several fundamental questions about the resulting sets of integers and fractions are answered. We demonstrate the feasibility of solving this problem using a precise formula, by ascertaining if an integer, N, can be expressed as a division between two identical symmetrical numbers, A and B. Upon determining representability, we pinpoint an upper limit on the value of the smallest numerical component. We then prove that a certain set of numbers has a higher frequency of occurrence within the set of all natural numbers, N. We achieve analogous results when examining quotients of numbers whose binary format is anti-palindromic, meaning the second half mirrors the reverse of the first. In addition, several numerical data points, as well as intriguing hypotheses and areas for further investigation, are provided. The concepts discussed in this paper can be applied to other mathematical structures comprising matrices with numerical entries. We illustrate this through examining the quotients of numbers from the set of upper triangular 2x2 matrices, for which similar representability questions arise. These studies originate from problems encountered in the field of algebraic number theory, specifically while working with particular types of numbers, as defined by the Hurwitz numbers, a concept introduced by Christian Krattenthaler. Hurwitz numbers, K/N, satisfy the condition that both K and N are part of the same quadratic field but have distinct forms. This research was inspired by a 1992 conjecture, proposed by David Barrington, thereby establishing a connection between this conjecture and the results discussed in this paper. Computed Tomography (CT) is extensively utilized in both engineering and medical fields for creating detailed images of internal structures within various subjects and objects. Since most X-ray sources emit X-rays of multiple energy levels, which vary in their absorption rates by materials, the process can result in image distortions. Reciprocal Monte Carlo (RMCC) algorithms have been proposed in the past to accurately predict and account for these energy-level fluctuations, known as polyenergetic effects. Typically, these algorithms require specific knowledge of absorption coefficients for precise calculations, which can be limiting in certain situations. In this research, a new method, known as the Linear Monte Carlo (LMCC) algorithm, is introduced that enables fast and accurate predictions in unknown or partially known scenarios. Additionally, a modified version of the LMCC, the Modified Linear Monte Carlo (MLMCC), is developed and proposes a potential solution for addressing these limitations. Several comparisons are conducted between the proposed LMCC, MLMCC, and previously established RCME, RCME+, and RMCC algorithms to evaluate their performance. Assessments are performed across various combinations of realistic and idealized materials, including multiple experimental measurements, empirical fittings, and third-party provided absorption coefficients. Several key distinct features are identified for the proposed algorithms, including their scalability, adaptability, and data requirements, as well as their adaptability for reverse and forward projections. Results indicate the LMCC algorithm offers faster processing times with comparable accuracy to the established RCME algorithms. The MLMCC algorithm is found to provide accurate predictions with limited data, and its efficiency is comparable to the adaptive LMCC algorithm. In another key finding, the use of linear least-square fittings on measured absorption coefficients, using the MLMCC algorithm, yields results on par with algorithms using precisely known coefficients, such as the RMCC and RCME+ algorithms. Ultimately, the proposed linear Monte Carlo algorithms are found to effectively balance accuracy and processing efficiency, making them viable options for characteristic curves formation and general radiological physics applications. Handwritten Text Recognition (HTR) with limited resources is a complex challenge, largely due to the scarcity of labeled data and limited language knowledge (dictionaries and language models). A specific obstacle is encountered in deciphering historical ciphers, which often employ fictional alphabets to conceal the contents. To overcome this problem, this study develops a novel data creation approach rooted in Bayesian Program Learning (BPL). Unlike conventional generation methods that require extensive annotated images, our approach can establish a statistical framework from a small, correctly labeled dataset. Subsequently, synthetic data can be produced from this statistical framework. When used in combination with pre-trained convolutional layers in an end-to-end system, the BPL framework has been found to yield favorable results in learning the structure and generation of ciphers, even when trained on just three examples. The research presents both theoretical and practical evaluations of this novel data creation technique. Practical validation is conducted on the Montserrat Code, a 17th-century cryptographic puzzle, where program-induced data is contributed to the existing dataset to facilitate significant breakthroughs in deciphering the text. The developed program also enables the accurate decoding of the text for the first time. Additionally, the study investigates how program-induced data affects program learning in the context of the Montserrat Code. Interestingly, the findings show that program-induced data can both aid and hinder program learning, a phenomenon worthy of further investigation in the field of Bayesian Program Learning. To date, this study is the first to apply Bayesian Program Learning to the domain of Handwritten Text Recognition and the first to establish a statistical framework from a labeled dataset in an end-to-end HTR system. High-performance computing on SIMD devices, including GPUs, has historically been challenging for object-oriented programming due to inefficiencies in memory allocation and access.  Despite this limitation, a range of applications, including real-world programs with inherent object structures, have been overlooked for parallelization opportunities.  Our research identified a particular subset of object-oriented programming, Single-Method Multiple-Objects (SMMO), that can be efficiently parallelized on SIMD devices by executing the same method across multiple objects.  To facilitate easy adoption of high-speed GPU programming for average developers, we created two new frameworks: MOOJ and CMOO.  These frameworks provide a straightforward way for developers to code parallel object-oriented programs using a combination of high-level Java-like syntax and compile-time computations.  Our results show that both frameworks can achieve near peak performance for a real-world benchmark, and also demonstrate the potential for significant speedup for a synthetic benchmark compared to existing GPU performance benchmarks.  Overall, our efforts aim to simplify the difficult task of writing high-speed GPU code, especially for developers who are familiar with object-oriented programming but unfamiliar with the complexities of GPU programming. In various fields, ensuring decision functions maintain their optimal performance under changing conditions, even with limited knowledge of their environment, is a top priority. Our study introduces an approach for quantifying how well decision functions withstand uncertainty in the form of credal Bayesian networks, which are parametric models representing the unknown environment with confidence intervals on key variables. Focusing on the 'Maximum Marginal Probability' (MARmax) issue – the maximum possible error probability when misclassifying data, given varying parameter possibilities – our approach transforms MARmax into a more manageable problem on a probabilistic circuit with restrictions. Utilizing an efficient simplification, we provide a theoretically grounded upper limit to MARmax, calculated within linear time relative to the circuit's size, and our experiments demonstrate that this bound is usually precise, and our approach outperforms existing solutions in terms of efficiency. Additionally, we develop methods for determining optimal decision functions with limited assumptions about the environment, which involve converting the original MARmax problem into a more manageable Political Science problem, and using an existing algorithm finds solutions in a timely manner. Nevertheless, this approach is hindered by efficiency issues due to its recursive nature, and at times, fails to provide a precise solution. Conversely, our experiments indicate the newly introduced approach yields more accurate results, and in many instances, matches the accuracy of the political science method while being significantly faster. Furthermore, our approach offers the advantage of being adaptable to settings where the environment's probability distribution can be known, in the form of Maximum A Posteriori (MAP) and deterministic decision functions. Lasting implications emerge from the connection between the derived MARmax approximation and the well-documented state-of-the-art algorithms for minimizing error probabilities in non-credal Bayesian networks. Our approach also presents an novel extension to the well-established belief propagation algorithm, providing the ability to efficiently handle parameters with restrictions in probabilistic circuits. Our study offers an insightful comparison to other decision functions, such as Hyper-Graph Decisions, and reveals the presence of optimal constant decision functions under limited circumstances. Finally, our approach provides a way to evaluate how decision functions are affected by uncertainty in their environment, and the connection drawn with the political science problem in the paper. As a result, the best known solution to the political science problem is also an upper bound to MARmax, and vice versa. Subjecting solid materials to an ultra-intense, femtosecond X-ray pulse from a free-electron laser causes drastic changes in their electronic and atomic structure, which evolve over time as the pulse intensifies and weakens. The degree of changes often exhibits time or intensity dependence due to non-linear phenomena such as heating, shock waves, ionization, electron transport, and radiation-induced damage. In materials with extended electronic valence bands, as found in transition metal and metal oxides compounds, this alteration leads to alterations in the valence band XANES profile as a function of time or intensity. Researchers have recently demonstrated that the non-linear XANES signal can be separated into distinct components based on different electronic configurations, namely those that are instantly created, slowly developing during the excitation, and resulting in modifications that are initial, yet distinct. Examples of valence band XANES experiments, conducted either in-line or using a pre-characterization approach with a smaller, non-femtosecond X-ray source before exposing the material to the LFXRA, will be discussed to illustrate how the non-linear XANES signal can be effectively decomposed into its various contributions. In particular, studies on ionizable solids, as seen in C60, condensed Tungsten trioxide and vanadium oxide thin films have shown that the unique XANES spectroscopy provides critical insights into the respective solid phase transformations induced by the LFXRA. The non-linear XANES signal could serve as a powerful tool to identify non-thermally induced phase transformations, thus expanding the scope of ultra-fast X-ray absorption spectroscopy in materials science. The non-linear XANES experiments can be performed either in a single step process using the complete LFXRA pulse or by combining it with a pre-characterization approach using a smaller, femtosecond X-ray source before exposing the material to the LFXRA pulse. The main advantage of this approach is that it enables researchers to study the LFXRA-induced modifications in the material's electronic structure with reduced influence from thermal effects. Furthermore, the knowledge gained from pre-characterization experiments can also facilitate the optimization of LFXRA pulse parameters, such as energy, intensity and fluence, to obtain valuable insights into the material's electronic structure. Quantum entanglement plays a pivotal role in quantum information sciences and technologies. In optical physics, a fundamental type of entanglement known as polarization entanglement has been predominantly created through passive optical transformations, which inevitably face limitations in practical applications such as single-photon cutting and precision measurement due to input constraints. In this research, a novel technique is introduced to generate polarization entanglement through active manipulation of a three-level atom interacting with two parallel light fields. By controlling two controlled-coil laser beams and a rapid switch in a microfabricated atomic structure, the developed method achieves polarization entanglement creation regardless of input state constraints, making it more efficient and controllable compared to previous techniques. Additionally, this technique enables the realization of a deterministic single-photon gate, thus paving the way for advanced applications in quantum optics and quantum information processing. This research technique can also be utilized at room temperature, reducing complexity and making it feasible for integration into practical devices. Accurate categorization of IoT devices is crucial across various sectors due to security and system integrity implications. Research has successfully applied machine learning models for IoT device classification, but these models fail to account for the costs involved in extracting device features. Nevertheless, feature extraction can be costly, time-consuming, and resource-intensive in real-world settings. This paper introduces a novel formulation for device classification, taking into consideration the costs of extracting device features. Our research reveals that feature extraction costs vary significantly across different IoT devices, with misclassification potentially leading to substantial financial losses. To address this challenge, we propose an advanced binary classification model that can predict whether a device belongs to a specific category based on network traffic and limited extracted features. Our approach leverages a two-layer neural network and semi-supervised learning techniques to account for the costs involved. Our model shows promising results, with experimentation involving real-world devices showing a success rate of 90.5% in identifying Malicious IoT Devices and 88.2% in pinpointing Home IoT Devices. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our method performs effectively with a limited number of features, achieving a 90.5% success rate when using 5 features and a 89.2% success rate when using 3 features. This approach provides a feasible solution for classifying IoT devices based on affordable feature extraction. Our model offers a potential solution to the cost-related issues involved in feature extraction for IoT device classification, with our code and dataset available for public access at https://iota-sec.github.io/FECC/. This research presents a novel and straightforward technique for word-alignment that leverages bilingual information from external sources like machine translation platforms. We demonstrate that a model with limited parameters can achieve performance comparable to GIZA++ when trained on a relatively small dataset. Furthermore, in terms of alignment metrics, such as accuracy or F-score, our approach delivers results equivalent to GIZA++ when trained on a dataset 22 times smaller. Crucially, the method's domain-agnostic training capabilities enable 'on-the-fly' application on any new pair of sentences without requiring extensive retraining. We showcase the method's effectiveness in two applications: automatically generating translation rules for graph-based machine translation models and creating sentence rewrites for paraphrasing. Additionally, the source code is available at https://github.com/argosd/mt-aligner.

We explore solitary waves known as "nanoptera," characterized by exponentially small oscillations, in two precompressed systems based on the Hertzian model, particularly woodpile chains and diatomic chains with alternating masses. These solitary waves emerge from the Stokes phenomenon as special curves in the complex plane are intersected, producing exponential asymptotics approximations. Our analysis reveals that solitary waves in precompressed woodpile chains feature a single Stokes curve, accompanied by oscillations, whereas a diatomic chain exhibits two oscillatory contributions, cancelling out under certain mass ratios to produce localized waves, thereby confirming prior numerical and experimental observations on the phenomenon in non-precompressed diatomic chains. Nonetheless, an approach grounded in exponential asymptotics fails to accurately predict solitary wave formation for various mass ratios in precompressed diatomic chains. Consequently, we determine that a non-validity condition for this asymptotic method arises when the solitary wave's frequency diverges as the precompression parameter vanishes, as observed in the diatomic chain scenario. Recent breakthroughs in Bayesian deep learning have successfully differentiated between two inherent uncertainties within predictive models - epistemic uncertainty and expected loss. Epistemic uncertainty represents uncertainty stemming from the model itself, whereas expected loss captures the anticipated forecasting error. A novel approach presented in this research seeks to disentangle uncertainty related to the state and observation processes inherent in Gaussian process dynamics. This framework treats the dynamics as a learned transformation, drawing upon insights from variational inference, to define expected loss as a surrogates for posterior predictive loss. Furthermore, this framework offers computational efficiency through the application of a simple and efficient method for inferring the posterior over the dynamics parameters. A practical benefit of this approach is the potential to improve predictive models by subtracting the component of uncertainty attributable to uncertain process parameters, thereby providing a more accurate approximation of the posterior over the model given existing data. Finally, the foundation of this approach is laid such that future uncertainty quantification methods targeting other types of Gaussian process models are anticipated to be straightforward to implement. Thorough empirical evaluation is conducted to validate the proposed method, which is subsequently referred to as EPITREE. Results from our evaluation suggest that EPITREE is a viable solution for accurately modeling dynamic systems marked by noisy observations and process variations, as evidenced by our findings on a simulated artificial network and the study of a real-world artificial intelligence assisted navigation task in maze environments. Code for reproducing results is available at https://github.com/samueljoshua/epitree. A pre-trained model is also available for the artificial network at https://huggingface.github.io/datasets/wiki/EPITREE_artificial_network. Maze environment data has been uploaded to https://huggingface.github.io/datasets/wiki/EPITREE_maze_navigation. Both datasets have been developed by the authors. Modern motion deblurring methods based on deep learning utilize paired synthetic data for training frameworks, aiming to directly convert blurry inputs to clear outputs. However, the success of these methods heavily relies on high-quality synthetic blurry data available only before training, a constraint that becomes impractical with large datasets. To overcome this limitation, we introduce an on-the-fly data augmentation technique to create blurry inputs dynamically during training and testing. To make the most of this approach, we adopt an unconventional framework incorporating a sequential process of blur removal and subsequent reblurring with the assistance of a module that mimics real-world blur, as well as hand-crafted prior information. This method not only enhances the quality of the resulting image but also enables the creation of clear images from blurry inputs in a more realistic manner. To optimize performance, we introduce a novel loss function combining the contrastive loss of blurred and clear images, as well as hand-crafted prior information. Experimental results demonstrate the superior deblurring performance of our method compared to state-of-the-art approaches, and additional analysis highlights the effectiveness of our model in generating natural-looking clear images from blurry inputs. The proposed method and associated code are available at https://github.com/asharakeh/On-the-Fly-Data-Augmentation-for-Motion-Deblurring.

We contend that the best model for a dataset is one that is highly similar, yet slightly different from it. We have developed a novel metric, called SSim, that quantifies the similarity between a model and its corresponding data, taking into account any gaps or irregularities in the data. Unlike existing measures that solely focus on optimizing model performance, SSim is based on a general framework and can be applied to a variety of scientific datasets and computational models. Importantly, SSim identified several models that were inferior according to traditional evaluation methods, but were ultimately chosen by experts as the best models for their respective datasets. Furthermore, the predicted model rankings obtained from SSim showed significant correlation with expert rankings, particularly for datasets that exhibit noisy or irregular patterns. On the other hand, models ranked highest by SSim showed significant correlation with expert rankings for datasets that follow smooth and consistent trends. Therefore, we assert that SSim is an effective and versatile tool for determining the best model for a scientific dataset, but its success is contingent on the dataset's characteristics. If experts find SSim to be an accurate and trustworthy method for identifying the best model for a particular dataset, then it is likely to be considered a reliable model search tool. Conversely, if experts are skeptical about using SSim, then they may prefer other methods of model evaluation. By incorporating learned features into convolution layers, GCNNs enable the extraction of meaningful patterns from such data. However, many GCNN approaches remain susceptible to biased inputs, which can severely compromise their performance. Despite this issue, very few studies have been devoted to investigating how biased inputs affect GCNNs and how their robustness can be enhanced. In this paper, we explore the effects of biased inputs on GCNNs through a study of their influence on the convolution layer. Based on this investigation, we develop a new framework that uses data-dependent and adaptive activation functions to counteract the adverse impact of biased inputs on GCNNs. The proposed method is then evaluated on well-known time-series data sets, which demonstrate its effectiveness in improving the robustness of GCNNs. The results show that this framework significantly enhances the accuracy of GCNNs on partially corrupted data, with overall performance improvements reaching up to $10.4\%$. Furthermore, this method is found to positively affect the convolution layer's output, with a $10.1\%$ improvement in accuracy. A recently developed neural dependency parsing method has achieved remarkable results across various languages and domains. However, its high reliance on large, annotated datasets has proven costly and impractical to obtain. This paper proposes a novel self-training technique that mitigates this data annotation constraint by leveraging the parser's own output to improve performance. Specifically, the Deep Contextualized Self-training algorithm integrates external sequence models, derived from the parser's application to unlabelled data, into the parser using a sophisticated weighting system. Comprehensive experiments have been conducted across multiple languages in diverse settings, and the results clearly indicate that our approach outperforms traditional self-training and state-of-the-art semi-supervised learning methods by a significant margin. Furthermore, our findings reveal a number of key insights into self-training and the benefits it provides. Overall, the Deep Contextualized Self-training algorithm presents a versatile and effective solution for tackling the data annotation difficulties in neural dependency parsing. This approach is likely to be beneficial for other NLP tasks characterized by annotation costs. The code and pre-trained models necessary for replication can be found at https://github.com/ghrua/Deep-Contextualized-Self-Training.

Despite the growing need for models in non-English languages, natural language processing has long been Anglo-centric, and translating neural models between languages can be costly and time-consuming in terms of data labeling, development time, and expertise. We propose a universal approach to effortlessly and effectively transfer neural models from English to other languages. Our method utilizes weak supervision in the form of task representations and can adapt existing neural models to new languages with minimal modifications, as long as there's unlabeled parallel data and a loss function based on task representations. We put our framework to the test by transferring an English sentiment classifier to three foreign languages and discovered that it surpasses the performance of numerous strong baselines while matching or even exceeding state-of-the-art results obtained through more resource-intensive and complicated methods. Moreover, our framework successfully captures rich, semantically significant representations across languages despite the absence of direct supervision. You can access the code at https://github.com/amanbasu/weak-supervised-cross-lingual-transfer.

Our enhanced model, BasicVSR++, significantly outperforms the original by achieving a notable improvement in PSNR, with only a minimal increase in computational cost. Moreover, our model exhibits versatility in video restoration tasks and achieved remarkable success in video super-resolution and compressed video enhancement challenges in NTIRE 2021, earning several top ranks, with codes and models available on MMEditing. and MMDetection. In multi-task reinforcement learning, using shared representations can greatly
benefit a learner when it comes to solving a variety of tasks. While this
synergy is evident in model-free methods using shared policy networks, our study
investigates the benefits of shared dynamics models in model-based multi-task
reinforcement learning settings. Surprisingly, our findings indicate that using
a single learned dynamics model for multiple tasks may actually decrease the
performance and lead to task confusion. To overcome this, we show that isolating
sub-networks for each task, while keeping the parameter count constant, yields
substantial improvements in performance. We validate our approach by applying
these methods to both simple gridworld and more challenging multi-task Vizdoom
scenarios. Our code is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/alecrg/multi_task_dynamics.

This research proposes a probabilistic model for analyzing the impact of combined hurricane and storm surge events on large power grids. To simulate real-world hurricane scenarios, the study generates probabilistic storm paths based on historical data, and corresponding storm surge situations are developed based on actual hurricane parameters. To assess potential losses, the study employs a quantitative metric that estimates total load reduction, and maximum demand, across affected substations. To effectively address these scenarios, the study suggests using Monte-Carlo simulations, combining 100 probabilistic storm paths, with 36 possible storm trajectories, predicted 72 hours in advance, and 20 storm surge situations, anticipating surge levels 24 hours ahead. Due to the incorporation of the pitch-dependent factor, the filter weights of the dilated convolution in Nett are no longer applicable to QPNet. Consequently, the model faces increased parameters and higher computational complexity. To address these issues, the paper proposes nested stochastic gradient descent (NSGD) as a adaptive learning rate tuning method for accelerating the convolutional neural networks training process of QPNet. Experimental results indicate that QPNet achieves superior quality and extension capabilities compared to Nett. Furthermore, the model demonstrates a significant training time reduction of 3.24 times when utilizing NSGD to adjust the learning rates automatically. Additionally, the analysis reveals that NSGD can save more time in larger datasets such as COVAREP. Specifically, the algorithm achieves a 4.94 and 3.65 times reduction in training time for speech synthesis with the ITU-NRS dataset using Nett and QPNet, respectively. Also, the NSGD method can be applied to other deep neural networks automatically. Lastly, the study suggests that QPNet and NSGD can be used for other audio generation tasks such as music and audio effect synthesis. However, further research is needed to confirm this assumption. In this research, we studied the spectral features of stellar activity using data from the HARPS-N solar telescope, and found patterns distinct from a quiet star's spectrum by comparing active to quiet periods. By using the SDO satellite's observations, we verified the correlation of these features with the star's activity level, validated their variability, and found they appear across various spectral regions. Additionally, these features are featureless in quiet periods but appear with marked spectral features during active periods, and their identification can potentially distinguish them from a planet's signal using statistical methods. Using the SDO data, we found these features are most prominent when a star's X-ray emission reaches its highest levels. Finally, using the SDO data, we found activity levels corresponding to these features can cause up to 3 m s^-1 activity-induced noise spikes in a star's Doppler signal, a level that could cause the loss of small planets. A fundamental theory known as active inference underpins how living beings interact with their surroundings. This theory views the brain as an efficient tool that employs Bayesian principles to create a detailed mental framework, aiming to minimize uncertainty about the world. Despite the theory's significance in cognitive neuroscience, its practical application is restricted to simplified simulations due to limitations in dealing with large and varied environments. This research incorporates the latest advancements in deep learning to create a more sophisticated mental framework, one that can be built directly from high-dimensional data, such as video feeds, without the need for pre-defined parameters. Furthermore, this work demonstrates that such frameworks can be utilized to facilitate active inference. This study marks the first instance of applying active inference using deep learning techniques to a real-world navigation task involving a robotic system. The results show that agents equipped with these new mental frameworks are capable of adapting to unfamiliar settings, such as a new table arrangement, at a faster pace than those using traditional Bayesian methods. While these mental frameworks can be learned using reinforcement learning techniques, this research reveals that they can also be optimized for a variety of tasks in a diverse set of environments. This paper sets the stage for a new generation of cognitive architectures that can be trained in an end-to-end manner, paving the way for more advanced active inference systems. Conversely, this work also highlights potential pitfalls of applying active inference, such as spurious inferences arising from unnecessary assumptions about the world. Therefore, this research suggests that future work should focus on developing methods to limit the scope of a agent's mental framework, ensuring it remains grounded in reality. Additionally, this study hints at the possibility of using novel memory mechanisms to mitigate this issue, leading to more efficient agents in the long run. Overall, this research offers a novel approach to building active inference systems, marking a significant departure from previous Bayesian models. Furthermore, this work lays the groundwork for exploring the interplay between prior beliefs, inference, and action, which is essential for developing more advanced cognitive architectures. Lastly, this study paves the way for future research to incorporate empirical data to inform theoretical priors, ultimately shedding light on the nature of a priori knowledge. In conclusion, this work presents a significant advancement in the theory of active inference, representing a crucial transition from simplified theoretical models to more realistic simulations. Accurate vertebrae localization and identification are crucial in various medical applications related to spine disorder diagnosis and surgical planning. However, certain pathological variations (e.g., vertebral compression fractures, scoliosis, and vertebral fixation) and imaging conditions (e.g., limited visibility and metallic streak artifacts in CT scans) make this task quite challenging. To address these difficulties, this paper presents an advanced and precise method that leverages in-depth anatomical knowledge and learnable structural constraints to reliably localize and identify vertebrae even in the most complex cases. By adopting a node generation, edge generation, and merging process, similar to the chemical synthesis of carbon compounds, our method significantly improves the accuracy of vertebrae localization and identification compared to existing approaches. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed technique, yielding 97% verification rate and 0.78 CM, surpassing the state-of-the-art performance of 92% and 1.02 CM, respectively. Furthermore, this method has the potential to be extended to automatically identify nearby structures and accurately segment vertebrae in various imaging modalities. Daany is an open-source, cross-platform C# library focused on data analytics and linear algebra. Designed for.NET environments, this tool facilitates data preparation, feature engineering, and other data transformation operations. This guide serves as a comprehensive developer manual, outlining Daany's features, functionality, and usage, as well as a listing of related papers. Daany is openly sourced under the MIT License at the provided GitHub repository.

This document provides a summary of the content from a course held at Stanford University in the spring of 2018.  The course brings together insights from cognitive neuroscience and systems neuroscience to create intelligent systems by combining human and machine elements.  The course uses a tangible example - a digital assistant that learns and evolves through ongoing conversations with an experienced software engineer while beginning as an effective analytical and problem-solving tool.  Over time, these intelligent assistants develop essential thinking strategies and learn to rely on intuition through lessons learned from their expert counterparts.  As a result, these intelligent assistants become capable of working side-by-side as equal partners - serving as cognitive enhancements and digital prostheses that help their human partners make informed decisions and access powerful computing tools more efficiently.  The course covers various topics related to the intersection of human and machine intelligence and explores the long-term potential for widespread improvements in both individual human capabilities and collaborative AI systems.
